Manifold Diagrams for Higher Categories
Lukas Heidemann

Abstract
We develop a graphical calculus of manifold diagrams which generalises string and surface diagrams to arbitrary dimensions. Manifold diagrams are pasting diagrams for ( ∞ , n ) (\infty,n) -categories that admit a semi-strict composition operation for which associativity and unitality is strict. The weak interchange law satisfied by composition of manifold diagrams is determined geometrically through isotopies of diagrams. By building upon framed combinatorial topology, we can classify critical points in isotopies at which the arrangement of cells changes. This allows us to represent manifold diagrams combinatorially and use them as shapes with which to probe ( ∞ , n ) (\infty,n) -categories, presented as n n -fold Segal spaces. Moreover, for any system of labels for the singularities in a manifold diagram, we show how to generate a free ( ∞ , n ) (\infty,n) -category.



Chapter 1
Introduction

String diagrams, Gray surface diagrams and extended topological quantum field theories
are bridges between geometry and the algebra of higher categories.
In this thesis we generalise string and surface diagrams to arbitrary
dimensions, to obtain an
n
-dimensional graphical calculus of manifold diagrams
for
(\infty,n)
-categories.
Whereas surface diagrams have vertices, edges, faces and volumes, an
n
-manifold
diagram consists of strata that are
k
-manifolds for all
0\leq k\leq n
,
each representing a
k
-codimensional cell of an
(\infty,n)
-category.

Higher category theory has promising applications throughout mathematics,
physics and computer science by
providing a common language to formally capture homotopy coherent algebraic structures that are otherwise difficult to describe or manipulate.
The expressivity of higher categories comes at the cost of complexity,
which has limited its applications in practice beyond homotopy theory.
The coherence structure alone that guarantees weak associativity, weak unitality
and the weak interchange law for the composition operations is highly non-trivial.
A graphical calculus like string diagrams for higher categories in arbitrary dimensions would enable more concrete calculations and simplify coherence of the composition operation.

While every
2
-category is equivalent to one in which
the coherence structure is strict, strictification is no longer possible
in general for
n
-categories when
n>2
without losing essential structure

[
Sim98
]
.
For example the fundamental
3
-groupoid
\Pi_{3}(S^{2})
of the
2
-sphere
S^{2}

cannot be equivalent to a strict
3
-groupoid since then the Eckmann-Hilton
argument would trivialise the
3
-cell that corresponds to the generator of

\pi_{3}(S^{2})\cong\mathbb{Z}
.
In principle, it is possible to explicitly write down the coherence laws for an
n
-category
for any
n\geq 0
, but the ensuing explosion of coherence axioms makes this approach unworkable.

We can therefore not fully avoid the complexity of the coherence laws without
losing the expressiveness of
n
-categories.
This does not preclude us in principle from strictifying at least part of the coherence structure, arriving at a semi-strict model of
n
-categories that is simpler than but still equivalent to the general theory.
The surface diagram calculus of
[
BMS18
]
is built upon Gray categories,
a semi-strict model of
3
-categories in which associativity and unitality of composition holds strictly and the interchange law remains weak.
This style of semi-strictification is a natural choice for a geometric model since it allows translating between composition of terms and gluing of subdiagrams.

So far there have been no known semi-strict models for
4
-categories (or higher)
in the style of Gray categories, with strict associativity and unitality but weak
interchange.
Teisi
[
Cra00
]
and the quasi-strict
4
-categories of
[
BV17
]

are candidates, but have not yet been proven equivalent to the general theory of
4
-categories.
Instead of finding a graphical calculus for a known semi-strict model
as in
[
BMS18
]
, we can go in the opposite direction
and characterise a semi-strict model
for
n
-categories by starting with the geometry of its graphical calculus
in the form of manifold diagrams.
The composition operation of the resulting theory simply juxtaposes
diagrams of varying sizes and therefore, generalising Moore paths, is strictly
associative and unital.

The most widely used models of higher categories to date are based on (abstract) homotopy theory.
Via the homotopy hypothesis, we can already understand a topological space as an
\infty
-groupoid:
the points are the objects, paths are
1
-morphisms, homotopies between paths are
2
-morphisms, etc.
The coherences are fully weak, but the complexity remains manageable via the wide range of tools of homotopy theory. Spaces or
\infty
-groupoids are the first in a sequence of types of
\omega
-categories with a decreasing amount of invertibility:
An
(\infty,n)
-category is an
\omega
-category
with the requirement that a
k
-morphism is invertible whenever
k\geq n
.
The case of
n=1
is particularly well understood, with most of
1
-category theory transferring to
(\infty,1)
-categories.

At first, it appears that moving from
n
-categories to
(\infty,n)
-categories only makes things harder for us.
But coherences are invertible, and so we can offload much of their complexity onto the homotopy theory of spaces.
This trick is already present in the string diagram calculus for plain, braided and
symmetric monoidal categories, where isotopies of the diagrams correspond to
the coherence laws in their algebraic formulation.
We can therefore rely on the geometric nature of manifold diagrams and describe
the weak interchange coherences directly as a space of isotopies rather than characterising them algebraically.

Homotopy theoretic models for higher categories are glued together from a category of basic shapes,
such as the simplices
\Delta
, multi-simplices
\Delta^{n}
, globular pasting diagrams
\Theta^{n}

and various versions of a category of cubes.
These shapes are typically optimised to be as minimal or basic as possible,
which is a good trade-off in situations where we want to prove general theorems.
There is however value in finding bigger and more structured shapes, as every object that is modelled from them automatically inherits their structure. This is preferable whenever we want to perform calculations on particular examples of higher categories.

I don’t like being tied to one particular shape of cell, particularly simplicial ones. When working with low-dimensional higher categories, like 2-categories and 3-categories, we use pasting diagrams with cells of many different shapes. I would like a notion of higher category that has an underlying sort of “higher computad” where we can talk about arbitrary pasting diagrams and “higher surface diagrams.”
Mike Shulman
-
[
Shu10
]

We identify the higher surface diagrams in this quote as our manifold diagrams.
Manifold diagrams are a particularly useful shape to do higher category theory.
Because manifold diagrams are composed by juxtaposition,
we can describe complex composites in a single shape.
While this composition operation does not satisfy a strict interchange law,
the coherences for weak interchange in
n
-manifold diagrams are isotopies
and therefore themselves
(n+1)
-diagrams.
Manifold diagrams are also well suited to describe freely generated higher categories.
The generating data for a free
n
-category is called an
n
-computad
and is typically defined inductively by specifying the generating
n
-morphisms whose domain
and codomain are
(n-1)
-morphisms in a free
(n-1)
-category.
This interleaved process is not ideal as the free
k
-categories are very hard to describe explicitly.
Because manifold diagrams are closed under composition and isotopy, we can sidestep the intermediate steps
and specify the generating data for all dimensions at once.

String diagrams were formalised as mathematical objects in
[
JS91
]

via topological graphs. The Gray surface diagram calculus of
[
BMS18
]

presents diagrams as a stratification of the
closed
3
-cube
{[0,1]}^{3}
which satisfies a series of conditions.
Trimble outlined the beginnings of an approach to
n
-manifold diagrams for arbitrary
n\geq 0
in an online note
[
Tri10
]
, which unfortunately has remained incomplete.
Dorn and Douglas described manifold diagrams
[
DD22
]
in arbitrary dimension for the purpose
of studying the combinatorialisability of smooth structures. However, they do not
consider how such diagrams would map to higher categorical structures.

Trimble’s note identified five essential ingredients that a theory of manifold diagrams would be built upon:
tameness
,
coincidences
,
progressivity
,
globularity
and
deformations
. We address each of these ingredients as follows.

Tameness seeks to avoid the wild phenomena that topology is famously
[
Gro97
]
filled with, such as space filling curves or Cantor spaces, which are far removed from any intuitive concept of a geometric shape.
Smooth geometry corrects some of them but also comes with various surprising features like infinite oscillations and spirals.
While there is a wealth of tools that are developed to deal with smooth manifolds,
the toolset for smooth stratified spaces is significantly sparser.
Smoothness is also non-trivial to maintain under many constructions.
Algebraic or analytic geometry is too rigid, since we need bump functions to glue diagrams.
Trimble’s note on surface diagrams therefore recommends o-minimal geometry, and specifically the o-minimal structure
\mathbb{R}_{\exp}
which extends algebraic sets with the exponential function.
The surface diagrams for Gray categories
[
BMS18
]
achieve tameness with piecewise linear geometry.
We follow their lead and base our notion of tameness on finite triangulations.

The string-diagram calculus for braided monoidal categories detects edge crossings and translates them into the braiding isomorphism.
Similarly, isotopies of Gray surface diagrams are translated into applications of the various coherence isomorphisms in the structure of a Gray
3
-category.
Lurie’s proof sketch for the cobordism hypothesis uses Morse theory to decompose manifolds into a finite sequence of segments, connected via Morse singularities that correspond to the higher cells generated by dualisability.
For a manifold diagram calculus we need a similar way to detect and classify critical points at which the relative positioning of strata changes in a way that is algebraically significant.

From the example of an edge crossing in a string diagram we can intuit that these critical points
are connected to projection:
when we project away the coordinate direction in which one edge passes over the other,
the projected edges intersect exactly at the height where the crossing occurred.
In
[
Tri10
]
these critical points are described in terms of
coincidence
.
It is common to define geometric structure by specifying the transformations that preserve it.
Framed combinatorial topology
[
DD21
,
Hei23
]
is a theory of tame geometry that is based around the concept of coincidence.
In §
3.1
we define a sequence of equivalence relations
\sim_{i}
on
\mathbb{R}^{n}

so that
x\sim_{i}y
whenever the last
i
coordinates of
x
and
y
agree.
We then equip stratified spaces with an embedding into
\mathbb{R}^{n}
, called an
n
-framing, and only allow
those transformations that are continuous, respect the stratification and preserve all coincidence relations
\sim_{i}
.

Tame
n
-framed stratified spaces such as
n
-manifold diagrams can be refined
by an
n
-mesh, making the structure that is encoded in the
n
-framing visible
in the stratification (see for example Figure
1.1
).
Meshes are defined inductively in §
3.2
as a sequence of

1
-dimensional mesh bundles, each adding one dimension at a time.
We concentrate on two types of meshes: open meshes that model the geometry of manifold diagrams,
and closed meshes that closely resemble commutative or pasting diagrams in higher dimensions.
Open and closed mesh bundles are classified by quasicategories
\cramped{\dot{\textup{M}}}^{n}
and
\cramped{\bar{\textup{M}}}^{n}
.
Meshes admit purely combinatorial and finite descriptions in terms of trusses,
which we explore in §
3.3
.
Trusses are classified by
1
-categories
\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n}\simeq\cramped{\dot{\textup{M}}}^{n}
and
\cramped{\bar{\textup{T}}}^{n}\simeq\cramped{\bar{\textup{M}}}^{n}
(see Figure
1.2
).

and its corresponding open
3
-mesh which detects the critical moment
at which the two strata pass over each other.

Figure 1.2
:

Starting with a string diagram on the left,
we can find the coarsest open
2
-mesh that refines it.
The open
2
-mesh can then be described as a combinatorial object
via the open
2
-truss on the right.

The edges in a string diagram have to progress in the direction from the source
to the target boundary of the diagram, without turning around or stalling.
This is the progressivity condition.
The manifold diagrams in
[
DD22
]

guarantee progressivity in higher dimensions by the framed conicality condition which requires that
each point has an open neighbourhood of the form
\textup{c}{L}\times\mathbb{R}^{k}

where
\textup{c}{L}
is a stratified cone.
Framed stratified isomorphisms can not exchange the coordinate order,
and so this framed conicality condition guarantees that on each
k
-dimensional
stratum
{S}
of an
n
-manifold diagram the projection
\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{k}
onto the last
k
coordinates restricts to an immersion
{S}\to\mathbb{R}^{k}
.
We modify the framed conicality requirement of

[
DD22
]

in §
4.2.1

and require that the open neighbourhoods in an
n
-manifold diagram
are refined by mesh atoms, which we identify in §
4.1

as the appropriate geometric shapes for cells in
(\infty,n)
-categories.

The globularity condition of a string diagram controls which strata can intersect
which boundary of the diagram. In particular it restricts vertices to lie strictly
within the interior of the diagram, while edges can intersect only the top and bottom
boundary. In §
4.2.2
we describe a generalisation of the globularity
condition to arbitrary dimensions, which allows
n
-manifold diagrams to be modelled
on top of any arbitrary closed
n
-mesh. This includes
n
-cubes of varying size,
to ensure semi-strict composition, but also more complex shapes that describe pasting
diagrams of
n
-manifold diagrams.

The last ingredient for
n
-manifold diagrams are their deformations or isotopies.
Isotopies of string diagrams for symmetric monoidal categories
are required to preserve the order of the incoming and outgoing edges of
every vertex, at least within some neighbourhood around the vertex. Without that condition, any map
A\otimes A\to A
expressed
in a string diagram would have to automatically be commutative.
The ordering condition for isotopies of string diagrams does not trivially generalise to isotopies of diagrams in higher dimensions since a cell can have adjacent cells of various dimensions in relative arrangements that can not be reduced to a linear order.
The notes
[
Tri10
]
identify this problem as well.
Our solution in §
4.2.3
requires that the
n
-framed
stratified bundles which represent isotopies of
n
-manifold diagrams
are
n
-framed stratified submersions, i.e. trivial up to
n
-framed
stratified isomorphism within a neighbourhood of any stratum.
This notion leaves enough flexibility for the interchange laws to arise as isotopies
while being strict enough to not impose additional relations on the cells
in the modelled
(\infty,n)
-categories.

Free plain, braided or symmetric monoidal categories can be generated via their
string diagram calculi by attaching labels to the strata, often presented via colours.
We demonstrate how to attach labels to manifold diagrams in §
4.4
,
characterising systems of admissible labels as diagrammatic computads.
Via the equivalence between meshes and trusses, such diagrammatic
n
-computads
can be seen alternatively but equivalently as combinatorial or geometric objects.
Using the theory of transverse configurations in FCT, developed in §
3.6
,
we can show that labelled manifold diagrams create free
(\infty,n)
-categories
from
n
-diagrammatic computads via an adjunction of
(\infty,1)
-categories

\mathbb{F}:\cramped{\textup{Cptd}}_{(\infty,n)}\rightleftarrows\textup{Cat}_{(\infty,n)}:\mathbb{U}
.

As a two-dimensional graphical calculus, string diagrams can be represented on paper, blackboards and screens.
Three-dimensional surface diagrams can still be rendered on a flat surface with projection, using artistic tricks to make them intelligible as needed.
The useability of a graphical notation then quickly declines when the dimension is increased beyond three.
Multiple decades had passed between appearances of string diagrams in the literature
[
GVNVN47
,
P+71
]
and their formalisation in
[
JS91
]
.
The authors of the latter paper partly attribute this delay to technological limitations
in printing at the time, which prevented graphical notations to escape from
the blackboard onto the printed page at scale.
The
homotopy.io
project posits that the use of manifold diagrams in higher dimensions similarly can be helped through a technological improvement.

homotopy.io
is a graphical proof assistant that enables a user
to inspect and manipulate low-dimensional slices and projections through an (in principle) arbitrary dimensional diagram in an
\omega
-category freely generated by a signature.
The conceptual model behind the freely generated
\omega
-category used for

homotopy.io
originates from
[
Dor23
]
, but has not previously been shown equivalent to established models.
Via our combinatorialisability results for manifold diagrams labelled in a diagrammatic computads, discussed in §
4.4
, we can describe the
free
\omega
-category generated by a
homotopy.io
signature
as an
n
-fold Segal space where
n
is the dimension of the highest dimensional generator in the (finite) signature.
In this way we demonstrate that the proof assistant has sound semantics in higher categories as claimed.

1.1
Related Work

The projects surrounding the cobordism hypothesis
[
Lur08b
,
CS19
,
GP22
]
and factorisation homology
[
AFR20
]
also establish a connection between geometry and category theory in higher dimensions, building upon decades of deep insights into the geometry of smooth manifolds.
These theories aim to study existing geometries that are of prior interest via the language and toolset of higher-dimensional categories.
Our aim in this thesis is to do the opposite:
we start with higher categories and want to elucidate their structure using geometry.
We therefore are afforded the opportunity to pick framed combinatorial topology as a theory of geometry that is tailored specifically to our purpose.

The graphical proof assistant Globular
[
BKV18
]

implemented a combinatorial encoding of the geometry of higher-dimensional
diagrams, based on the data structure described in
[
BV17
]
.
This data structure, and therefore also the proof assistant, relied
on an explicit classification of generators for the weak interchange law,
such as braids, braid naturality, etc. So far this explicit classification
was not extended beyond dimension four, which limits the expressive power of the system.
Dorn’s thesis
[
Dor23
]
is the conceptual origin of the ideas of
framed combinatorial topology. Instead of attempting to classify algebraic
generators for the weak interchange structure, the singular interval bundles
of
[
Dor23
]
mirror the geometry of higher-dimensional diagrams
directly.
This theory admits an alternative mathematical formulation in terms
of the zigzag construction, an implementation as a data structure,
and algorithms to construct and type check isotopies of diagrams step by step
[
RV19
,
HRV22
]
.
The proof assistant
homotopy.io

[
CHH+24
]
was then developed based on these results.

The framed combinatorial topology (FCT) project
[
DD21
]

aimed to apply the combinatorial theory of geometry beyond higher categorical
diagrams, with a focus on computability in combinatorial topology.
FCT introduced trusses, derived from the singular interval bundles of
[
Dor23
]
,
and meshes, which serve as a bridge
between the geometry of stratified spaces in
\mathbb{R}^{n}
and the combinatorics of trusses.
This was applied in
[
DD22
]
to explore combinatorialisability
of smooth structures.
Trusses and meshes were discovered independently in the author’s attempts to
give geometric meaning to the zigzag construction of
[
RV19
,
HRV22
]
, and were realised with techniques of higher category theory in
[
Hei23
]
. To avoid fragmentation, we have decided to
adopt the terminology of framed combinatorial topology.
Our formulation of meshes in terms of quasicategories is more technically
convenient for the purposes of this thesis. Moreover, our meshes are not required
to have continuous boundaries, allowing us to express embeddings between meshes
as the inert bordisms in
\cramped{\dot{\textup{M}}}^{n}
and
\cramped{\bar{\textup{M}}}^{n}
,
described in §
3.5
. This is essential for the theory of
diagrammatic spaces which we develop in §
4.1
.

The idea of strictifying higher categorical structures by probing them with
shapes that admit strict composition operations themselves originated from
[
KV
]
,
which attempted to strictify associativity, unitality and the interchange law for
\infty
-groupoids.
This was shown to be impossible by Simpson in
[
Sim98
]
,
who suggested compromising via a semi-strict model in which unitality is weak.
The diagrammatic sets of
[
Had19
]
build upon this idea and are conjectured to be a semi-strict model for
\omega
-categories, particularly well-suited for defining the Gray tensor product
[
Had21
]

and admitting a computer implementation
[
HK23a
,
HK23b
]
.
While this model does admit a geometric realisation similar to manifold diagrams,
each cell must have at least one stratum in its domain and codomain, respectively.
These additional strata prevent any non-trivial braiding to be performed directly by isotopy,
instead relying on the coherence structure of the weak units.

The theory of
(\infty,n)
-categories is determined essentially uniquely,
up to a choice of direction for each dimension
[
BS20
]
.
We use complete
n
-fold Segal spaces as the model for
(\infty,n)
-categories,
originally defined in
[
Bar05
]
and popularised by
[
Lur08b
]
.
Our construction of the
n
-diagrammatic spaces
\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n}(-)
and
\cramped{\mathbb{E}}^{n}(-)

with
n
-manifold diagrams that are orthogonal to a closed
n
-mesh is derived
from the technique used in
[
Lur08b
]
to construct the
n
-fold Segal space
of
n
-corbordisms.
Our universal bundles

\cramped{\bar{\mathfrak{M}}}^{n}:\cramped{\bar{\textup{M}}}^{n}_{*}\to\cramped{\bar{\textup{M}}}^{n}

and

\cramped{\dot{\mathfrak{M}}}^{n}:\cramped{\dot{\textup{M}}}^{n}_{*}\to\cramped{\dot{\textup{M}}}^{n}

that classify closed and open
n
-meshes
are inspired by the bundle
\mathcal{E}\textup{xit}\to\mathcal{B}\textup{un}

of
[
AFR17
]
, although their concrete implementation as quasicategories differs substantially.
Our
n
-diagrammatic computads were loosely inspired by the geometric structures of
[
GP22
]
.

Chapter 2
Background

In this chapter we broadly review the notions from the theories of
(\infty,1)
-categories,
polynomial functors and stratified spaces that form the basis of our constructions.
We assume knowledge of ordinary category theory. We do not claim originality
for any concepts in this chapter beyond their presentation.

2.1
(\infty,1)
-Categories

An
(\infty,1)
-category is an
\omega
-category in which all
k
-morphisms for
k>1
are invertible.
Equivalently, we can see an
(\infty,1)
-category
\mathcal{C}
as a collection of objects together with a space
of
1
-morphisms
\mathcal{C}(X,Y)
for any pair of objects, equipped with a composition operation that is associative and unital up to homotopy.

(\infty,1)
-categories are the natural place for homotopy coherent mathematics,
and we will make constant use of them throughout this thesis.
The theory of
(\infty,1)
-categories closely matches the theory of ordinary
1
-categories.
We will commonly refer to
(\infty,1)
-categories simply as
\infty
-categories.
For a proper introduction to
\infty
-category theory we refer to
[
Cis19
,
Rez
,
Lur08a
]
.
Most of the definitions and results in this section are common,
and can be found in the cited introductory texts;
we will only cite specific items that are not as well known.

2.1.1
Quasicategories and Kan Complexes

Similar to picking a basis in linear algebra, we pick a model for
\infty
-categories.
By now there are multiple choices of such a model which have been shown to be equivalent in the appropriate way.
For the purposes of this thesis we mostly work with quasicategories,
which are the most well developed at this point.

Definition 2.1.1.1
.

We denote by
\Delta
the category of finite non-empty ordinals,
whose objects are the linearly ordered sets

[n]:=\{0\leq 1\leq\cdots\leq n\}

for all natural numbers
n\geq 0
.
The maps in
\Delta
are order-preserving functions.
We denote by for some
n,m\geq 0
and any monotone sequence

0\leq i_{0}\leq\cdots\leq i_{n}\leq m
we denote by

\langle i_{0},\ldots,i_{k}\rangle

the map
[n]\to[m]
which sends
j\in[n]
to
i_{j}\in[m]
.
A
simplicial set
is a functor
\Delta^{\textup{op}}\to\textup{Set}
,
and a map of simplicial sets is a natural transformation of functors.
We denote by
sSet
the
1
-category of simplicial sets.
For
k\geq 0
we write
\Delta[k]
for the simplicial set
given by the representable functor
\textup{sSet}(-,[k])
.
When
X
is a simplicial set, we call an element
X([k])

a
k
-simplex
of
X
; by the Yoneda lemma there is a natural bijection
between
X([k])
and the set of maps
\Delta[k]\to X
.
The
boundary
of the
k
-simplex
\Delta[k]
is the union of all subsimplices
\Delta[k-1]\hookrightarrow\Delta[k]
.
For
0\leq i\leq k
the
i
th horn
\Lambda^{i}[k]
is the union of all
subsimplices
\Delta[k-1]\hookrightarrow\Delta[k]

except the one which corresponds to the inclusion

[k-1]\hookrightarrow[k]

that misses
i\in[k]
.
We write
X*Y
for the
join
of two simplicial sets
X
and
Y
.

2.1.1.2
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a
1
-category and
f:A\to B
,
g:X\to Y
maps in
\mathcal{C}
.
We write
f\boxslash g
when for every (solid) diagram in
\mathcal{C}
of the form

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{B}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{Y}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}

there exists a dashed map
B\to Y
that makes the diagram commute.
In this case we say that
f
has the
left lifting property
with respect to

g
, or equivalently that
g
has the
right lifting property
with respect
to
f
.
For a set
S
of maps in
\mathcal{C}
we write
\operatorname{llp}(S)
for the subcategory
of
\mathcal{C}
consisting of maps
g
such that
f\boxslash g
for all
f\in S
.
The set
\operatorname{llp}(S)
is closed under composition, pullbacks, products and retracts
where they exist in
\mathcal{C}
.
Dually we write
\operatorname{rlp}(S)
for
the subcategory of
\mathcal{C}
consisting of maps
f
such that
f\boxslash g
.
Then
\operatorname{rlp}(S)
is closed under composition, pushouts, coproducts and retracts
where they exist in
\mathcal{C}
.

2.1.1.3
.

A
quasicategory
is a simplicial set
\mathcal{C}
such that the unique
map
!_{\mathcal{C}}:\mathcal{C}\to\Delta[0]
has the right lifting property with respect to
all inner horn inclusions
\Lambda^{i}[k]\hookrightarrow\Delta[k]
for
0<i<k
.
When
\mathcal{C}
is a quasicategory, the
objects
of
\mathcal{C}
are the
0
-simplices
and the
maps
of
\mathcal{C}
are the
1
-simplices.
An inner horn
\Lambda^{1}[2]\to\mathcal{C}
is a composable sequence of two maps in
\mathcal{C}
,
and the existence of a filler
\Delta[2]\to\mathcal{C}
guarantees that the sequence has a composite.
The fillers of inner horns
\Lambda^{i}[k]\to\mathcal{C}
when
k>2
ensure that the composite
is unique up to equivalence, and that composition is weakly associative and unital.

2.1.1.4
.

Every
1
-category
\mathcal{C}
induces a quasicategory
\textup{N}\mathcal{C}
by taking its nerve.
The nerve of
\mathcal{C}
is the simplicial set whose
k
-simplices are functors

[k]\to\mathcal{C}
, i.e. composable sequences in
\mathcal{C}
of length
k

together with a choice of composites. Because composites in a
1
-category are
uniquely determined, the nerve
\textup{N}\mathcal{C}
has unique fillers for all inner
horns. Conversely, every simplicial set with unique fillers for all inner horns
is isomorphic to the nerve of a
1
-category. Moreover, the nerve construction
extends to a fully faithful functor

\textup{N}:\textup{Cat}\hookrightarrow\textup{sSet}
.
We will therefore conflate
1
-categories with their nerve.

2.1.1.5
.

The nerve functor
\textup{N}:\textup{Cat}\hookrightarrow\textup{sSet}
has a left adjoint

\textup{h}:\textup{sSet}\to\textup{Cat}
which sends a simplicial set
X
to its
homotopy category

\textup{h}(X)
. When
\mathcal{C}
is a quasicategory, the homotopy category
\textup{h}(\mathcal{C})

admits the following description: The objects of
\textup{h}(\mathcal{C})
are the
0
-simplices
of
\mathcal{C}
and the maps from
x
to
y
in
\textup{h}(\mathcal{C})
are equivalence classes
of
1
-simplices from
x
to
y
in
\mathcal{C}
, where two
1
-simplices are identified
when there is a
2
-simplex

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{y}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{x}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{z}}
id
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}

Then the composition operation is uniquely determined, well-defined,
unital and associative due to the inner horn fillers for
\mathcal{C}
.
We say that a map in
\mathcal{C}
is an
equivalence
if it is sent to an
isomorphism in
\textup{h}(\mathcal{C})
by the adjunction unit

\mathcal{C}\to\textup{N}(\textup{h}(\mathcal{C}))
.

2.1.1.6
.

A
Kan complex
is a simplicial set
X
such that the unique map

!_{X}:X\to\Delta[0]
has the right lifting property with respect
to all horn inclusions
\Lambda^{i}[k]\hookrightarrow\Delta[k]
.
A Kan complex is therefore in particular a quasicategory. The fillers for the outer horns

\Lambda^{0}[k]
and
\Lambda^{k}[k]
guarantee that every map of a Kan complex
is invertible. Kan complexes therefore serve as a model of
\infty
-groupoids or spaces.

2.1.1.7
.

For any topological space
X
we can define a simplicial set
\operatorname{Sing}(X)

whose
k
-simplices are continuous maps from the topological standard
simplex
{|\Delta[k]|}\to X
. An object in
\operatorname{Sing}(X)
is a point in
X
.
A map is a path
\gamma:{|\Delta[1]|}\to X
. Famously composition of
paths with constant length can not be made associative or unital, but
it is associative and unital up to homotopy.
Every topological horn inclusion
{|\Lambda^{i}[k]|}\hookrightarrow{|\Delta[k]|}

admits a retraction, with which we can construct horn fillers for
\operatorname{Sing}(X)
.
Therefore,
\operatorname{Sing}(X)
is a Kan complex.
The functor
\operatorname{Sing}:\textup{Top}\to\textup{sSet}
has a left adjoint,
the geometric realisation functor
|-|:\textup{sSet}\to\textup{Top}
.

2.1.1.8
.

When
\mathcal{C}
is a quasicategory, the
core
of
\mathcal{C}
is the largest
simplicial subset
\operatorname{core}(\mathcal{C})\hookrightarrow\mathcal{C}
whose
1
-simplices
must be equivalences in
\mathcal{C}
. In other words, the core of
\mathcal{C}
is
the largest Kan complex contained within
\mathcal{C}
.

2.1.1.9
.

When
\mathcal{C}
and
\mathcal{D}
are quasicategories, the product of simplicial
sets
\mathcal{C}\times\mathcal{D}
is a quasicategory as well. Similarly, the
coproduct
\mathcal{C}\sqcup\mathcal{D}
is again a quasicategory.
For any simplicial set
X
and a quasicategory
\mathcal{C}
we write

\textup{Fun}(X,\mathcal{C})
for the simplicial set whose
k
-simplices are maps

\Delta[k]\times X\to\mathcal{C}
. Then
\textup{Fun}(X,\mathcal{C})
is a quasicategory
itself, whose objects are
functors
from
X
to
\mathcal{C}
and whose maps
are
natural transformations
. We write
\textup{Cat}_{\infty}(X,\mathcal{C})
for the
core of
\textup{Fun}(X,\mathcal{C})
.
The quasicategory of functors
\textup{Fun}(\Delta[1],\mathcal{C})

is the
arrow category
of
\mathcal{C}
, equipped with functors

\textup{dom},\textup{cod}:\textup{Fun}(\Delta[1],\mathcal{C})\to\mathcal{C}
that sends a map to
its domain and codomain, respectively.
For any pair of objects
x
,
y
in
\mathcal{C}
we can take the pullbacks
of simplicial sets

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{C}(x,y)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\textup{Fun}(\Delta[1],\mathcal{C})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Delta[0]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{C}\times\mathcal{C}}}
{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\textup{dom},\textup{cod})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(x,y)}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{C}_{x/}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\textup{Fun}(\Delta[1],\mathcal{C})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Delta[0]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{C}}}
{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}
dom
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{C}_{/y}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\textup{Fun}(\Delta[1],\mathcal{C})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Delta[0]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{C}}}
{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}
cod
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces y}

The simplicial set
\mathcal{C}(x,y)
is a Kan complex that represents the

mapping space
from
x
to
y
in
\mathcal{C}
. The simplicial sets
\mathcal{C}_{x/}

and
\mathcal{C}_{/y}
are the
slice categories
of
\mathcal{C}
under
x
and over
y
.
More generally for functors
f:\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{C}
and
g:\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}
of quasicategories, we define the
comma categories
via the pullbacks of simplicial sets

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{(f/g)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\textup{Fun}(\Delta[1],\mathcal{C})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{B}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{C}\times\mathcal{C}}}
{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\textup{dom},\textup{cod})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f\times g}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{C}_{f/}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\textup{Fun}(\Delta[1],\mathcal{C})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{A}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{C}}}
{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}
dom
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{C}_{/g}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\textup{Fun}(\Delta[1],\mathcal{C})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{B}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{C}}}
{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}
cod
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}

2.1.1.10
.

A map of simplicial sets
f:X\to Y
is a
Kan equivalence
when
its geometric realisation
|f|:|X|\to|Y|
is a weak homotopy equivalence
of topological spaces. The map
f:X\to Y
is a
categorical equivalence

when for every quasicategory
\mathcal{C}
the map
\textup{Cat}_{\infty}(Y,\mathcal{C})\to\textup{Cat}_{\infty}(X,\mathcal{C})
,
induced by precomposition with
f
, is a Kan equivalence.

2.1.1.11
.

Let
f:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}
be a functor between quasicategories.
Then
f
is
fully faithful
if for each pair of objects
x
,
y
in
\mathcal{C}

the induced map
\mathcal{C}(x,y)\to\mathcal{D}(f(x),f(y))

is a Kan equivalence.
An object
d
in
\mathcal{D}
is in the
essential image
of

f
when there exists an object
c
in
\mathcal{C}
and an equivalence

f(c)\to d
in
\mathcal{D}
.
The functor
f
is
essentially surjective
when every object
of
\mathcal{D}
is in the essential image of
f
.
A functor between quasicategories is a categorical equivalence if and only
if it is fully faithful and essentially surjective.

2.1.1.12
.

A functor
f:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}
between quasicategories is a categorical equivalence if and only
if there exists a functor
g:\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{C}
and natural equivalences

f\circ g\simeq\textup{id}_{\mathcal{D}}
as well as
g\circ f\simeq\textup{id}_{\mathcal{C}}
.

2.1.1.13
.

Let
f:X\to Y
be a map of simplicial sets. Suppose that for every

k\geq 0
and every (solid) diagram of simplicial sets

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\partial\Delta[k]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Delta[k]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{Y}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces v}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces w}

there exists a map
w:\Delta[k]\to Y
which makes the upper left
square commute strictly together with a natural equivalence
f\circ w\simeq u
.
Then
f
is a Kan equivalence by
[
KS15
, Lemma 4.3]
.
Moreover if
Y
is a Kan complex, then so is
X
.
The analogous claim holds for categorical equivalences and quasicategories.

2.1.1.14
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a quasicategory and
X\subseteq\mathcal{C}
a simplicial
set contained in
\mathcal{C}
. Then
X
is a
subcategory
of
\mathcal{C}

if it is closed under composition, i.e. when the inclusion map

X\hookrightarrow\mathcal{C}
has the right lifting
property with respect to the horn inclusion
\Lambda^{1}[2]\to\Delta[2]
.
In this case
X\hookrightarrow\mathcal{C}
has the right lifting property
with respect to all
\Lambda^{i}[k]\hookrightarrow\Delta[k]

for
0<i<k
and so
X
is itself a quasicategory.
A subcategory
\mathcal{D}\subseteq\mathcal{C}
is
full
if the inclusion map

\mathcal{D}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{C}
is fully faithful. A subcategory

\mathcal{D}\subseteq\mathcal{C}
is
wide
if
\mathcal{D}
contains all
objects of
\mathcal{C}
.

2.1.1.15
.

A pair of functors
L:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}
and
R:\mathcal{D}\to\mathcal{C}

between quasicategories form an adjunction when there exist natural
transformations
\eta:\textup{id}_{\mathcal{D}}\to R\circ L
and
\varepsilon:L\circ R\to\textup{id}_{\mathcal{C}}
,
called the
unit
and
counit
,
together with
2
-simplices

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{L}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{L\circ R\circ L}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{L}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\textup{id}_{L}\circ\eta}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\textup{id}_{R}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varepsilon\circ\textup{id}_{L}}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{R}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{R\circ L\circ R}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{R}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\eta\circ\textup{id}_{R}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\textup{id}_{R}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\textup{id}_{R}\circ\varepsilon}

in
\textup{Fun}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D})
and
\textup{Fun}(\mathcal{D},\mathcal{C})
.
In this case we write
L\dashv R
and
L:\mathcal{C}\rightleftarrows\mathcal{D}:R
.
The data of an adjunction is determined uniquely up to equivalence by just
L
or

R
individually, as long as it exists.
The adjunction is an
adjoint equivalence
whenever both the unit and
counit are natural equivalences.

2.1.1.16
.

Let
I
be a simplicial set.
Then the left and right cones
I^{\triangleleft}
and
I^{\triangleright}

are defined by the pushouts of simplicial sets

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Delta[0]\times I}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Delta[1]\times I}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Delta[0]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{I^{\triangleleft}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\langle 0\rangle\times\textup{id}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Delta[0]\times I}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Delta[1]\times I}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Delta[0]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{I^{\triangleright}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\langle 1\rangle\times\textup{id}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}

The cones let us define limits and colimits as follows:
Suppose that
\mathcal{C}
is a quasicategory and
\hat{f}:I^{\triangleleft}\to\mathcal{C}
a map of
simplicial sets which restricts to the map
f:I\to\mathcal{C}
.
Then
\hat{f}
is a
limit diagram
whenever the restriction map

\mathcal{C}_{/\hat{f}}\to\mathcal{C}_{/f}

is a categorical equivalence.

Colimit diagrams
are defined dually.
Let
\textup{const}_{I}:\mathcal{C}\to\textup{Fun}(I,\mathcal{C})
be the constant diagram functor.
A right adjoint of
\textup{const}_{I}
, when it exists, computes limits of all
I
-shaped
diagrams; similarly a left adjoint of
\textup{const}_{I}
computes colimits of
I
-shaped
diagrams.

2.1.1.17
.

Suppose that
\mathcal{C}
is a quasicategory and

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{X_{0}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{X_{1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{X_{2}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{Y_{0}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{Y_{1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{Y_{2}}}
{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}

a commutative diagram in
\mathcal{C}
in which the square on the right
is a pullback square. Then the square on the left is a pullback square
if and only if the overall diagram composes to a pullback square.

2.1.1.18
.

Suppose that
\mathcal{C}
is a quasicategory and

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces B}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces D}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces W}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces C}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Z}

a commutative diagram in
\mathcal{C}
in which the left, back and right square

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{B}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{C}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{D}}
{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{B}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{Y}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{D}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{W}}
{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{Y}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{Z}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{W}}
{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}

are all pullback squares. Then also the front square

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{C}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{Z}}

is a pullback square.

2.1.2
Localisation and Model Categories

2.1.2.1
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a quasicategory and
W
a subset of the set of maps in
\mathcal{C}
.
The
localisation
of
\mathcal{C}
at
W
is a quasicategory
\mathcal{C}[W^{-1}]

together with a functor
\gamma:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}[W^{-1}]
so that for
every quasicategory
\mathcal{D}
the functor
\textup{Cat}_{\infty}(\mathcal{C}[W^{-1}],\mathcal{D})\to\textup{Cat}_{\infty}(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{D})

induced by
\gamma
is fully faithful, and its essential image consists of those functors

f:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}
which sends maps in
W
to equivalences in
\mathcal{D}
.
The localisation always exists and is determined uniquely up to equivalence.
Even when
\mathcal{C}
is a
1
-category, the localisation of
\mathcal{C}
at some set
may not be equivalent to a
1
-category. Every quasicategory arises as the
localisation of a
1
-category.

2.1.2.2
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a quasicategory and
W
a subset of the set of maps in
\mathcal{C}
.
Then
W
satisfies the
2
-out-of-
3
property
if whenever
f:x\to y
and
g:y\to z
are composable maps in
\mathcal{C}
and two of

f
,
g
,
g\circ f
are in
W
, then so is the third.
In particular if
W
is the set of equivalences in
\mathcal{C}
, then it satisfies
the
2
-out-of-
3
property.

2.1.2.3
.

For any Grothendieck universe
U
we have a
1
-category
\textup{sSet}_{U}
of

U
-small simplicial sets. Then the quasicategory of
U
-small
spaces

\textup{S}_{U}
is the localisation of
\textup{sSet}_{U}
at the Kan equivalences.
The quasicategory of
U
-small
\infty
-categories
(\textup{Cat}_{\infty})_{U}
is the
localisation of
\textup{sSet}_{U}
at the categorical equivalences.
We largely ignore size issues, and therefore drop the Grothendieck
universe from the notation to write
S
and
\textup{Cat}_{\infty}
.

Localisations are difficult to work with in general.
However, there are tools that use additional structure on a relative category

(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{W})
to enable us to perform computations in the localisation
\mathcal{C}[\mathcal{W}^{-1}]

via constructions purely in
\mathcal{C}
.
Model categories are one such tool.
We will quickly review the parts of the theory of model categories that are relevant to this thesis,
but refer to the literature for proofs or more in depth discussion.

2.1.2.4
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a
1
-category that is complete and cocomplete.
A
model structure

S
on
\mathcal{C}
consists of three wide subcategories

\textup{W}_{S}
,
\textup{Fib}_{S}
and
\textup{Cof}_{S}
of
\mathcal{C}
such that

1.

\textup{W}_{S}
,
\textup{Fib}_{S}
and
\textup{Cof}_{S}
are closed under retract.

2.

(\textup{W}_{S}\cap\textup{Cof}_{S})\boxslash\textup{Fib}_{S}
and
\textup{Cof}_{S}\boxslash(\textup{W}_{S}\cap\textup{Fib}_{S})
.

3.

Each map in
\mathcal{C}
factors as a map in
\textup{W}_{S}\cap\textup{Cof}_{S}
followed by a map in
\textup{Fib}_{S}
.

4.

Each map in
\mathcal{C}
factors as a map in
\textup{Cof}_{S}
followed by a map in
\textup{W}_{S}\cap\textup{Fib}_{S}
.

The
1
-category
\mathcal{C}
together with the model structure
S

form a
model category

(\mathcal{C},S)
.
The maps in
\textup{W}_{S}
,
\textup{Fib}_{S}
and
\textup{Cof}_{S}
are called the

weak equivalences
,
fibrations
and
cofibrations

of
S
. A fibration or cofibration is
trivial
or
acyclic

when it is also in
\textup{W}_{S}
. An object
X
in
\mathcal{C}
is

fibrant
when the unique map
X\to*
into the terminal
object of
\mathcal{C}
is a fibration. An object
X
in
\mathcal{C}

is
cofibrant
when the unique map
\emptyset\to X

from the initial object is a cofibration.
The model structure is
cofibrantly generated
when there exist
sets of maps
I
,
J
in
\mathcal{C}
such that
\textup{Fib}_{S}=\operatorname{rlp}(I)

and
\textup{Fib}_{S}\cap\textup{W}_{S}=\operatorname{rlp}(J)
.
The model category is
combinatorial
when
\mathcal{C}
is a
locally presentable category and the model structure is cofibrantly generated.

2.1.2.5
.

The
Kan-Quillen model structure

Kan
on the category
sSet

of simplicial sets is the unique model structure
on
sSet
whose cofibrations are the monomorphisms and the fibrant
objects are Kan complexes.
The weak equivalences are the Kan equivalences as defined above.
It is cofibrantly generated by the sets

\displaystyle I

\displaystyle:=\{\Lambda^{i}[k]\hookrightarrow\Delta[k]\mid 0\leq i\leq k,k\geq 1\}

\displaystyle J

\displaystyle:=\{\partial\Delta[k]\hookrightarrow\Delta[k]\mid k\geq 0\}

We call the fibrations in
\textup{Fib}_{\textup{Kan}}
the
Kan fibrations
.
Since
sSet
is locally presentable, the model category
(\textup{sSet},\textup{Kan})

is combinatorial.

2.1.2.6
.

The
Joyal model structure

Joyal
is the unique model structure on

sSet
whose cofibrations are the monomorphisms and the fibrant
objects are quasicategories.
Its weak equivalences are the categorical equivalences.
It is cofibrantly generated by the sets

\displaystyle I

\displaystyle:=\{\Lambda^{i}[k]\hookrightarrow\Delta[k]\mid 0<i<k\}\cup\{\Delta[0]\hookrightarrow E[1]\}

\displaystyle J

\displaystyle:=\{\partial\Delta[k]\hookrightarrow\Delta[k]\mid k\geq 0\}

A fibration in
\textup{Fib}_{\textup{Joyal}}
is a
categorical fibration
.
The trivial fibrations in
\textup{Fib}_{\textup{Joyal}}\cap\textup{W}_{\textup{Joyal}}
agree with
the trivial fibrations of the Kan-Quillen model structure.
Since
sSet
is locally presentable, the model category
(\textup{sSet},\textup{Joyal})

is combinatorial.
We say that a map in
sSet
is an
inner fibration
whenever it has the right lifting property with respect to the set

\{\Lambda^{i}[k]\hookrightarrow\Delta[k]\mid 0<i<k\}

Lemma 2.1.2.7
.

Suppose that
f:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}
is a map of simplicial sets such that

\mathcal{C}
is a quasicategory and
\mathcal{D}
is the nerve of a
1
-category.
Then
f
is an inner fibration.

Proof.

Suppose that
0<i<k
and we have a lifting problem

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Lambda^{i}[k]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{C}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Delta[k]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{D}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tau^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sigma}

(2.1)

Because
\mathcal{C}
is a quasicategory, we have an inner horn filler

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Lambda^{i}[k]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{C}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Delta[k]}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tau^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tau}

Then
f\circ\tau
and
\sigma
are both solutions to the lifting problem

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Lambda^{i}[k]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{D}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Delta[k]}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f\circ\tau^{\prime}}

By assumption
\mathcal{D}
is the nerve of a
1
-category and so
f\circ\tau=\sigma
.
Therefore,
\tau
is a solution to the lifting problem (
2.1
).
∎

2.1.2.8
.

Suppose that
(\mathcal{C},S)
is a model category and
\mathcal{I}
is a small
1
-category.
Let
\mathcal{W}
be the wide subcategory of
\textup{Fun}(\mathcal{I},\mathcal{C})
consisting of
the pointwise weak equivalences, i.e. those natural transformations whose
components are weak equivalences in
\textup{W}_{S}
.
Then the universal property of the localisation induces a functor of
\infty
-categories

\textup{Fun}(\mathcal{I},\mathcal{C})[\mathcal{W}^{-1}]\longrightarrow\textup{Fun}(\mathcal{I},\mathcal{C}[\textup{W}_{S}^{-1}])

By
[
Cis19
, Theorem 7.9.8.]
this functor is an equivalence.
Therefore, every diagram in the localisation
X:\mathcal{I}\to\mathcal{C}[\textup{W}_{S}^{-1}]

can be
rectified
to a diagram
\hat{X}:\mathcal{I}\to\mathcal{C}

in the model category:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{I}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{C}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{C}[\textup{W}_{S}^{-1}]}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\hat{X}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}

In particular every diagram of
\infty
-categories in
\textup{Cat}_{\infty}

or spaces in
S

rectifies to a diagram in the
1
-category of simplicial sets.

2.1.2.9
.

A
Reedy category
is a
1
-category
\mathcal{I}
together with an
ordinal
\alpha
and a degree functor
\deg:\mathcal{I}\to\alpha
and
two wide subcategories
\mathcal{I}_{+}
and
\mathcal{I}_{-}
which together satisfy:

1.

Each non-identity map in
\mathcal{I}_{+}
strictly raises the degree.

2.

Each non-identity map in
\mathcal{I}_{-}
strictly lowers the degree.

3.

Each map of
\mathcal{I}
factors uniquely as a map in
\mathcal{I}_{-}
followed by a map in
\mathcal{I}_{+}
.

Whenever
\mathcal{I}
is a Reedy category, then its opposite
\mathcal{I}^{\textup{op}}
can
also be equipped with the structure of a Reedy category.
The category
\Delta
is a Reedy category with the degree functor

\deg:\Delta\to\omega
which sends
[n]
to
n\in\omega
,
where
\Delta_{+}
and
\Delta_{-}
are the injective and surjective maps.
When
(\mathcal{C},S)
is a model category and
\mathcal{I}
a Reedy category,
we can equip
\textup{Fun}(\mathcal{I},\mathcal{C})
with the
Reedy model structure

\textup{Reedy}(\mathcal{I},S)
that presents the quasicategory of functors

\textup{Fun}(\mathcal{I},\mathcal{C}[\textup{W}_{S}^{-1}])
.

2.1.2.10
.

Let
(\mathcal{C},S)
be a model category and
X\in\mathcal{C}
an object.
Let
U:\mathcal{C}_{/X}\to\mathcal{C}
be the forgetful functor from the slice
category. Then
\mathcal{C}_{/X}
admits a
slice model structure

S_{/X}
with

\displaystyle\textup{W}_{S_{/X}}

\displaystyle:=\{f\in\textup{Arr}(\mathcal{C}_{/X})\mid U(f)\in\textup{W}_{S}\}

\displaystyle\textup{Fib}_{S_{/X}}

\displaystyle:=\{f\in\textup{Arr}(\mathcal{C}_{/X})\mid U(f)\in\textup{Fib}_{S}\}

\displaystyle\textup{Cof}_{S_{/X}}

\displaystyle:=\{f\in\textup{Arr}(\mathcal{C}_{/X})\mid U(f)\in\textup{Cof}_{S}\}

The slice model structure is cofibrantly generated and combinatorial whenever

(\mathcal{C},S)
is.

2.1.2.11
.

Let
(\mathcal{C},S)
and
(\mathcal{D},T)
be model categories.
An adjunction
L:\mathcal{C}\rightleftarrows\mathcal{D}:R
is a

Quillen adjunction

whenever the following equivalent conditions are satisfied:

1.

L
preserves cofibrations and trivial cofibrations.

2.

R
preserves fibrations and trivial fibrations.

3.

L
preserves cofibrations and
R
preserves fibrations.

4.

L
preserves trivial cofibrations and
R
preserves fibrations.

In this case we denote the Quillen adjunction by

L:(\mathcal{C},S)\rightleftarrows(\mathcal{D},T):R

and say that
L
,
R
are left and right Quillen functors, respectively.
By Ken Brown’s Lemma left Quillen functors preserve weak equivalences
between cofibrant objects and right Quillen functors preserve weak equivalences
between fibrant objects.
By
[
Maz21
, Theorem 1.1.]
the Quillen
adjunction induces a derived adjunction

\mathbb{L}:\mathcal{C}[\textup{W}_{S}^{-1}]\rightleftarrows\mathcal{D}[\textup{W}_{T}^{-1}]:\mathbb{R}

between the quasicategories obtained by localisation.

2.1.2.12
.

The identity functors form a Quillen adjunction

\textup{id}:(\textup{sSet},\textup{Joyal})\rightleftarrows(\textup{sSet},\textup{Kan}):\textup{id}

between the Joyal and Kan model structures on simplicial sets,
which induces an adjunction
\textup{Cat}_{\infty}\rightleftarrows\textup{S}
.
The right adjoint is the inclusion
\textup{S}\hookrightarrow\textup{Cat}_{\infty}

of spaces into
\infty
-categories, while the left adjoint

\textup{k}:\textup{Cat}_{\infty}\to\textup{S}
produces a space
\textup{k}(\mathcal{C})
from an
\infty
-category
\mathcal{C}

by freely inverting all maps.
We also call
\textup{k}(\mathcal{C})
the
classifying space
of
\mathcal{C}
.

2.1.2.13
.

Let
(\mathcal{C},S)
be a model structure and
\mathcal{I}
a Reedy category.
Then the adjunction between the constant diagram functor and the limit functor

\textup{const}:(\mathcal{C},S)\rightleftarrows(\textup{Fun}(\mathcal{I},\mathcal{C}),\textup{Reedy}(\mathcal{I},S)):\lim

is a Quillen adjunction so that the induced adjunction

\textup{const}:\mathcal{C}[\textup{W}_{S}^{-1}]\rightleftarrows\textup{Fun}(\mathcal{I},\mathcal{C}[\textup{W}_{S}^{-1}]):\lim

determines
\mathcal{I}
-shaped limits in the
\infty
-category
\mathcal{C}[\textup{W}_{S}^{-1}]
.
In particular when
X:\mathcal{I}\to\mathcal{C}
is a diagram in the
1
-category
\mathcal{C}
that is fibrant in the Reedy model structure,
then the localisation functor
\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}[\textup{W}_{S}^{-1}]
preserves the limit of
X
.
Analogously, the adjunction

\operatorname*{colim}:(\textup{Fun}(\mathcal{I},\mathcal{C}),\textup{Reedy}(\mathcal{I},S))\rightleftarrows(\mathcal{C},S):\textup{const}

is a Quillen adjunction
and so the localisation
\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}[\textup{W}_{S}^{-1}]
preserves colimits of Reedy cofibrant diagrams.

2.1.2.14
.

Suppose that
(\mathcal{C},S)
is a model category.
When we let

\mathcal{I}:=\{0\rightarrow 1\leftarrow 2\},

then an
\mathcal{I}
-shaped limit is a pullback.
The category
\mathcal{I}
is a Reedy category so that a diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X(0)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X(1)}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X(2)}

is fibrant in
(\textup{Fun}(\mathcal{I},\mathcal{C}),\textup{Reedy}(S))
when the objects

X(0)
,
X(1)
and
X(2)
are all fibrant in
(\mathcal{C},S)

and
X(2)\to X(1)
is a fibration.
This allows us to compute pullbacks in
\mathcal{C}[\textup{W}^{-1}]

via certain pullbacks in
\mathcal{C}
.
The pullbacks of quasicategories above all have this form and
therefore represent pullbacks of
\infty
-categories.

2.1.2.15
.

Let
(\mathcal{C},S)
be a model category and
f:X\to Y
a map in
\mathcal{C}
.
Then the adjunction
\Sigma_{f}\dashv f^{*}
between the slice categories is
a Quillen adjunction for the slice model structures

\Sigma_{f}:(\mathcal{C}_{/X},S_{/X})\rightleftarrows(\mathcal{C}_{/Y},S_{/Y}):f^{*}

2.1.2.16
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be an
\infty
-category.
A
reflective localisation
of
\mathcal{C}
is a full subcategory

i:\mathcal{D}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{C}
such that the inclusion functor
has a left adjoint
L:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}
.
We say that a map
f:X\to Y
in
\mathcal{C}
is
\mathcal{D}
-local when for every
object
D\in\mathcal{D}
, precomposition with
f
induces an equivalence

\mathcal{C}(Y,D)\to\mathcal{C}(X,D).

Then
L:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}
is the localisation functor which freely
inverts the
\mathcal{D}
-local maps in
\mathcal{C}
.

2.1.2.17
.

A diagram
X:\mathcal{I}^{\triangleleft}\to\mathcal{D}
is a limit diagram
if and only if
i\circ X:\mathcal{I}^{\triangleleft}\to\mathcal{C}
is a limit
diagram.
A colimit in
\mathcal{D}
is computed by first taking the colimit in
\mathcal{C}
and then
applying the functor
L
to the result.

2.1.2.18
.

Let
(\mathcal{C},S)
be a model category and
W
a collection of maps in
\mathcal{C}
.
The
left Bousfield localisation
of
(\mathcal{C},S)
at
W
is,
if it exists, the unique model structure
S[W^{-1}]
on
\mathcal{C}

with the same cofibrations
\textup{Cof}_{S[W^{-1}]}=\textup{Cof}_{S}

so that the weak equivalences
\textup{W}_{S[W^{-1}]}
are those maps of

\mathcal{C}
that become equivalences in the localisation
\mathcal{C}[(\textup{W}_{S}\cup W)^{-1}]
.
Then the identity functor
\textup{id}:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}
induces a Quillen
adjunction
\textup{id}:(\mathcal{C},S[W^{-1}])\rightleftarrows(\mathcal{C},S):\textup{id}
.
The derived adjunction
\mathcal{C}[\textup{W}_{S[W^{-1}]}]\rightleftarrows\mathcal{C}[\textup{W}_{S}]

has a fully faithful right adjoint so that
\mathcal{C}[\textup{W}_{S[W^{-1}]}]

is a reflective subcategory of
\mathcal{C}[\textup{W}_{S}]
.

2.1.3
Fibrations

2.1.3.1
.

A map of simplicial sets
p:X\to Y
is an isofibration if it is
an inner fibration and for every object
x_{0}
of
X
and every
equivalence
f:y_{0}\to y_{1}
in
Y
with
p(x_{0})=y_{0}
there exists
an equivalence
\hat{f}:x_{0}\to x_{1}
in
X
with
p(\hat{f})=f
.
Whenever
\mathcal{E}
and
\mathcal{K}
are quasicategories, a map

p:\mathcal{E}\to\mathcal{K}
is an isofibration if and only if it
is a categorical fibration.

2.1.3.2
.

A map of simplicial sets
p:E\to K
is a
left fibration

if it has the right lifting property against all horn inclusions

\Lambda^{i}[k]\to\Delta[k]
with
0\leq i<k
.
Dually, a map of simplicial sets
p:E\to K
is a
right fibration

when it has the right lifting property against all horn inclusions

\Lambda^{i}[k]\to\Delta[k]
with
0<i\leq k
.
Both left and right fibrations are closed under pullback and composition.

2.1.3.3
.

Let
K
be a simplicial set. The
covariant model structure
over
K

is the unique model structure
\textup{Cov}(K)
on the slice category
\textup{sSet}_{/K}
whose fibrant
objects are the left fibrations and whose cofibrations are the monomorphisms.
For any map
f:K\to L
of simplicial sets, the induced base change adjunction between
the slice categories
\Sigma_{f}:\textup{sSet}_{/K}\rightleftarrows\textup{sSet}_{/L}:f^{*}

is a Quillen adjunction for the covariant model structures.
Moreover, when
f
is also a categorical equivalence, then the adjunction is a
Quillen equivalence.
When
\mathcal{K}
is a quasicategory, the covariant model structure represents a full
\infty
-subcategory

\textup{LFib}(\mathcal{K})
of
(\textup{Cat}_{\infty})_{/\mathcal{K}}
.
There is an equivalence of
\infty
-categories

\textup{LFib}(\mathcal{K})\simeq\textup{Fun}(\mathcal{K},\textup{S})

that is natural in
\mathcal{K}
.
The functor
\textup{LFib}(\mathcal{K})\to\textup{Fun}(\mathcal{K},\textup{S})
is called

straightening
and its inverse
unstraightening
.
Given a left fibration
p:\mathcal{E}\to\mathcal{K}
over a quasicategory

\mathcal{K}
which straightens to a functor
F:\mathcal{K}\to\textup{S}
,
we can compute the Kan complex which represents the space
F(x)

for an object
x\in\mathcal{K}
by taking the pullback of
simplicial sets

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{F(x)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{E}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Delta[0]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{K}}}
{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x}

2.1.3.4
.

Dually, the right fibrations over a simplicial set
K
are the fibrant
objects of the
contravariant model structure

\textup{Contr}(K)
,
which is compatible with base change. When
\mathcal{K}
is a quasicategory,
the contravariant model structure represents a full
\infty
-subcategory

\textup{RFib}(\mathcal{K})
of
(\textup{Cat}_{\infty})_{/\mathcal{K}}
.
There is an equivalence of
\infty
-categories

\textup{RFib}(\mathcal{K})\simeq\textup{Fun}(\mathcal{K}^{\textup{op}},\textup{S})

that is natural in
\mathcal{K}
.
The functor
\textup{RFib}(\mathcal{K})\to\textup{Fun}(\mathcal{K}^{\textup{op}},\textup{S})
is called

straightening
and its inverse
unstraightening
.

2.1.3.5
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a quasicategory. A
presheaf
on
\mathcal{C}
is a functor

\mathcal{C}^{\textup{op}}\to\textup{S}
and a map of presheaves is a natural transformation
of such functors. Presheaves on
\mathcal{C}
organise into the quasicategory

\textup{P}(\mathcal{C}):=\textup{Fun}(\mathcal{C}^{\textup{op}},\textup{S})
.
Since
S
is complete and cocomplete, and limits and colimits in a functor
category are computed pointwise, it follows that
\textup{P}(\mathcal{C})
is also complete and cocomplete.
The
\infty
-category of presheaves
\textup{P}(\mathcal{C})
can be presented by the contravariant model structure over
\mathcal{C}
or the covariant model structure over
\mathcal{C}^{\textup{op}}
.

2.1.3.6
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a quasicategory and
x
an object of
\mathcal{C}
.
Then the projection from the slice category
\mathcal{C}_{x/}\to\mathcal{C}

under
x
is a left fibration, which represents the covariant functor

\mathcal{C}(x,-):\mathcal{C}\to\textup{S}
.
Similarly, the projection from the slice category
\mathcal{C}_{/x}\to\mathcal{C}

over
x
is a right fibration, representing the contravariant functor

\mathcal{C}(-,x):\mathcal{C}^{\textup{op}}\to\textup{S}
.
The functor
\mathcal{C}(-,x)
is called the
representable presheaf
for
x
.

2.1.3.7
.

Let
X
be a simplicial set.
The
twisted arrow construction

\operatorname{Tw}(X)
of
X
is the simplicial set
whose
k
-simplices are the maps
[k]^{\textup{op}}*[k]\to X
.
This defines a right adjoint functor
\operatorname{Tw}(-):\textup{sSet}\to\textup{sSet}

together with a natural projection map
\operatorname{Tw}(X)\to X^{\textup{op}}\times X

that is induced by the inclusion
[k]^{\textup{op}}\sqcup[k]\hookrightarrow[k]^{\textup{op}}*[k]
.
When
\mathcal{C}
is a quasicategory, the projection map
\operatorname{Tw}(\mathcal{C})\to\mathcal{C}^{\textup{op}}\times\mathcal{C}
is a left fibration which, via the equivalence
\textup{LFib}(\mathcal{C}^{\textup{op}}\times\mathcal{C})\simeq\textup{Fun}(\mathcal{C}^{\textup{op}}\times\mathcal{C},\textup{S})
,
represents the mapping space functor

\mathcal{C}(-,-):\mathcal{C}^{\textup{op}}\times\mathcal{C}\to\textup{S}
.
Expanding the definitions, we see that a
k
-simplex of
\operatorname{Tw}(\mathcal{C})

corresponds to a diagram in
\mathcal{C}
of the form

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{s_{0}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{s_{1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\cdots}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{s_{k-1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{s_{k}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{t_{0}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{t_{1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\cdots}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{t_{k-1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{t_{k}}}

2.1.3.8
.

The
Yoneda embedding
is the fully faithful functor

\mathcal{C}\hookrightarrow\textup{P}(\mathcal{C})
which sends an object
x
of
\mathcal{C}

to the representable presheaf
\mathcal{C}(-,x):\mathcal{C}^{\textup{op}}\to\textup{S}
.
The Yoneda embedding can be constructed concretely by starting with the left
fibration
\operatorname{Tw}(\mathcal{C})\to\mathcal{C}^{\textup{op}}\times\mathcal{C}
, obtaining the
functor
\mathcal{C}(-,-):\mathcal{C}^{\textup{op}}\times\mathcal{C}\to\textup{S}
and
then applying the adjunction
(\mathcal{C}^{\textup{op}}\times-)\dashv\textup{Fun}(\mathcal{C}^{\textup{op}},-)
.

2.1.3.9
.

Let
f:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}
be a functor between quasicategories.
Then precomposition with
f
induces a functor
f^{*}:\textup{P}(\mathcal{D})\to\textup{P}(\mathcal{C})
.
The functor
f^{*}
has a left adjoint
f_{!}:\textup{P}(\mathcal{C})\to\textup{P}(\mathcal{D})

and a right adjoint
f_{*}:\textup{P}(\mathcal{C})\to\textup{P}(\mathcal{D})
.
When the quasicategories of presheaves are presented using
the covariant model structures, the adjunction
f_{!}:\textup{P}(\mathcal{C})\rightleftarrows\textup{P}(\mathcal{D}):f^{*}
is the derived adjunction of the Quillen adjunction

\Sigma_{f}:(\textup{sSet}_{/\mathcal{C}},\textup{Cov}(\mathcal{C}))\rightleftarrows(\textup{sSet}_{/\mathcal{D}},\textup{Cov}(\mathcal{D})):f^{*}
.
When the functor
f
is fully faithful, then so are the left and right adjoints

f_{!},f_{*}:\textup{P}(\mathcal{C})\to\textup{P}(\mathcal{D})
.

2.1.3.10
.

Let
\mathcal{B}
be a quasicategory and
\mathcal{W}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{B}

a wide subcategory. Then the slice category
\textup{sSet}_{/\mathcal{B}}

admits a model structure
\textup{Cov}(\mathcal{B},\mathcal{W})
, called the

\mathcal{W}
-local covariant model structure
, that presents the
quasicategory
\textup{Fun}(\mathcal{B}[\mathcal{W}^{-1}],\textup{S})
.
The cofibrations are the monomorphisms and the fibrant objects
are the left fibrations
p:\mathcal{E}\to\mathcal{B}
that restrict to
a Kan fibration
p^{\prime}
over the wide subcategory
\mathcal{W}
of
\mathcal{B}
:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{E}\times_{{B}}\mathcal{W}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{E}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{W}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{B}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p^{\prime}}
{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}

2.1.3.11
.

A left fibration
p:E\to B
is a
left covering map
when the lifts
against the horn inclusions

\Lambda^{i}[k]\hookrightarrow\Delta[k]

with
0\leq i<k
are unique.
Ignoring size issues, for every right covering map
p:E\to B
there is a unique
pullback square of simplicial sets

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{E}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\textup{Set}_{*}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{B}}
Set
{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}

where
\textup{Set}_{*}\to\textup{Set}
is the functor from pointed sets to sets
which forgets the point.
Analogously, right fibrations with unique lifts are the
right covering maps
,
and classify functors into
\textup{Set}^{\textup{op}}
.

2.1.3.12
.

Let
p:E\to B
be an inner fibration of simplicial sets.
A map
f:\Delta[1]\to B
in
E
is
p
-cartesian

if for every
k\geq 2
and every diagram of the form

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Delta[1]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Lambda^{k}[k]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{E}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Delta[k]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{B}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\langle k-1,k\rangle}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}

there exists a lift
\Delta[k]\to E
that makes the diagram commute.
Dually a map
f
in
E
is
p
-cocartesian
if it is
p^{\textup{op}}
-cartesian
as a map of
E^{\textup{op}}
. Both
p
-cartesian and
p
-cocartesian maps are closed
under composition in
E
.

2.1.3.13
.

Let
p:E\to B
be an inner fibration of simplicial sets.
Then
p
is a
cartesian fibration
if for every object
e_{1}
of
E

and every map
f:b_{0}\to b_{1}
in
B
with
p(e_{1})=b_{1}
there exists
a
p
-cartesian map
\hat{f}:e_{0}\to e_{1}
in
E
with
p(\hat{f})=f
.
Dually
p
is a
cocartesian fibration
when
p^{\textup{op}}:E^{\textup{op}}\to B^{\textup{op}}
is a cartesian fibration.
Both cartesian and cocartesian fibrations are closed under pullback and composition.

2.1.3.14
.

A
marked simplicial set
is a simplicial set
X
together with a subset

T\subseteq X([1])
which contains all degenerate
1
-simplices;
we say that a
1
-simplex is
marked
when it is contained in
T
.
A map of marked simplicial sets from
(X,T)
to
(Y,S)
is a map of
simplical sets
f:X\to Y
such that the induced map
X([1])\to Y([1])

sends elements of
T
to elements of
S
. Marked simplicial sets and
their maps form a
1
-category
\textup{sSet}^{+}
, which is a quasi-topos and therefore
complete, cocomplete and locally cartesian closed.
There is a functor
(-)_{\flat}:\textup{sSet}^{+}\to\textup{sSet}
which forgets the marking.
The forgetful functor has a left adjoint
(-)^{\flat}:\textup{sSet}\to\textup{sSet}^{+}
which
sends a simplicial set
X
to the marked simplicial set
X^{\flat}
in which
only the degenerate
1
-simplices of
X
are marked.
The forgetful functor also has a right adjoint
(-)^{\sharp}:\textup{sSet}\to\textup{sSet}^{+}

so that every
1
-simplex of
X^{\sharp}
is marked.

2.1.3.15
.

Let
p:E\to B
be a cartesian fibration. We then write

E^{\natural}
for the marked simplicial set whose underlying simplicial
set is
E
and in which a map is marked when it is
p
-cartesian.
This is called the
natural marking
of
p
.
The
cartesian model structure
over
B
is the unique model structure

\textup{Cart}(B)
on the slice category
\textup{sSet}^{+}_{/B^{\sharp}}
whose cofibrations
are those maps whose underlying map of simplicial sets is a monomorphism and whose fibrant objects are the cartesian fibrations
with the natural marking.
When
\mathcal{B}
is a quasicategory, the cartesian model structure over
\mathcal{B}

represents a subcategory
\textup{Cart}(\mathcal{B})
of the
\infty
-category
(\textup{Cat}_{\infty})_{/\mathcal{B}}
.
We then have a straightening/unstraightening equivalence

\textup{Cart}(\mathcal{B})\simeq\textup{Fun}(\mathcal{B}^{\textup{op}},\textup{Cat}_{\infty}).

When
p:\mathcal{E}\to\mathcal{B}
is a cartesian fibration which straightens
to a functor
F:\mathcal{B}^{\textup{op}}\to\textup{Cat}_{\infty}
, we can compute the
\infty
-category

F(b)
for any
b\in\mathcal{B}
as a quasicategory by taking the pullback of
simplicial sets

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{F(b)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{E}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Delta[0]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{B}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces b}

2.1.3.16
.

When
\mathcal{B}=\Delta[0]
we have an isomorphism of
1
-categories

\cramped{\textup{sSet}^{+}}_{/\Delta[0]^{\sharp}}\cong\textup{sSet}^{+}
. The cartesian model structure
over
\Delta[0]
therefore induces a model structure on the category
\textup{sSet}^{+}
of
marked simplicial sets. The fibrant objects in this model structure
are the quasicategories
\mathcal{C}
equipped with the
natural marking

\mathcal{C}^{\natural}
in which the marked maps are the equivalences of
\mathcal{C}
.
This model structure presents the
\infty
-category
\textup{Cat}_{\infty}
, and a fibrant
replacement is computed by localising at the marked maps.

2.1.3.17
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a quasicategory.
Then
\textup{cod}:\textup{Fun}(\Delta[1],\mathcal{C})\to\mathcal{C}

is a cocartesian fibration which sends an object
x\in\mathcal{C}
to the slice
category
\mathcal{C}_{/x}
over
x
and a map
f:x\to y
to the functor

\Sigma_{f}:\mathcal{C}_{/x}\to\mathcal{C}_{/y}
given by postcomposition.
When
\mathcal{C}
has all pullbacks, the functor
\textup{cod}:\textup{Fun}(\Delta[1],\mathcal{C})\to\mathcal{C}
is also a cartesian fibration which sends a map
f:x\to y
in
\mathcal{C}

to the pullback functor
f^{*}:\mathcal{C}_{/y}\to\mathcal{C}_{/x}
.
In this case
\Sigma_{f}
is the left adjoint of
f^{*}
.

2.1.3.18
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a quasicategory. We then have projection maps

\textup{dom}:\operatorname{Tw}(\mathcal{C})\to\mathcal{C}^{\textup{op}}
and
\textup{cod}:\operatorname{Tw}(\mathcal{C})\to\mathcal{C}

from the twisted arrow construction of
\mathcal{C}
. These maps are cocartesian
fibrations which straighten to the functors
\mathcal{C}\to\textup{Cat}_{\infty}

which send
x\in\mathcal{C}
to
\mathcal{C}_{x/}
and
\mathcal{C}_{/x}^{\textup{op}}
,
respectively.

Lemma 2.1.3.19
.

Suppose that we have a commutative diagram of quasicategories

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{E}\times_{\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{C}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{E}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{B}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{C}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{D}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q^{*}r}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r^{*}q}
{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r}

in which the square is a pullback square, the map
r:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}

is a categorical fibration and
p
is a cocartesian fibration.
Suppose further that a map in
\mathcal{E}
is
p
-cocartesian if and only
if it is sent to an equivalence by
q:\mathcal{E}\to\mathcal{D}
.
Then the top row of the diagram composes to a cocartesian fibration

p\circ q^{*}r
. Moreover, a map in
\mathcal{E}\times_{\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{C}
is

(p\circ q^{*}r)
-cocartesian if and only if it is sent to an equivalence
by
r^{*}q:\mathcal{E}\times_{\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}
.

Proof.

The map
q^{*}r:\mathcal{E}\times_{\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{C}
is a categorical fibration
since it is the pullback of the categorical fibration
r
.
Therefore
q^{*}r

is in particular an inner fibration. The cocartesian fibration
p:\mathcal{E}\to\mathcal{B}

is also an inner fibration, and so the composite map
p\circ q^{*}r
is an inner fibration.

Suppose that we have a map
(g,h):(e_{0},c_{0})\to(e_{1},c_{1})
in
\mathcal{E}\times_{\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{C}

such that
h
is an equivalence, and suppose further that we have
a lifting problem of the form

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Delta[1]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Lambda^{0}[0]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{E}\times_{\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{C}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Delta[k]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{B}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\langle 0,1\rangle}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(g,h)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\sigma^{\prime},\tau^{\prime})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p\circ q^{*}r}

(2.2)

Because
h
is an equivalence, so is the map
r(h)=q(g)
in
\mathcal{D}
.
By assumption we then have that
g
is
p
-cocartesian, and so there
exists a solution to the induced lifting problem

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Delta[1]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Lambda^{0}[0]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{E}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Delta[k]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{B}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\langle 0,1\rangle}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sigma^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sigma}

The map
r
is a categorical fibration and
h
is an equivalence in
\mathcal{C}
.
We can therefore find a solution to the lifting problem

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Delta[1]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Lambda^{0}[0]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{C}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Delta[k]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{D}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\langle 0,1\rangle}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tau^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces q\circ\sigma}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tau}

Then the lifts
\sigma:\Delta[k]\to\mathcal{E}
and
\tau:\Delta[k]\to\mathcal{C}

together define a solution
(\sigma,\tau)
for the lifting problem (
2.2
). It follows that
(g,h)
is
(p\circ q^{*}r)
-cocartesian.

It remains to show that
p\circ q^{*}r
has enough cocartesian lifts.
Whenever
(e_{0},c_{0})
is an object of
\mathcal{E}\times_{\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{C}

and
f:b_{0}\to b_{1}
is a map in
\mathcal{B}
with
p(e_{0})=b_{0}
,
there exists a
p
-cocartesian lift
g:b_{0}\to b_{1}
with

p(g)=f
.
Then the map
q(g):q(b_{0})\to q(b_{1})
is an equivalence in
\mathcal{D}
.
The categorical fibration
r
is in particular an isofibration, and so
there exists a lift
h:c_{0}\to c_{1}
in
\mathcal{C}
with
r(h)=q(g)
so that

h
is an equivalence.
The maps
g
and
h
together determine a map
(e_{0},c_{0})\to(e_{1},c_{1})

in the pullback
\mathcal{E}\times_{\mathcal{D}}\mathcal{C}
which is a
(p\circ q^{*}r)
-cocartesian
lift of
f
since
h
is an equivalence.
∎

2.1.3.20
.

Suppose that
\mathcal{K}
is an
\infty
-category,
then the inclusion functor
\textup{coCart}(\mathcal{K})\hookrightarrow(\textup{Cat}_{\infty})_{/\mathcal{K}}

has a left adjoint which sends a functor
f:\mathcal{E}\to\mathcal{K}

F
over
\mathcal{K}
.
Following

, Theorem 4.5]
,
we can construct

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}

Similarly the free cartesian fibration
G

2.1.3.21
.

Suppose that
f:\mathcal{E}\to\mathcal{K}
is a functor of
\infty
-categories.
We can obtain a cocartesian fibration
R
via the twisted arrow construction
by composing the top row in the diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\operatorname{Tw}(\mathcal{K})\times_{\mathcal{K}}\mathcal{E}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\operatorname{Tw}(\mathcal{K})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{K}^{\textup{op}}}}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{K}}}
{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}
cod
