\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}

The cocartesian fibration
R
represents the functor

\mathcal{K}^{\textup{op}}\to\textup{Cat}_{\infty}

which sends an object
k\in\mathcal{K}
to the slice category

\mathcal{K}_{k/}\times_{\mathcal{K}}\mathcal{E}
.
This is the same functor as represented by the free cartesian fibration of
f
.

2.1.3.22
.

Let
\mathcal{K}
be an
\infty
-category.
The inclusion
\textup{S}\hookrightarrow\textup{Cat}_{\infty}
together with its left
adjoint induce an adjunction on arrows categories

\textup{Fun}(\mathcal{K},\textup{Cat}_{\infty})\rightleftarrows\textup{Fun}(\mathcal{K},\textup{S})
.
Then using the straightening/unstraightening equivalences for cocartesian
and left fibrations over
\mathcal{K}
, we see how to compute the
free left
fibration
from a cocartesian fibration:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\textup{Fun}(\mathcal{K},\textup{Cat}_{\infty})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\textup{Fun}(\mathcal{K},\textup{S})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\textup{coCart}(\mathcal{K})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\textup{LFib}(\mathcal{K})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\dashv}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\dashv}

We then see that the free left fibration induced by some functor
p:\mathcal{E}\to\mathcal{K}

is obtained by first replacing it with the free cocartesian fibration:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{(\textup{Cat}_{\infty})_{/\mathcal{K}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\textup{coCart}(\mathcal{K})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\textup{LFib}(\mathcal{K})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\dashv}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\dashv}

The dual applies for cartesian fibrations and right fibrations:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{(\textup{Cat}_{\infty})_{/\mathcal{K}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\textup{Cart}(\mathcal{K})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\textup{RFib}(\mathcal{K})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\dashv}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\dashv}

2.1.3.23
.

Suppose we have a left fibration
p:\mathcal{E}\to\mathcal{C}
that represents a presheaf

\mathcal{F}:\mathcal{C}^{\textup{op}}\to\textup{S}

and a map of quasicategories
f:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}
.
Because the postcomposition functor
\Sigma_{f}:(\textup{sSet}_{/\mathcal{C}},\textup{Cov}(\mathcal{C}))\to(\textup{sSet}_{/\mathcal{D}},\textup{Cov}(\mathcal{D}))

is a left Quillen functor and every object in the covariant model structure over
\mathcal{C}
is
cofibrant, the composite map
\Sigma_{f}p=f\circ p:\mathcal{E}\to\mathcal{D}

represents the presheaf
f_{!}\mathcal{F}
.
The map
f\circ p
itself is not a left fibration in general, but by taking
the free left fibration of
f\circ p
we can find a fibrant replacement that
represents the presheaf
f_{!}\mathcal{F}
.

2.1.4
Segal Spaces

Complete Segal spaces are an alternative model for
\infty
-categories
[
Rez01
]
,
which generalises to a model for
(\infty,n)
-categories
[
Bar05
,
Lur08b
]
.

2.1.4.1
.

An order-preserving map of finite non-empty ordinals
\alpha:[t]\to[k]
is
inert

if
\alpha(i)=\alpha(0)+i
for all
i\in[t]
.
We write
\Delta^{\textup{int}}
for the wide subcategory of
\Delta
consisting of the
inert maps, and
\Delta_{\leq 1}
for the full subcategory of
\Delta

that contains
[0]
and
[1]
.
A simplicial space
\mathcal{F}:\Delta^{\textup{op}}\to\textup{S}
is a
Segal space

if for all
k\geq 0
the natural map

\mathcal{F}([k])\longrightarrow\lim(\Delta_{\leq 1}\times_{\Delta}\Delta^{\textup{int}}_{/[k]}\longrightarrow\Delta\xrightarrow{\;\mathcal{F}\;}\textup{S})

is an equivalence of spaces. In other words, for every
k\geq 1
we
have an equivalence

\mathcal{F}([k])\simeq\underbrace{\mathcal{F}([1])\times_{\mathcal{F}([0])}\cdots\times_{\mathcal{F}([0])}\mathcal{F}([1])}_{\text{$k$ times}}

We interpret this property as follows: for every composable sequence
of maps in
\mathcal{F}
, the space of compatible choices of composites
is contractible.
The Segal spaces form a reflective subcategory
\operatorname{Seg}(\Delta)
of
\textup{P}(\Delta)
.

2.1.4.2
.

A Segal space
\mathcal{F}\in\operatorname{Seg}(\Delta)
is
complete
if it
is local for the unique map
E[1]\to\Delta[0]

from the free contractible groupoid with two objects
E[1]
.
Complete Segal spaces are a model of
\infty
-categories:
For every
\infty
-category
\mathcal{C}
we have a presheaf on
\Delta

which sends
[k]
to the space of functors
[k]\to\mathcal{C}
.
This defines a fully faithful functor

\textup{Cat}_{\infty}\hookrightarrow\textup{P}(\Delta)
,
the
\infty
-categorical version of the nerve

\textup{N}:\textup{Cat}\hookrightarrow\textup{sSet}
.
Then a presheaf is in the essential image of the inclusion

\textup{Cat}_{\infty}\hookrightarrow\textup{P}(\Delta)

precisely if it is a complete Segal space.

An
(\infty,n)
-category is an
\omega
-category in which
a
k
-cell must be invertible if
k>n
.
There are multiple equivalent models of
(\infty,n)
-categories.
In particular quasicategories and complete Segal spaces are models of

(\infty,n)
-categories for
n=1
.
For general
n\geq 0
we will present
(\infty,n)
-categories as complete
n
-fold
Segal spaces.

2.1.4.3
.

For any
n\geq 0
we write
\Delta^{n}
for the
n
-fold product of the
category
\Delta
with itself:

\Delta^{n}:=\underbrace{\Delta\times\cdots\times\Delta}_{\text{$n$ times}}

We will sometimes use the following abbreviated notation for objects of
\Delta^{n}
:

[k_{1},\ldots,k_{n}]:=([k_{1}],\ldots,[k_{n}])

A presheaf
\mathcal{F}:\Delta^{n,\textup{op}}\to\textup{S}
is a
n
-uple Segal space

if for all
k_{1},\ldots,k_{n}\geq 0
the natural map

\mathcal{F}([k_{1},\ldots,k_{n}])\longrightarrow\lim(\Delta^{n}_{\leq 1}\times_{\Delta^{n}}\Delta^{\textup{int},n}_{/[k_{1},\ldots,k_{n}]}\longrightarrow\Delta\xrightarrow{\;\mathcal{F}\;}\textup{S})

is an equivalence of spaces.
The
n
-uple Segal spaces form a reflective subcategory
\operatorname{Seg}(\Delta^{n})

of
\textup{P}(\Delta^{n})
.

2.1.4.4
.

An
n
-uple Segal space
\mathcal{F}
is
globular
when

\mathcal{F}([0]):\Delta^{n-1,\textup{op}}\to\textup{S}
is a constant diagram
and
\mathcal{F}([i])
is a globular
(n-1)
-uple Segal space for all
i\geq 0
.
Globular
n
-uple Segal spaces are also called
n
-fold Segal spaces

and form a reflective subcategory
\operatorname{Seg}^{\textup{g}}(\Delta^{n})
of
\textup{P}(\Delta^{n})
.

2.1.4.5
.

An
n
-fold Segal space
\mathcal{F}
is
complete
when the Segal space

\mathcal{F}([-,0,\ldots,0]):\Delta^{\textup{op}}\to\textup{S}
is complete and
the
(n-1)
-fold Segal space
\mathcal{F}([1])
is complete.
The complete
n
-fold Segal spaces form a reflective subcategory of

\textup{P}(\Delta^{n})
which we denote by
\textup{Cat}_{(\infty,n)}
.

2.2
Polynomial Functors

2.2.0.1
.

When
\mathcal{C}
is an
\infty
-category with pullbacks,
every map
f:X\to Y
in
\mathcal{C}
induces a pullback functor

f^{*}:\mathcal{C}_{/Y}\to\mathcal{C}_{/X}
that is right adjoint to the
postcomposition functor
\Sigma_{f}:\mathcal{C}_{/X}\to\mathcal{C}_{/Y}
.
We say that
f
is
exponentiable
when the pullback functor

f^{*}:\mathcal{C}_{/Y}\to\mathcal{C}_{/X}
also has a right adjoint
\Pi_{f}:\mathcal{C}_{/X}\to\mathcal{C}_{/Y}
.
An
\infty
-category
\mathcal{C}
is
locally cartesian closed
when it has pullbacks
and every map in
\mathcal{C}
is exponentiable.

Example 2.2.0.2
.

For every
1
-category
\mathcal{C}
, the
1
-category
\textup{Fun}(\mathcal{C}^{\textup{op}},\textup{Set})

of discrete presheaves on
\mathcal{C}
is locally cartesian closed.
This includes the
1
-category of sets
\textup{Set}\cong\textup{Fun}(*,\textup{Set})
and the
1
-category of simplicial sets
\textup{sSet}\cong\textup{Fun}(\Delta,\textup{Set})
.
Analogously, the
\infty
-category of presheaves
\textup{P}(\mathcal{C})=\textup{Fun}(\mathcal{C}^{\textup{op}},\textup{S})
on any
\infty
-category
\mathcal{C}
is locally cartesian closed, including the
\infty
-category of spaces
S
.

Example 2.2.0.3
.

The
1
-category of categories
Cat
has all pullbacks but is
not
locally cartesian closed.
An exponentiable map in
Cat
is known as a Conduché fibration.
The
\infty
-category
\textup{Cat}_{\infty}
also is
not
locally cartesian closed.
The exponentiable maps in
\textup{Cat}_{\infty}
are called the
exponentiable fibrations

[
AFR20
]
.

Definition 2.2.0.4
.

A
polynomial
in an
\infty
-category
\mathcal{C}
is a diagram in
\mathcal{C}
of the form

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Z}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces W}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces h}

The
polynomial functor
induced by the polynomial is the composite functor

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{C}_{/X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{C}_{/Y}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{C}_{/Z}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{C}_{/W}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Pi_{g}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Sigma_{h}}

provided that
f^{*}
and
\Pi_{g}
exist.

2.2.0.5
.

Suppose that
\mathcal{C}
is an
\infty
-category with a terminal object
*

and products.
Then the slice category of
\mathcal{C}
over the terminal object
\mathcal{C}_{/*}

is equivalent to
\mathcal{C}
itself.
We will be mostly interested in polynomial functors induced by a polynomial of the form

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces*}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces Y}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces*}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces!_{X}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces!_{Y}}

where
!_{X}
and
!_{Y}
are the (essentially) unique maps into the terminal object
and
f
is exponentiable.
In this case we abbreviate
(!_{X})^{*}=(X\times-)
and
\Sigma_{Y}:=\Sigma_{!_{X}}

and write
f[-]:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}
for the induced polynomial functor

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{C}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{C}_{/X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{C}_{/Y}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{C}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X\times-}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Pi_{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Sigma_{Y}}

The theory of polynomial functors for
1
-categories is well-developed
[
GK13
,
Spi20
]
.
For
\infty
-categories the literature is much sparser; we refer to
[
GHK22
]

for the special case of polynomial functors on the
\infty
-category of spaces
S
.
For our purposes we need polynomial functors on
\textup{Cat}_{\infty}
, which we approach via quasicategories
by constructing polynomial functors on the
1
-category
sSet
of simplicial sets.

Lemma 2.2.0.6
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a locally cartesian closed
1
-category with a terminal object
and
f:E\to B
a map in
\mathcal{C}
.
Whenever
A
,
X
are objects in
\mathcal{C}
,
there is a bijection between maps of simplicial sets

\varphi:A\to f[X]

and diagrams of the form

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{E\times_{B}A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{E}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{B}}
{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}

Moreover this bijection is natural in
A
and
X
.

Proof.

The polynomial functor
f[-]:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}
is the composite

f[-]=\Sigma_{B}\circ\Pi_{f}\circ(E\times-)
.
The functor
\Sigma_{B}:{\mathcal{C}}_{/B}\to\mathcal{C}
sends an object

X\to B

of the slice category over
B

to the domain
X
.
Therefore, any map
\varphi:A\to f[X]
induces a map

\alpha:A\to B
so that the diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Sigma_{B}\Pi_{f}(E\times X)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{B}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varphi}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Pi_{f}(E\times X)}

represents a map in the slice category
\mathcal{C}_{/B}
.
The dependent product functor
\Pi_{f}
is the right adjoint of the pullback functor

f^{*}
.
Then the bijection

\textup{sSet}_{/B}((A,\alpha),\Pi_{f}(E\times X))\cong\textup{sSet}_{/E}(f^{*}(A,\alpha),E\times X)

sends
\varphi
to a map
\varphi_{1}
in the slice
category
\mathcal{C}_{/E}
over
E
which fits into the diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{E\times X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{E\times_{B}A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{E}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{B}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{*}\alpha}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varphi_{1}}
{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha}

We then let
\varphi_{2}
be the composite of
\varphi_{1}
with the product projection

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{E\times_{B}A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{E\times X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{X}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varphi_{1}}

Each step in the construction of
\varphi_{2}
from
\varphi
is invertible.
∎

Observation 2.2.0.7
.

Suppose that
\mathcal{C}
is a locally cartesian closed
1
-category with a terminal object
*

and
f:E\to K
a map in
\mathcal{C}
.
By Lemma
2.2.0.6
there is a bijection
natural between maps
A\to f[*]
and diagrams

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{*}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{E\times_{B}A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{E}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{K}}
{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}

(2.3)

Since
*
is the terminal object of
\mathcal{C}
, the map

E\times_{B}A\to*
is uniquely determined.
Therefore the diagram (
2.3
) is uniquely determined
by the map
A\to K
.
It follows that the map
f[*]\to K
is an isomorphism.

2.2.1
Maps of Polynomials

Construction 2.2.1.1
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a locally cartesian closed
1
-category with a terminal object
and suppose that we have a diagram in
\mathcal{C}
of the form

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{E_{0}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{E_{1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{K}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}

(2.4)

Then (
2.4
) induces a natural transformation

g[-]\to f[-]
.
In components, we can construct this natural transformation as follows.
When
A
and
X
are objects of
\mathcal{C}
,
then by Lemma
2.2.0.6
there is a bijection between
maps
A\to g[X]
and diagrams of the form

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{E_{1}\times_{K_{1}}A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{E_{1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{K}}
{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}

(2.5)

Then (
2.5
) fits into the right side of the diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{E_{0}\times_{K}A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{E_{1}\times_{K}A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{E_{0}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{E_{1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{K}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{K}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}

(2.6)

in which the two diagonal squares are pullback squares.
The left hand square then determines a map
A\to f[X]
.

Construction 2.2.1.2
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a locally cartesian closed
1
-category with a terminal object
and suppose that we have a pullback square in
\mathcal{C}
of the form

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{E_{0}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{E_{1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{K_{0}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{K_{1}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}

(2.7)

Then (
2.7
) induces a natural transformation

f[-]\to g[-]

between the polynomial functors so that the component on any object
X\in\mathcal{C}

makes the following diagram commute and into a pullback square:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{f[X]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{g[X]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{K_{0}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{K_{1}}}

In components, this natural transformation is constructed as follows.
When
A
and
X
are objects of
\mathcal{C}
,
then by Lemma
2.2.0.6
there is a bijection between
maps
A\to f[X]
and diagrams of the form

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{E_{0}\times_{K_{0}}A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{E_{0}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{K_{0}}}
{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}

(2.8)

Then (
2.8
) fits into the left side of the diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{E_{0}\times_{K_{0}}A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{E_{1}\times_{K_{1}}A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{E_{0}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{E_{1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{K_{0}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{K_{1}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}

(2.9)

in which the two diagonal squares are pullback squares and the front
square of the cube is the pullback square (
2.7
).
Then the back square of the cube is a pullback as well,
and so the induced map between the pullbacks

E_{0}\times_{K_{0}}A\to E_{1}\times_{K_{1}}A

must be an isomorphism.
Therefore, there exists a unique map
E_{1}\times_{K_{1}}A\to X
which makes the
overall diagram (
2.9
) commute.
Then the right side of (
2.9
) uniquely corresponds to a map

A\to g[C]
.

Construction 2.2.1.3
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a locally cartesian closed
1
-category with a terminal object.
Suppose that we have a commutative diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{E_{0}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{E_{1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{E_{0}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{K_{0}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{K_{1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{K_{0}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{0}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{0}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r}

in
\mathcal{C}
in which the rows compose to the identity.
Then we have natural transformations

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{f_{0}[-]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{f_{1}[-]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{f_{0}[-]}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces I}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces R}

that compose to the identity so that for every object
X\in\mathcal{C}

the following diagram commutes

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{f_{0}[X]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{f_{1}[X]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{f_{0}[X]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{K_{0}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{K_{1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{K_{0}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces I_{X}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces R_{X}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r}

For any
X\in\mathcal{C}
we only describe the component
I_{X}
explicitly;
the component
R_{X}
can be constructed analogously.
By Lemma
2.2.0.6
there is a bijection between maps

A\to f_{0}[X]
and diagrams of the form

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{E_{0}\times_{K_{0}}A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{E_{0}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{K_{0}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varphi}
{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{0}}

(2.10)

Then (
2.10
) fits twice into the induced diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces X}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{E_{0}\times_{K_{0}}A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{E_{1}\times_{K_{1}}A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{E_{0}\times_{K_{0}}A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{E_{0}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{E_{1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{E_{0}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces A}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{K_{0}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{K_{1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{K_{0}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varphi_{0}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varphi_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varphi_{0}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i^{\prime}}

(2.11)

Because
r
is a retraction of
i
it follows that the induced map

E_{1}\times_{K_{1}}A\to E_{0}\to E_{0}\times_{K_{0}}A

is a retraction as well.
Therefore, there is a unique map

\varphi_{1}
which completes the diagram (
2.11
).
By applying Lemma
2.2.0.6
to the middle slice of
(
2.11
) we therefore have a map
A\to f_{1}[X]
.

2.2.2
Composition of Polynomials

Definition 2.2.2.1
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a locally cartesian closed
1
-category
with a terminal object
and
f:E\to K
a map in
\mathcal{C}
.
Then for any object
X\in\mathcal{C}
we define

f_{*}[X]

via the pullback

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{f_{*}[X]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{E}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{f[X]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{K}}
{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}

By letting
X
vary
this defines a functor
f_{*}[-]:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}
together
with a natural transformation

f_{*}[-]\longrightarrow f[-].

Observation 2.2.2.2
.

Suppose that
f:E\to K
is a map in a locally cartesian closed
1
-category
\mathcal{C}

with a terminal object.
When we evaluate the functor
f_{*}[-]:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{C}
on
the terminal object
1
, the result
f_{*}[1]
is defined via the pullback

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{f_{*}[1]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{E}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{f[1]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{K}}
{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}

Since the bottom map
f[1]\to K
is an isomorphism it therefore follows
that also
f_{*}[1]\to E
is an isomorphism.
In particular the pullback square is an isomorphism
in the arrow category of
\mathcal{C}

between
f
and
the map
f_{*}[1]\to f[1]
.

Observation 2.2.2.3
.

Suppose that
f:E\to K
is a map in a locally cartesian closed
1
-category
\mathcal{C}

with a terminal object.
When
X
is an object of
\mathcal{C}
then the projection map

f_{*}[X]\to f[X]

is uniquely characterised via Lemma
2.2.0.6

by a diagram of the form

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{E\times_{K}f[X]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{E}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{f[X]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{K}}
{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}

But by definition we have
f_{*}[X]=E\times_{K}f[X]
.
Therefore, we have a natural map

f_{*}[X]\longrightarrow X

for every object
X
of
\mathcal{C}
.

Lemma 2.2.2.4
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a locally cartesian closed
1
-category
with a terminal object
*

and let
f:E_{0}\to K_{0}
,
g:E_{1}\to K_{1}
a pair of maps in
\mathcal{C}
.
Then the composite functor
X\mapsto g[f[X]]
is again a polynomial
functor which is induced by the map

f_{*}[g[*]]\times_{g[*]}g_{*}[*]\to f[g[*]]

Proof.

We observe that there is a diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{f_{*}[g[*]]\times_{g[*]}g_{*}[*]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{f_{*}[g[*]]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{f[g[*]]]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{g_{*}[*]\times f_{*}[*]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{g[*]\times f_{*}[*]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{g_{*}[*]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{g[*]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{f_{*}[*]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{f[*]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces*}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces*}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces*}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}

in which every square is a pullback square.
We then refer to
[
GK13
, Proposition 1.12]
.
∎

2.2.3
Polynomial Functors of Quasicategories

In general, polynomial functors on
sSet
do not induce polynomial functors
on
\textup{Cat}_{\infty}
. Flat categorical fibrations
[
Lur17
, B.3]
are
the implementation of exponential fibrations in terms of quasicategories.

2.2.3.1
.

An inner fibration
p:{X}\to\Delta[2]
is
flat
if
the induced map
{X}\times_{\Delta[2]}\Lambda^{1}[2]\hookrightarrow{X}

is a categorical equivalence. An inner fibration
p:E\to K
is
flat
if
for every
2
-simplex
\sigma:\Delta[2]\to K
the pullback

\sigma^{*}p:E\times_{K}\Delta[2]\to\Delta[2]
is flat.
Flat inner fibrations are closed under composition, taking opposites,
products, equivalence in the arrow category and pullback along any map of
simplicial sets.

Lemma 2.2.3.2
.

Suppose we have a diagram of simplicial sets

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{X}\times_{\mathcal{Y}}A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{X}\times_{\mathcal{Y}}B}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{X}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{B}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{Y}}}
{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}
{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}

in which both squares are pullback squares,

\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}
is a flat categorical fibration between
quasicategories
and
A\to B
is a categorical equivalence.
Then the map

\mathcal{X}\times_{\mathcal{Y}}A\longrightarrow\mathcal{X}\times_{\mathcal{Y}}B

is a categorical equivalence as well.

Proof.

This is
[
Lur17
, Corollary B.3.15]
.
∎

Lemma 2.2.3.3
.

Let
f:E\to K
be an inner fibration.
Then
f
is flat if and only if for every
2
-simplex
\sigma:\Delta[2]\to K

the map

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\textup{Fun}_{/K}((\Delta[2],\sigma),(E,f))}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\textup{Fun}_{/K}((\Delta[1],\sigma\circ\langle 0,2\rangle),(E,f))}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\langle 0,2\rangle}^{*}}

has weakly contractible fibres.

Proof.

Via
[
Lur17
, Remark B.3.9]
.
∎

Proposition 2.2.3.4
.

Let
f:\mathcal{E}\to\mathcal{B}
be a flat categorical fibration between quasicategories.
Then the polynomial functor
f[-]:\textup{sSet}\to\textup{sSet}
represented by
f
satisfies:

1.

f[-]
preserves categorical fibrations.

2.

f[\mathcal{C}]\to\mathcal{B}
is a categorical fibration for any quasicategory
\mathcal{C}
.

3.

f[-]
preserves quasicategories.

4.

f[-]
preserves categorical equivalences between quasicategories.

Proof.

The polynomial functor
f[-]
is the composite

sSet
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\textup{sSet}_{/\mathcal{E}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\textup{sSet}_{/\mathcal{B}}}}
sSet
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathcal{E}^{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Pi_{f}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Sigma_{\mathcal{B}}}

We equip
sSet
with the Joyal model structure and the slice categories

\textup{sSet}_{/\mathcal{E}}
and
\textup{sSet}_{/\mathcal{B}}
with the slice model structures
over the Joyal model structure.
The product functor
(\mathcal{E}\times-)
is a right Quillen functor because
\mathcal{E}
is a quasicategory and therefore fibrant.
Because
f
is a flat categorical fibration, the dependent product functor

\Pi_{f}

is a right Quillen functor by
[
Lur17
, Proposition B.4.5]
.
Therefore, the composite
\Pi_{f}\circ\mathcal{E}^{*}
is also a right Quillen functor.

Let
p:X\to Y
be a categorical fibration.
Right Quillen functors preserve fibrations, and so

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{f[X]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{f[Y]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{B}}}

is a fibration in the slice model structure
\textup{sSet}_{/\mathcal{B}}
,
and so by definition of the slice model structure
f[X]\to f[Y]

is a categorical fibration.
Let
\mathcal{C}
be a quasicategory then
\mathcal{C}\to*
is a categorical fibration,
and so
f[\mathcal{C}]\to f[*]\cong\mathcal{B}
is a categorical fibration as well.
Moreover since
\mathcal{B}
is assumed to be a quasicategory, it follows that
f[\mathcal{C}]
is also a quasicategory.

Let
\varphi:\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{D}
be a categorical equivalence between quasicategories.
By Ken Brown’s Lemma the right Quillen functor
\Pi_{f}\circ\mathcal{E}^{*}
preserves weak
equivalences between fibrant objects, and so
\varphi
induces a weak equivalence

f[\mathcal{C}]\to f[\mathcal{D}]
over
\mathcal{B}
.
∎

Lemma 2.2.3.5
.

Suppose that we have a pullback square of quasicategories

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{E}_{0}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{E}_{1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{B}_{0}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{B}_{1}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{0}}
{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varphi}

We suppose further that both
f_{0}
and
f_{1}
are flat categorical fibrations
and that
\varphi
is a categorical equivalence.
Then for every quasicategory
\mathcal{C}
the induced map

f_{0}[\mathcal{C}]\longrightarrow f_{1}[\mathcal{C}]

from Construction
2.2.1.2
is a categorical equivalence.

Proof.

The map fits into a pullback square

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{f_{0}[\mathcal{C}]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{f_{1}[\mathcal{C}]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{B}_{0}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{B}_{1}}}
{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varphi}

The vertical maps are categorical fibrations by Proposition
2.2.3.4

and therefore the square is a homotopy pullback.
Because
\varphi
is a categorical equivalence it then follows that also

f_{0}[\mathcal{C}]\to f_{1}[\mathcal{C}]
is a categorical equivalence.
∎

Lemma 2.2.3.6
.

Suppose that we have a commutative square of quasicategories

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{E}_{0}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{E}_{1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{E}_{0}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{B}_{0}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{B}_{1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{B}_{0}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{0}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{0}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces i}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces r}

such that the rows compose to the identity.
We suppose further that both
f_{0}
and
f_{1}
are flat categorical fibrations
and that
i
,
i^{\prime}
are categorical equivalences.
Then for every quasicategory
\mathcal{C}
the components

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{f_{0}[\mathcal{C}]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{f_{1}[\mathcal{C}]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{f_{0}[\mathcal{C}]}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces I_{\mathcal{C}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces R_{\mathcal{C}}}

of the natural transformations from Construction
2.2.1.3
are categorical equivalences.

2.3
Geometry

2.3.1
Topology and Simplices

2.3.1.1
.

By
topological space
we will generally mean a
\Delta
-generated topological
space
[
Dug03
,
FR08
]
. Topological
spaces and continuous maps then organise into a
1
-category

Top
that is cartesian closed and presentable.

2.3.1.2
.

The
topological
n
-simplex

{|\Delta[n]|}
is the subspace

{|\Delta[n]|}:=\{(x_{0},\ldots,x_{n})\mid x_{0}+\cdots+x_{n}=1\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+1}.

This convention is referred to as
barycentric coordinates
.
The topological simplices organise into a cosimplicial object

{|\Delta[\bullet]|}:\Delta\to\textup{Top}
. Since
Top
is cocomplete,
we then have an induced nerve/realisation adjunction

|-|:\textup{sSet}\rightleftarrows\textup{Top}:\operatorname{Sing}.

2.3.1.3
.

A
triangulation
of a topological space
X
consists of a poset

P
together with an isomorphism of topological spaces
|P|\cong X
.
A topological space
X
is
triangulable
if there exists a triangulation
of
X
. A triangulation
|P|\cong X
is
finite
when
P
is a
finite poset, and
locally finite
as long as
P_{/p}
is finite for all
p\in P
.
A triangulable space is compact if and only if it admits a finite triangulation;
it is locally compact if and only if it has a locally finite triangulation.

Remark 2.3.1.4
.

Triangulations are usually defined in terms of simplicial complexes.
A simplicial complex is a pair
(V,S)
consisting of a set
V
and a
set
S
of non-empty subsets of
V
which together satisfy the following
conditions:

1.

When
\sigma\in S
and
\tau\subseteq\sigma
then
\tau\in S
.

2.

When
v\in V
then
\{v\}\in S
.

Elements of
V
and
S
are referred to as
vertices
and
simplices
.
Then in particular
S
is a poset when ordered by set inclusion.
The geometric realisation of the simplicial complex
(V,S)
as commonly
defined is isomorphic to
|S|
.
Conversely, for every poset
P
the
flag complex
of
P
is the simplicial
complex whose vertices are the elements of
P
and whose simplices are
the images of any injective monotone map
[n]\to P
for any
n\geq 0
.
Then the geometric realisation of the flag complex of
P
is isomorphic to
|P|
.

We will use finiteness of triangulations to ensure tameness of topological spaces.
In order for the notion of tameness to also allow for some non-compact topological spaces,
we will use finite relative triangulations.

Definition 2.3.1.5
.

A
relative triangulation
of a topological space
X
consists of a poset

P
and a downwards closed subposet
P_{0}\subseteq P
such that
X
is isomorphic
to
|P|\setminus|P_{0}|
. The relative triangulation is
finite

when
P
is finite.

2.3.2
Stratified Spaces

Stratified spaces are topological spaces that are composed out of distinguished parts,
which are called the strata.
For example, a simplicial complex or CW complex is a stratified space whose strata are the interiors of the simplices or cells, respectively.
Stratified spaces are also commonly used for spaces with singularities, such as algebraic varieties or pseudomanifolds.
We use stratified spaces to define manifold diagrams.
There is substantial literature on stratified spaces, especially in the smooth case.
However, the field is sufficiently fragmented that there is no standard notion
which we can assume to be known or agreed upon.
We therefore give a quick overview over the type of stratified space that we will
use throughout this thesis.
The ideas in this section are due to
[
Nan
,
DW22
,
Lur17
,
Waa24
]
.

2.3.2.1
.

The
Alexandroff topology
on a poset is the topology
the underlying set of
P
in which a subset
U\subseteq P
is open
exactly if it is upwards closed, i.e. if for every
x\in U
and
x\leq y

also
y\in P
.
By sending a poset to the topological space with the Alexandroff topology,
we obtain a fully faithful functor
\textup{Alex}:\textup{Pos}\hookrightarrow\textup{Top}
.

2.3.2.2
.

A
pre-stratified space

{X}
is a topological space
X
together with a poset

\cramped{\mathbb{P}}({{X}})
and a continuous map
\cramped{\mathbb{s}}({{X}}):X\to\cramped{\mathbb{P}}({{X}})
.
For any
p\in\cramped{\mathbb{P}}({{X}})
we denote by
{X}_{p}:=\cramped{\mathbb{s}}({{X}})^{-1}(p)

the
stratum
of
{X}
over
p
.
The category of pre-stratified spaces is the comma category
\textup{Top}/\textup{Alex}

for the inclusion functor
\textup{Alex}:\textup{Pos}\hookrightarrow\textup{Top}
which equips a poset with its Alexandroff topology.

2.3.2.3
.

The
stratified
n
-simplex

\|\Delta[n]\|
is the topological
n
-simplex

{|\Delta[n]|}=\{(x_{0},\ldots,x_{n})\mid x_{0}+\cdots+x_{n}=1\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n+1}

presented in barycentric coordinates such that
\cramped{\mathbb{P}}({\|\Delta[n]\|}):=[n]
and

\cramped{\mathbb{s}}({\|\Delta[n]\|})(x):=\max\{i\in[n]\mid x_{i}>0\}.

A map
\gamma:\|\Delta[1]\|\to{X}
of pre-stratified spaces is called
an
exit path
in
{X}
.

0
1

0
1
2

Figure 2.1
:
The stratified standard simplices
\|\Delta[1]\|
and
\|\Delta[2]\|
.

2.3.2.4
.

A pre-stratified space
{X}

carries the
\Delta_{s}
-topology

when its underlying topological space
\operatorname{U}({X})
has the final
topology with respect to all stratified maps
\|\Delta[k]\|\to{X}

for all
k\geq 0
.
A pre-stratified space
{X}
is
surjectively stratified
when
the map
\cramped{\mathbb{s}}({{X}}):X\to\cramped{\mathbb{P}}({{X}})
surjective.
In other words,
{X}
is surjectively stratified when its strata are non-empty.
A
stratified space
is a pre-stratified space
{X}
that carries
the
\Delta_{s}
-topology, is surjectively stratified and satisfies the following
condition:
Whenever
x_{0},x_{1}\in{X}
satisfy

\cramped{\mathbb{s}}({{X}})(x_{0})\leq\cramped{\mathbb{s}}({{X}})(x_{1})
then there exists a sequence
of exit paths
\gamma_{0},\ldots,\gamma_{k}:\|\Delta[1]\|\to{X}
such that

\gamma_{0}(0)=x_{0}
,
\gamma_{k}(1)=x_{1}
and
\gamma_{i-1}(1)=\gamma_{i}(0)
for all

1\leq i\leq k
.

2.3.2.5
.

The category of stratified spaces
Strat
is the full subcategory of
\textup{Top}/\textup{Alex}
.
We write
\operatorname{U}(-):\textup{Strat}\to\textup{Top}
for the functor which forgets the stratification and sends a stratified space to its
underlying topological space
.
The category
Strat
is a coreflective subcategory of the comma category

\textup{Top}/\textup{Alex}
, i.e. the inclusion functor

\textup{Strat}\hookrightarrow\textup{Top}\downarrow\textup{Alex}

has a right adjoint.
In particular
Strat
is presentable, complete and cocomplete.

2.3.2.6
.

Let
f:{X}\to{Y}
be a map of stratified spaces.

1.

The map
f
is a
refinement map
when its underlying map
of topological spaces
\operatorname{U}(f):\operatorname{U}({X})\to\operatorname{U}({Y})

is an isomorphism and
\cramped{\mathbb{P}}({f}):\cramped{\mathbb{P}}({{X}})\to\cramped{\mathbb{P}}({{Y}})

is surjective. In this case we say that
{X}
is a
refinement

of
{Y}
or, equivalently, that
{Y}
is a
coarsening
of
{X}
.

2.

The map
f
is
open
when
\operatorname{U}(f):\operatorname{U}({X})\to\operatorname{U}({Y})
is an open embedding of topological spaces and
f
restricts to a refinement map onto its image.

3.

The map
f
is a
constructible embedding
when its map on posets

\cramped{\mathbb{P}}({f}):\cramped{\mathbb{P}}({{X}})\to\cramped{\mathbb{P}}({{Y}})
is injective and there is a pullback
square of topological spaces

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{X}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{Y}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\cramped{\mathbb{P}}({{X}})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\cramped{\mathbb{P}}({{Y}})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cramped{\mathbb{s}}({{X}})}
{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cramped{\mathbb{s}}({{Y}})}

In this situation we say that
{X}
is a
constructible subspace

of
{Y}
.

2.3.2.7
.

The stratified
n
-simplices define a cosimplicial object

\|\Delta[-]\|:\Delta\to\textup{Strat}.

Since
Strat
is cocomplete, we have an induced nerve/realisation adjunction

\|-\|:\textup{sSet}\rightleftarrows\textup{Strat}:\textup{Exit}

The functor
\|-\|:\textup{Strat}\to\textup{sSet}
preserves finite products.

2.3.2.8
.

For every poset
P
, interpreted as a simplicial set via its nerve, we have
a stratified space
\|P\|
. The underlying unstratified space of

\|P\|
is the geometric realisation
|P|
. The stratified
space
\|P\|
is glued together via a colimit in
Strat
from stratified simplices
\|\Delta[k]\|

for each flag of
P
given by an injective map
\Delta[k]\hookrightarrow P
.
A
triangulation
of a stratified space
{X}
is a poset
S

together with a refinement map
\|S\|\to{X}
.
A stratified space
{X}
is
triangulable
when it admits
a triangulation.

2.3.2.9
.

Concretely, the functor
Exit
sends a stratified space
{X}
to the
simplicial set
\textup{Exit}({X})
whose
k
-simplices are the maps of stratified
spaces
\|\Delta[k]\|\to{X}
.
We say that the stratified space
{X}
is
fibrant
if the simplicial set

\textup{Exit}({X})
is a quasicategory; in this case
\textup{Exit}({X})
represents
the
\infty
-category of exit paths
in
{X}
.
A map
f:{X}\to{Y}
of stratified spaces is a
stratified weak equivalence

when the induced map
\textup{Exit}(f):\textup{Exit}({X})\to\textup{Exit}({Y})
is a categorical equivalence.
The unit
\eta_{X}:X\to\textup{Exit}(\|X\|)
of the adjunction
\|-\|\dashv\textup{Exit}
is a monomorphism and a categorical
equivalence. In particular
\eta_{X}
is an acyclic cofibration in the Joyal
model structure.

Remark 2.3.2.10
.

The terminology appears to imply that we could equip
Strat
with a model structure.
Unfortunately this is not possible
[
Nan
]
.
More recently it has been shown that
Strat
admits a left semi-model structure
[
Waa24
]
,
but we will not need this result here.
The localisation of
Strat
at the stratified weak equivalences is a reflective

\infty
-subcategory of
\textup{Cat}_{\infty}
consisting of layered
\infty
-categories:
An
\infty
-category
\mathcal{C}
is
layered
when every endomorphism is an automorphism.
Equivalently
\mathcal{C}
is layered when there exists a poset
P
and a conservative functor

\mathcal{C}\to P
.

2.3.2.11
.

A stratified space
{X}
satisfies the
frontier condition
when for
each
p\leq q
in
\cramped{\mathbb{P}}({{X}})
the stratum
{X}_{p}
is contained
within the closure of
{X}_{q}
within
{X}
.
Equivalently, a stratified space
{X}
satisfies the frontier condition
when for every pair of points
x_{0},x_{1}\in{X}
with
\cramped{\mathbb{P}}({{X}})(x_{0})\leq\cramped{\mathbb{P}}({{X}})(x_{1})
there exists an exit path
\gamma:\|\Delta[1]\|\to{X}
with

\gamma(0)=0
and
\gamma(1)=1
.
Every fibrant stratified space satisfies the frontier condition.

2.3.2.12
.

Let
{L}
be a compact and Hausdorff stratified space.
The
stratified cone

\textup{c}{L}
is the pushout of stratified spaces

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\{0\}\times{L}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{*}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\|\Delta[1]\|\times{L}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\textup{c}{L}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}

In particular the base poset of
\cramped{\mathbb{P}}({\textup{c}{L}})

is the left cone

\cramped{\mathbb{P}}({{L}})^{\triangleleft}
, i.e. the union of
\cramped{\mathbb{P}}({{L}})

with an additional minimal element
\bot
.
A stratified space
{X}
is
conical
if for every point
x\in{X}

with
p=\cramped{\mathbb{s}}({{X}})(x)

there exists an open neighbourhood
{U}
of
x
in
{X}
,
an open neighbourhood
V
of
x
in its stratum
{X}_{p}
and a compact
Hausdorff stratified space
{L}
so that
{U}
is isomorphic as a stratified
space to
\textup{c}{L}\times V
.
Every conical stratified space is fibrant.
For every poset
P
the stratified geometric realisation
\|P\|
is conical,
and so in particular
\|P\|
is fibrant.

Remark 2.3.2.13
.

The stratified cone
\textup{c}{L}
can be defined for any stratified space
{L}

via the teardrop topology (see for instance
[
Lur17
, Definition A.5.3]
).
When
{L}
is compact and Hausdorff the general definition agrees with the pushout.

We will make use of an alternative characterisation of triangulations for
stratified spaces.

2.3.2.14
.

Let
T
be a subset of the maps of
\Delta[k]
which includes all the degenerate
maps so that
(\Delta[k],T)
is a marked simplicial set. Denote by

\pi:[k]\to P
the quotient of the poset
[k]
which identifies

i,j\in[k]
when the map
i\to j
is contained within
T
.
We then let
\|\Delta[k],T\|^{+}
be the stratification of

{|\Delta[k]|}
over the poset
P
with stratifying map

\cramped{\mathbb{s}}({\|\Delta[k],T\|^{+}}):=\pi\circ\cramped{\mathbb{s}}({\|\Delta[k]\|}).

This defines a nerve/realisation adjunction

\|-\|^{+}:\textup{sSet}^{+}\rightleftarrows\textup{Strat}:\textup{Exit}^{+}

A stratified space
{X}
is triangulable if and only if there exists a
marked poset
P
together with an isomorphism of stratified spaces

\|P\|^{+}\cong{X}
.
For every marked poset
P
the unit
\eta_{S}:S\to\textup{Exit}^{+}(\|S\|^{+})

of the adjunction
\|-\|^{+}\dashv\textup{Exit}^{+}
is a marked equivalence.

Remark 2.3.2.15
.

Presenting triangulable stratified spaces via marked simplicial sets is unusual.
A more common approach defines a combinatorial analogue of
Strat
via the
comma category of
sSet
over the inclusion
\textup{Pos}\hookrightarrow\textup{sSet}
.
We haven chosen to use marked simplicial sets instead for additional flexibility.
Concretely we make use of a map of marked simplicial sets
S\to\mathcal{C}^{\natural}

from a marked poset
S
to a quasicategory with natural marking
\mathcal{C}^{\natural}
,
which can not be expressed in
\textup{sSet}/\textup{Pos}
in general.

2.3.2.16
.

A map of stratified spaces
p:{E}\to{B}
is a
(stratified) trivial bundle

when there exists a stratified space
{F}
such that
p
is isomorphic over
{B}

to the projection map
{F}\times{B}\to{B}
.
A map of stratified spaces
p:{E}\to{B}
is a

stratified fibre bundle
if for every point
b\in{B}

with
i=\cramped{\mathbb{s}}({{B}})(b)

there exists an open neighbourhood
U\subseteq{B}_{i}
within
the stratum that contains
b
such that
p
restricts to a stratified trivial
bundle
{E}\times_{{B}}U\to U
.

2.3.2.17
.

Let
p:{X}\to{Y}
be a stratified fibre bundle such that
the induced map of simplicial sets
\textup{Exit}(p)
is an inner fibration.
Then
\textup{Exit}(p)
is an isofibration.

2.3.3
PL Stratified Pseudomanifolds

Definition 2.3.3.1
.

A stratified space
{X}
is a
PL stratified pseudomanifold

if
\operatorname{U}({X})
is piecewise linear and
for every
x\in{X}
there exists a compact PL stratified pseudomanifold
{L}
, called the
link
, and a PL stratified embedding

u:\mathbb{R}^{i}\times\textup{c}{L}\hookrightarrow{X}

such that
u(0,*)=x
.

Remark 2.3.3.2
.

The definition of a PL stratified pseudomanifold appears circular but is recursive:
The link
{L}
at some point of a PL stratified pseudomanifold
{X}

has fewer strata than
{X}
.
Our definition differs slightly from the variants typically found in the literature:

1.

PL stratified pseudomanifolds are most often defined via a filtration
instead of a stratification. With stratifications defined as above,
this makes no difference.

2.

The literature concentrates on PL stratified
n
-pseudomanfolds
{X}
for
some
n\geq 0
, which are restricted to contain only strata of dimension up to
n

so that the
n
-dimensional strata in
{X}
form a dense subspace.

3.

In some sources it is typical to assume that a stratified PL
n
-pseudomanifold
has no strata of dimension
n-1
. This is due to technical difficulties that
arise in intersection homology if such strata were allowed.
We do not use intersection homology and so this restriction does not make sense for our purposes.

Observation 2.3.3.3
.

Suppose that
{X}
is a PL stratified pseudomanifold.
Then each stratum of
{X}
is a connected PL manifold.
Since
{X}
is locally conical it is fibrant.
Moreover
{X}
satisfies the frontier condition.

Proposition 2.3.3.4
.

Let
{X}
be a stratified space that admits a locally
finite triangulation and let

A=(A_{i}\mid i\in I)
be a locally
finite family of closed PL subspaces of
\operatorname{U}({X})
.
Then there exists a coarsest refinement

{Y}\to{X}

such that
{Y}
is a PL stratified pseudomanifold
and
A_{i}
is a union of strata in
{Y}
for each
i\in I
.

Proof.

This follows from the theory of intrinsic dimension developed in
[
Arm67
]
.
Concretely we can construct
{Y}
as follows.
We say that a triangulation of
{X}
is adapted to the family
A
when
each
A_{i}
is a subcomplex of the triangulation.
The intrinsic dimension
\textup{dim}(x)
of a point
x\in{X}
is the largest
k\geq 0
such that there exists an triangulation of
{X}
adapted to
A

for which
x
is within the interior of a
k
-simplex.
Then
\textup{dim}:\operatorname{U}({X})\to\mathbb{N}^{\textup{op}}
defines a pre-stratification
which induces the desired stratification
{Y}
by splitting the strata into path-connected components.
∎

Observation 2.3.3.5
.

The coarsest stratification is determined locally
since the intrinsic dimension is a local property.
In the situation of Proposition
2.3.3.4

suppose that
{U}\subseteq{X}
is an open PL subspace.
Then the coarsest PL stratified pseudomanifold that refines
{U}

and is adapted to

A_{i}\cap{U}
for all
i\in I

agrees with
{Y}\cap{U}
.

Lemma 2.3.3.6
.

Let
{X},{Y}
be stratified spaces
with locally finite stratifications
that satisfy the frontier condition,
and let
f:\operatorname{U}({X})\to\operatorname{U}({Y})
be a map of the underlying topological spaces.
Then
f
respects the stratification if and only if

f^{-1}(\textup{cl}({Y}_{p}))
is a union of strata
for all
p\in\cramped{\mathbb{P}}({{Y}})
.

Proof.

Because
{X}
satisfies the frontier condition,
there is an order-preserving isomorphism between
the closed sets in
\cramped{\mathbb{P}}({{X}})

and the closed subsets of
X
which are unions of strata.
The same holds for
{Y}
as well.
Because
\cramped{\mathbb{P}}({{X}})
,
\cramped{\mathbb{P}}({{Y}})

are locally finite, they are sober.
But then the claim follows since a map between the posets
is the same as a frame map.
∎

Lemma 2.3.3.7
.

Let
{A}
,
{X}
be stratified spaces that
both satisfy the frontier condition and admit locally finite
triangulations.
Suppose further that
f:\operatorname{U}({A})\to\operatorname{U}({X})
a PL map between the underlying topological spaces
such that the fibres of
f
intersect finitely many strata.
Then there exists a coarsest refinement
{B}\to{A}

such that
f
becomes a stratified map
{B}\to{X}

and
{B}
is a PL stratified pseudomanifold.

Proof.

By Lemma
2.3.3.6
a refinement

{B}\to{A}
makes
f
into a stratified map

{B}\to{X}
if and only
if for each
p\in\cramped{\mathbb{P}}({X})
the preimage

f^{-1}(\textup{cl}({X}_{p}))
is a union of strata in
{B}
.
But then the claim follows by Proposition
2.3.3.4
.
∎

2.3.4
Open Mapping Cylinders

The mapping cylinder of a map of topological spaces is a common construction
in algebraic topology. For stratified spaces, there are multiple versions
of this construction, one of which is the open mapping cylinder
[
AFR17
]
.

Construction 2.3.4.1
.

Suppose that
{X}_{\bullet}:[k]\to\textup{Strat}
is a sequence of
open maps of stratified spaces
f_{i}:{X}_{i-1}\to{X}_{i}

for
1\leq i\leq k
.
Then the
k
-fold open mapping cylinder

\cramped{\textup{Cyl}}_{\textup{o}}({X}_{\bullet})

is the stratified space obtained as the quotient of the disjoint union

\coprod_{i\in[k]}{X}_{i}\times\|\Delta[k]\|_{\geq i}

by the smallest equivalence relation
\sim
such that

(x,b)\sim(f_{i}(x),b)
whenever
1\leq i\leq k
,
x\in{X}_{i-1}

and
b\in\|\Delta[k]\|_{\geq i}
.
There is a natural projection map

\cramped{\textup{Cyl}}_{\textup{o}}({X}_{\bullet})\longrightarrow\|\Delta[k]\|

so that the
k
-fold open mapping cylinder defines a functor

\cramped{\textup{Cyl}}_{\textup{o}}^{k}(-):\textup{Fun}(\Delta[k],\textup{Strat})\longrightarrow\textup{Strat}_{/\|\Delta[k]\|}

Observation 2.3.4.2
.

For any order-preserving map
[k]\to[s]
, the
k
-fold and
s
-fold
open mapping cylinder functors are compatible with the pullback of maps
of stratified spaces:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\textup{Fun}(\Delta[s],\textup{Strat})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\textup{Strat}_{/\Delta[s]}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\textup{Fun}(\Delta[k],\textup{Strat})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\textup{Strat}_{/\Delta[k]}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cramped{\textup{Cyl}}_{\textup{o}}^{s}(-)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cramped{\textup{Cyl}}_{\textup{o}}^{k}(-)}

Observation 2.3.4.3
.

Suppose that
{X}_{\bullet}:[k]\to\textup{Strat}
is a sequence of
open maps of stratified spaces. Then the inclusion map
{X}_{k}\to\cramped{\textup{Cyl}}_{\textup{o}}({X}_{\bullet})

has a retraction.

Lemma 2.3.4.4
.

Suppose that we have a diagram of stratified spaces

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{{X}_{0}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{{X}_{1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\cdots}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{{X}_{k-1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{{X}_{k}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{{B}_{0}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{{B}_{1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\cdots}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{{B}_{k-1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{{B}_{k}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varphi_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{0}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varphi_{k}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{k-1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{k}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\psi_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\psi_{k}}

such that each
\textup{Exit}(f_{i})
is an isofibration
and the rows consist of open maps of stratified spaces.
Let
\pi:\cramped{\textup{Cyl}}_{\textup{o}}^{k}({X}_{\bullet})\to\cramped{\textup{Cyl}}_{\textup{o}}^{k}({B}_{\bullet})
be the induced map between
the
k
-fold open mapping cylinders of the rows.
Then
\textup{Exit}(\pi)
is an isofibration.

Proof.

Suppose that we have a lifting problem of the form

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\|\Lambda^{i}[k]\|}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\cramped{\textup{Cyl}}_{\textup{o}}^{k}({X}_{\bullet})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\|\Delta[k]\|}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\cramped{\textup{Cyl}}_{\textup{o}}^{k}({Y}_{\bullet})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sigma^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\pi}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tau}

for some
0<i<k
.
By induction on
k\geq 0
we can reduce to the case that
\sigma^{\prime}(k)

is contained within the image of
{X}_{k}\times\|\Delta[k]\|_{\geq k}\to\cramped{\textup{Cyl}}_{\textup{o}}^{k}({X}_{\bullet})
.
Since
\textup{Exit}(f_{k})
is an isofibration, we then have a solution to the lifting problem

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\|\Lambda^{i}[k]\|}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\cramped{\textup{Cyl}}_{\textup{o}}({X}_{\bullet})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{{X}_{k}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\|\Delta[k]\|}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\cramped{\textup{Cyl}}_{\textup{o}}({B}_{\bullet})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{{B}_{k}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sigma^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f_{k}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tau}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\rho}

We then define an extension
\sigma:\|\Delta[k]\|\to\cramped{\textup{Cyl}}_{\textup{o}}^{k}({X}_{\bullet})

of
\sigma^{\prime}
by letting
\sigma(b):=[\rho(b),\tau(b)]
for all

b\in\|\Delta[k]\|\setminus\|\Lambda^{i}[k]\|
.
This defines a solution to our original lifting problem.
∎

Lemma 2.3.4.5
.

Suppose that
\varphi:{X}\to{Y}
is an open map of stratified spaces
such that
{Y}
is fibrant.
Let
\pi:\cramped{\textup{Cyl}}_{\textup{o}}(\varphi)\to\|\Delta[1]\|
be the projection map
from the open mapping cylinder and let
\gamma:\|\Delta[1]\|\to\cramped{\textup{Cyl}}_{\textup{o}}(\varphi)
be a section of
\pi

such that
\textup{Exit}(\cramped{\textup{Cyl}}_{\textup{o}}(\varphi))\to\textup{Exit}({Y})
sends
\gamma

to an equivalence.
Then
\gamma
is
\textup{Exit}(\pi)
-cocartesian.

Proof.

Suppose that we have a lifting problem

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\|\Delta[1]\|}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\|\Lambda^{0}[k]\|}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\cramped{\textup{Cyl}}_{\textup{o}}(\varphi)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\|\Delta[k]\|}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\|\Delta[1]\|}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\langle 0,1\rangle}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\gamma}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sigma^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\tau}

We then obtain an induced lifting problem

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\|\Lambda^{i}[k]\|}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\cramped{\textup{Cyl}}_{\textup{o}}(\varphi)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{{Y}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\|\Delta[k]\|}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\sigma^{\prime}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\rho}

which has a solution because
{Y}
is fibrant.
We then define an extension
\sigma:\|\Delta[k]\|\to\cramped{\textup{Cyl}}_{\textup{o}}(\varphi)

of
\sigma^{\prime}
by letting
\sigma(b):=[\rho(b),\tau(b)]
for all

b\in\|\Delta[k]\|\setminus\|\Lambda^{i}[k]\|
.
This defines a solution to our original lifting problem.
∎

Lemma 2.3.4.6
.

Suppose that
\varphi:{X}\to{Y}
is an open map of fibrant stratified spaces. Let
\pi:\cramped{\textup{Cyl}}_{\textup{o}}(\varphi)\to\|\Delta[1]\|
be the projection map
from the open mapping cylinder. Then
\textup{Exit}(\pi)
is a cocartesian fibration.

Proof.

By Lemma
2.3.4.4
the map
\textup{Exit}(\pi)
is an isofibration.
To show that
\textup{Exit}(\pi)
is cocartesian, it suffices to show that the identity
exit path
\textup{id}:\|\Delta[1]\|\to\|\Delta[1]\|
has an
\textup{Exit}(\pi)
-cocartesian
lift starting at any
x\in{X}
.
We let
\gamma:\|\Delta[1]\|\to\cramped{\textup{Cyl}}_{\textup{o}}(\varphi)
be the map defined by

\gamma(t)=[x,t]
, then
\gamma
is
\textup{Exit}(\pi)
-cocartesian by Lemma
2.3.4.5
.
∎

Chapter 3
Framed Combinatorial Topology

3.1
Framed Stratified Spaces and Bundles

We study stratifications that are embedded into Euclidean space.
In particular, we are interested in the relative arrangement of the strata.
For this purpose we equip a stratified space
{X}
with an
n
-framing, which is an embedding of
the underlying topological space
\operatorname{U}({X})
into
\mathbb{R}^{n}
, and allow only those
transformations that preserve the projections.
This allows us to detect and give algebraic significance to the changes in relative arrangement of strata, which will be useful for our theory of manifold diagrams.

Definition 3.1.0.1
.

For every
0\leq m\leq n
there is a projection map

\mathbb{R}^{n}\cong\mathbb{R}^{n-m}\times\mathbb{R}^{m}\to\mathbb{R}^{m}

onto the last
m
coordinates in the Euclidean standard basis.
We will denote this map by
\pi^{m}
assuming that
n
will be clear from the context.
For any
0\leq m\leq n
we define an equivalence relation
\sim_{m}
on
\mathbb{R}^{n}

so that
x\sim_{m}y
for
x,y\in\mathbb{R}^{n}
whenever
\pi^{m}(x)=\pi^{m}(y)
.

Definition 3.1.0.2
.

An
n
-framed stratified space is a stratified space
{X}
together
with a continuous embedding of the underlying topological space

\operatorname{fr}({X}):\operatorname{U}({X})\hookrightarrow\mathbb{R}^{n}
.
A map of
n
-framed stratified spaces
\varphi:{X}\to{Y}

is a map of stratified spaces such that for all
0\leq m\leq n
and
elements
x_{1},x_{2}\in{X}
we have

\operatorname{fr}({X})(x_{1})\sim_{m}\operatorname{fr}({X})(x_{2})\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\operatorname{fr}({Y})(\varphi(x_{1}))\sim_{m}\operatorname{fr}({Y})(\varphi(x_{2}))

The
n
-framed stratified spaces and their maps form a
1
-category

\textup{FrStrat}^{n}
.

In
2
-dimensional diagrams we adopt the convention that, unless specified
otherwise, the first coordinate axis goes from left to right on the page
while the second coordinate axis goes from bottom to top.
This is consistent with a common convention on how to draw string diagrams.

.

Suppose we have a stratification
{X}
of the plane
\mathbb{R}^{2}
with two
0
-strata:

-strata,

Definition 3.1.0.5
.

An
n
-framed stratified bundle
is a map

f:{E}\to{B}

of stratified spaces
together with a continuous embedding

\operatorname{fr}(f):\operatorname{U}({E})\hookrightarrow\mathbb{R}^{n}\times\operatorname{U}({B})
over
\operatorname{U}({B})
.
A map of
n
-framed stratified bundles
f
and
g
is a diagram
of stratified spaces

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{E}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{D}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{B}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varphi}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces g}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\psi}

such that for every point
b\in{B}
the map on fibres

{E}\times_{{B}}\{b\}\to{D}\times_{{A}}\{\psi(b)\}

is a map of
n
-framed stratified spaces with the induced framing.
The
n
-framed bundles and their maps form a
1
-category
\textup{FrBun}^{n}
.

Observation 3.1.0.6
.

We have a fully faithful inclusion functor
\textup{FrStrat}^{n}\hookrightarrow\textup{FrBun}^{n}

which sends an
n
-framed stratified space
{X}
to the
n
-framed
stratified bundle
{X}\to\|\Delta[0]\|
.

Construction 3.1.0.7
.

Suppose that
f:{E}\to{B}
is an
n
-framed stratified bundle
and
\psi:{A}\to{B}
a map of stratified spaces.
When

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{{A}\times_{{B}}{E}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{{E}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{{A}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{{B}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varphi}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\psi^{*}f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\psi}

is the pullback in
Strat
, we can equip
\psi^{*}f
with a canonical framing

\operatorname{fr}(\psi^{*}f)
induced by
\operatorname{fr}(f)
.
This is a cartesian lift for the functor
\textup{FrBun}^{n}\to\textup{Strat}
which sends
an
n
-framed stratified bundle
\varphi:{E}\to{B}
to the
stratified base space
{B}
.

Remark 3.1.0.8
.

Typically, constructions based on bundles and pullback run into coherence issues, with pullbacks only being defined up to isomorphism.
Via the framing of an
n
-framed bundle

f:{E}\to{B}
we can canonically treat
the underlying space
\operatorname{U}({E})

as a subspace of
\mathbb{R}^{n}\times\operatorname{U}({B})
.
We can also present the set of elements of the poset
\cramped{\mathbb{P}}({{E}})

of strata as a quotient of the points
\operatorname{U}({E})
.
This provides a canonical representative for every isomorphism class and thus a functorial strictification.
We will use this trick implicitly for any constructions based on framed stratified bundles that we will define below.

Definition 3.1.0.9
.

An
n
-framed stratified bundle
f:{E}\to{B}
is a
submersion

when for every point
x\in{E}
there exists an open embedding
of
n
-framed stratified bundles

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{{U}\times{V}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{{E}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{{V}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{{B}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces u}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces v}

such that
x
is in the image of
u
.

Lemma 3.1.0.10
.

Framed stratified submersions are closed under pullback.

Definition 3.1.0.11
.

Let
f:{X}\to{Y}
be an
n
-framed stratified bundle
and
g:{Y}\to{Z}
an
m
-framed stratified bundle.
The
composite framing
on
g\circ f:{X}\to{Z}
is
the
(n+m)
-framing obtained as the composite of the individual framings

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\operatorname{U}({X})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{R}^{n}\times\operatorname{U}({Y})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{R}^{n}\times\mathbb{R}^{m}\times\operatorname{U}({Z})=\mathbb{R}^{n+m}\times\operatorname{U}({Z})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\operatorname{fr}(f)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{R}^{n}\times\operatorname{fr}(g)}

Construction 3.1.0.12
.

Let
f:{X}\to{A}
be an
n
-framed stratified bundle
and
g:{Y}\to{B}
an
m
-framed stratified bundle.
Then the
framed product

f\rtimes g
is the map of stratified spaces

{X}\times{Y}\to{A}\times{B}

equipped with the induced
(n+m)
-framing

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\operatorname{U}({X}\times{Y})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\mathbb{R}^{n}\times\operatorname{U}({A})\times\mathbb{R}^{m}\times\operatorname{U}({B})\cong\mathbb{R}^{n+m}\times\operatorname{U}({A}\times{B})}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\operatorname{fr}(f)\times\operatorname{fr}(g)}

For each
n,m\geq 0
the framed product defines a functor

-\rtimes-:\textup{FrBun}^{n}\times\textup{FrBun}^{m}\longrightarrow\textup{FrBun}^{n+m}

Remark 3.1.0.13
.

Since the coordinate order in a framing is significant, the framed product
is not symmetric up to framed isomorphism. We use the asymmetric symbol

\rtimes
instead of
\times
to indicate this in the notation.

Definition 3.1.0.14
.

An
n
-framed stratified bundle

f:{E}\to{B}

is
tame
when
{E}
and
\mathbb{R}^{n}\times{B}
have
finite relative triangulations such that
the framing

\operatorname{fr}(f):\operatorname{U}({E})\hookrightarrow\mathbb{R}^{n}\times\operatorname{U}({B})

is a simplicial map.
An
n
-framed stratified bundle is
essentially tame

when it is isomorphic in
\textup{FrBun}^{n}
to a tame
n
-framed stratified bundle.

Example 3.1.0.15
.

Our notion of tameness for bundles is stricter than that which would be imposed by
o-minimality without additional conditions.
Consider for example the stratified spaces
{X}
and
{B}
,
written as the union of their strata:

\displaystyle\operatorname{U}({B}):=

\displaystyle\ \{(x,y)\mid 0\leq x\leq y\leq 1\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{2}

\displaystyle\operatorname{U}({X}):=

\displaystyle\ \{((1-y)\tfrac{x}{y},x,y)\mid 0\leq x\leq y\leq 1,0<y\}

\displaystyle\cup

\displaystyle\ \{(t,0,0)\mid 0<t<1\}\cup\{(1,0,0)\}\cup\{(0,0,0)\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{3}

Then the projection onto the last two coordinates induces a
1
-framed stratified
bundle
f:{X}\to{B}
which is not essentially tame, although it is semi-algebraic.

Example 3.1.0.16
.

Consider the
3
-framed stratified spaces
{X},{Y},{Z}
which each consist of a single stratum
given by the following subspaces of
\mathbb{R}^{3}
:

\displaystyle{X}

\displaystyle:=\{(0,0,t)\mid t\in\mathbb{R}\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{3},

\displaystyle{Y}

\displaystyle:=\{(1,t\sin(\tfrac{1}{t}),t)\mid t\in\mathbb{R}\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{3},

\displaystyle{Z}

\displaystyle:=\{(1,0,t)\mid t\in\mathbb{R}\}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{3}.

Then
{X}
and
{Z}
are tame but
{Y}
is not. However, as
3
-framed stratified
spaces we have
{Y}\cong{Z}
and so
{Y}
is essentially tame.
The difference is important since the union
{X}\cup{Z}
remains tame,
while the union
{X}\cup{Y}
is not even essentially tame.

Definition 3.1.0.17
.

The
frame order
on
\mathbb{R}^{n}
is the smallest partial order
\leq_{\textup{fr}}

such that for all points

x=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\in\mathbb{R}^{n}
and
y=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{n})\in\mathbb{R}^{n}

and
0\leq i<n
we have

x\sim_{i}y\land x_{n-i}<y_{n-i}\quad\Rightarrow\quad x\leq_{\textup{fr}}y

Observation 3.1.0.18
.

The frame order on
\mathbb{R}^{n}
is the lexicographic order where elements of

\mathbb{R}^{n}
are seen as sequences in
(\mathbb{R},\leq)
in reverse coordinate order.

Definition 3.1.0.19
.

Let
X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}
be a subset and
p\in\mathbb{R}^{n}
a point.
We say that
x\in X
is the
framed projection
of
p
onto
X

when it is the unique point in
X
that minimises the pointwise absolute value

|x-p|

in the frame order
\leq_{\textup{fr}}
on
\mathbb{R}^{n}
.
In that case we write
\operatorname{proj}_{\textup{fr}}(X,p)=x
.

3.2
Meshes

Meshes are framed stratified spaces in which all the information that is
detected by framed stratified isomorphisms is visible in the stratification.
Meshes organise into mesh bundles, and in the coordinate order prescribed by
the framing, an
n
-mesh bundle is built inductively as the framed composite
of
1
-mesh bundles that each add a single dimension.

We define two flavours of meshes:
Closed meshes are akin to commutative or pasting diagrams for higher categories,
and are glued together from compatible families of closed cells.
Open meshes are the Poincaré duals of closed meshes and model a form of higher-dimensional string diagrams.

We begin with closed meshes, which are technically simpler to manipulate than open ones. In §
3.2.1
we define closed
1
-mesh bundles and explore their properties. In particular, we see how closed
1
-mesh bundles are classified by a quasicategory
\cramped{\bar{\textup{M}}}^{1}
, equivalent to
\Delta^{\textup{op}}
.
Our results on closed
1
-mesh bundles then transfer to closed
n
-mesh bundles
in §
3.2.2
, which are classified by a quasicategory
\cramped{\bar{\textup{M}}}^{n}
.
We can equip closed
n
-mesh bundles with labels in any quasicategory
\mathcal{C}
,
leading to a quasicategory
\cramped{\bar{\textup{M}}}^{n}(\mathcal{C})
in §
3.2.3
.
Via the packing construction of §
3.2.4
we then see that
\cramped{\bar{\textup{M}}}^{n+m}(\mathcal{C})\simeq\cramped{\bar{\textup{M}}}^{n}(\cramped{\bar{\textup{M}}}^{m}(\mathcal{C}))
.
We define open
n
-mesh bundles in §
3.2.5
and transfer the relevant results from closed
n
-mesh bundles via a compactification construction. The result is a quasicategory
\cramped{\dot{\textup{M}}}^{n}(\mathcal{C})
which classifies open
n
-mesh bundles with labels in
\mathcal{C}
.
In §
3.2.6
we explore grids, a special case of open and closed
n
-meshes, to show that the
n
-fold products
\Delta^{n,\textup{op}}
and
\Delta^{n}
are subcategories of
\cramped{\bar{\textup{M}}}^{n}
and
\cramped{\dot{\textup{M}}}^{n}
, respectively.

3.2.1
Closed
1
-Meshes

Definition 3.2.1.1
.

A
closed
1
-mesh
is a stratified space

{X}
such that the underlying space is a non-empty closed bounded interval
\operatorname{U}({X})\subset\mathbb{R}

and every stratum is either an open interval or an isolated point.
The former strata are called
regular
,
the latter
singular
.
A point
x\in{X}
is
regular
or

singular
if it is contained in a stratum that
is regular or singular, respectively.

We visualise a closed
1
-mesh by a line on which the singular strata are marked with a dot:

singular
regular

There is a closed
1
-mesh with any positive number of singular strata:

etc.

Closed
1
-meshes organise into compatible families via closed
1
-mesh bundles.

Definition 3.2.1.2
.

A
closed
1
-mesh bundle
is a
1
-framed
stratified bundle
\xi:{X}\to{B}

that satisfies the following conditions:

1.

\xi
is a stratified fibre bundle.

2.

For every
b\in{B}
the fibre
\xi^{-1}(b)
is a closed
1
-mesh.

3.

The singular points in all fibres form a closed subset of
{X}
.

4.

The framing map
\operatorname{fr}(\xi):\operatorname{U}({X})\hookrightarrow\mathbb{R}^{1}\times\operatorname{U}({B})
is a closed embedding.

We denote by
\textup{sing}({X})
the subspace consisting of the singular points of
{X}
.
