, as we outlined earlier in Definition
3.6.2.2
.
Moreover there is a diagram of forgetful maps

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\cramped{\bar{\textup{M}}}^{n}(C^{\textup{op}})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\textup{Conf}^{n}(C)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\cramped{\dot{\textup{M}}}^{n}(C)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\cramped{\bar{\textup{M}}}^{n}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\textup{Conf}^{n}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\cramped{\dot{\textup{M}}}^{n}}}

Lemma 3.6.2.13
.

The projection maps

\displaystyle\mathfrak{C}\textup{onf}^{n}_{\textup{L}}

\displaystyle:\textup{Conf}^{n}_{\textup{L}}\to\textup{Conf}^{n}

\displaystyle\mathfrak{C}\textup{onf}^{n}_{\textup{LR}}

\displaystyle:\textup{Conf}^{n}_{\textup{LR}}\to\textup{Conf}^{n}

\displaystyle\mathfrak{C}\textup{onf}^{n}_{\textup{R}}

\displaystyle:\textup{Conf}^{n}_{\textup{R}}\to\textup{Conf}^{n}

are flat categorical fibrations.

Proof.

The map
\mathfrak{C}\textup{onf}^{n}_{\textup{L}}
is a pullback of
\cramped{\bar{\mathfrak{M}}}^{n}:\cramped{\bar{\textup{M}}}^{n}_{*}\to\cramped{\bar{\textup{M}}}^{n}
which is a flat
categorical fibration by Lemma
3.2.3.7
.
Similarly the map
\mathfrak{C}\textup{onf}^{n}_{\textup{R}}
is a pullback of the flat categorical fibration

\cramped{\dot{\mathfrak{M}}}^{n}:\cramped{\dot{\textup{M}}}^{n}_{*}\to\cramped{\dot{\textup{M}}}^{n}
.
Since the intersection
\xi\cap f
is a closed
n
-mesh bundle,
by Lemma
3.2.2.4
the induced map

\textup{Exit}(\xi\cap f)
is a flat categorical fibration.
Then we can proceed analogously as in the proof of Lemma
3.2.3.7
to see that
\mathfrak{C}\textup{onf}^{n}_{\textup{LR}}
must be flat as well.
∎

Proposition 3.6.2.14
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a quasicategory.
Then the projection
\textup{Conf}^{n}(\mathcal{C})\to\textup{Conf}^{n}
is a categorical
fibration.
In particular
\textup{Conf}^{n}(\mathcal{C})
is a quasicategory.

Proof.

By Lemma
3.6.2.13
the maps

\mathfrak{C}\textup{onf}^{n}_{\textup{L}}
,
\mathfrak{C}\textup{onf}^{n}_{\textup{LR}}
and
\mathfrak{C}\textup{onf}^{n}_{\textup{R}}
are flat categorical
fibrations.
The projections
\operatorname{Tw}(\mathcal{C})\to\mathcal{C}^{\textup{op}}
and

\operatorname{Tw}(\mathcal{C})\to\mathcal{C}
are categorical fibrations and
\operatorname{Tw}(\mathcal{C})

a quasicategory.
When we equip the diagram (
3.19
) with the forgetful
maps into
\textup{Conf}^{n}
, it follows by Proposition
2.2.3.4
that
the resulting diagram in the slice category
\textup{sSet}_{/\textup{Conf}^{n}}

is fibrant in the slice model structure. Moreover the maps

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\textup{Conf}^{n}_{\textup{LR}}(\mathcal{C}^{\textup{op}})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\textup{Conf}^{n}_{\textup{LR}}(\operatorname{Tw}(\mathcal{C}))}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\textup{Conf}^{n}_{\textup{LR}}(\mathcal{C})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\textup{Conf}^{n}}}

are fibrations in the slice model category.
Therefore the limit
\textup{Conf}^{n}(\mathcal{C})\to\textup{Conf}^{n}
is fibrant as well
and thus a categorical fibration.
∎

3.6.3
Characterising Configurations of
1
-Meshes

Let us for now restrict our attention to transverse configurations of
1
-meshes,
and build up to the result that for any
1
-category
\mathcal{C}
there is a natural
equivalence
\textup{Conf}^{1}(\mathcal{C})\simeq\operatorname{Tw}(\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{1}(\mathcal{C}))
.
We start with the unlabelled case and construct a map
\textup{Conf}^{1}\to\operatorname{Tw}(\Delta)
.

Observation 3.6.3.1
.

Let
\xi\pitchfork f
be a transverse configuration of a closed
1
-mesh bundle

\xi:{X}\to\|\Delta[0]\|
and an open
1
-mesh bundle

f:{M}\to\|\Delta[0]\|
.
We have a finite ordinal
\textup{sing}(\xi)
whose elements correspond
to the singular strata of
{X}
, and a finite ordinal

\textup{reg}(f)
whose elements are the regular strata of
{M}
.
Then we can define a map

\textup{sing}(\xi)\longrightarrow\textup{reg}(f)

which sends a singular stratum to the regular stratum that it is contained in.
This is well-defined by the transversality condition and is order-preserving.
We can therefore assign to each object of
\textup{Conf}^{1}
an object of
the twisted arrow category
\operatorname{Tw}(\Delta)
.

Lemma 3.6.3.2
.

Observation
3.6.3.1
extends uniquely to a functor
in the diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\cramped{\bar{\textup{M}}}^{1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\textup{Conf}^{1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\cramped{\dot{\textup{M}}}^{1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Delta^{\textup{op}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\operatorname{Tw}(\Delta)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Delta}}
sing
reg

Proof.

Since
\operatorname{Tw}(\Delta)
is a
1
-category, it suffices to construct a functor
of
1
-categories

\textup{h}(\textup{Conf}^{1})\longrightarrow\operatorname{Tw}(\Delta).

Observation
3.6.3.1
specifies the action on objects.
A map of
\textup{h}(\textup{Conf}^{1})
is represented by
a transverse configuration
\xi\pitchfork f
of a closed
1
-mesh bundle

\xi:{X}\to\|\Delta[1]\|
and an open
1
-mesh bundle

f:{M}\to\|\Delta[1]\|
.
Let us denote respectively by
\xi_{0}
,
\xi_{1}
and by
f_{0}
,
f_{1}
the
restrictions of the
1
-mesh bundles
\xi
and
f
to the endpoints of the stratified interval
\|\Delta[1]\|
.
We then obtain a twisted square of finite ordinals

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\textup{sing}(\xi_{0})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\textup{sing}(\xi_{1})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\textup{reg}(f_{0})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\textup{reg}(f_{1})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\textup{sing}(\xi)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\textup{reg}(f)}

(3.20)

We argue that this twisted square commutes by following the action
of the maps on an element
i_{1}\in\textup{sing}(\xi_{1})
.
The element
i_{1}
corresponds to a singular point
x\in{X}
.
Since by Lemma
3.2.1.9
the
map
\textup{Exit}(\xi)
is a right covering map, there exists a unique filler for

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\|\Delta[0]\|}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{{X}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\|\Delta[1]\|}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\|\Delta[1]\|}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces x}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\langle 1\rangle_{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\xi}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\gamma}

where
\gamma
may only intersect singular strata of
{X}
.
When we let
i_{0}\in\textup{sing}(\xi_{0})
be the index of the singular point
\gamma(0)
,
the exit path
\gamma
witnesses that
\textup{sing}(\xi)(i_{1})=i_{0}
.
By transversality the exit path
\gamma
that traverses only singular strata of

{X}
can intersect only regular strata of
{M}
.
Let
j_{0}\in\textup{reg}(f_{0})
and
j_{1}\in\textup{reg}(f_{1})
be the indices of the regular
strata of
f_{0}
and
f_{1}
that contain the points
\gamma(0)
and
\gamma(1)
.
When we interpret
\gamma
as an exit path in the regular subspace of
{M}
,
by construction of
reg
we have that
\textup{reg}(f)(i_{0})=i_{1}
.
We have thus shown that on the element
i_{1}\in\textup{sing}(\xi_{1})
the twisted
square of maps (
3.20
) acts by

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{i_{0}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{i_{1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{j_{0}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{j_{1}}}

It follows that (
3.20
) commutes.
Moreover
sing
and
reg
are invariant under equivalences of the
1
-mesh bundles.
The maps
\textup{sing}(\xi_{0})\to\textup{reg}(\xi_{0})
and
\textup{sing}(\xi_{1})\to\textup{reg}(\xi_{1})

respect equivalences of transverse configurations, since changing these maps
would require moving a singular stratum of the closed mesh through a singular stratum of the open one, violating transversality on the way.
Therefore the construction of the twisted square (
3.20
)
respects the quotient defining the set of maps in
\textup{h}(\textup{Conf}^{1})
.
Functoriality of
\textup{h}(\textup{Conf}^{1})\to\operatorname{Tw}(\Delta)
requires that the
twisted squares of the form (
3.20
) composes
horizontally, which follows directly from functoriality of
sing
and
reg

individually.
∎

Proposition 3.6.3.3
.

The map
\textup{Conf}^{1}\to\operatorname{Tw}(\Delta)
is a trivial fibration.

Proof.

Suppose we are given a lifting problem

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\partial\Delta[k]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\textup{Conf}^{1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Delta[k]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\operatorname{Tw}(\Delta)}}

We construct a lift by a case distinction on
k\geq 0
.

1.

When
k=0
the
0
-simplex
\Delta[0]\to\operatorname{Tw}(\Delta)
classifies an order-preserving map

v:[a]\to[b]
.
Let
f:{M}\to\|\Delta[0]\|
be an open mesh bundle so that
\textup{reg}(f)=[b]
.
Then we can construct a closed mesh bundle
\xi:{X}\to\|\Delta[0]\|

with
\textup{sing}(\xi)=[a]
such that the
i
th singular stratum is contained in the

v(i)
th regular stratum of
f
.
The pair
\xi\pitchfork f
is a transverse configuration and classifies a lift
\Delta[0]\to\textup{Conf}^{1}
.

2.

For
k=1
we are given a twisted square of finite non-empty ordinals

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[a_{0}]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[a_{1}]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[b_{0}]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[b_{1}]}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces v_{0}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces v_{1}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\alpha}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\beta}

and a transverse configuration
\xi^{\prime}\pitchfork f^{\prime}
of a closed
1
-mesh bundle

\xi^{\prime}:{X}^{\prime}\to\partial\|\Delta[1]\|
and an open
1
-mesh bundle

f^{\prime}:{M}^{\prime}\to\partial\|\Delta[1]\|
.
We write
\xi_{0}
,
\xi_{1}
and
f_{0}
,
f_{1}
for the restrictions of
\xi^{\prime}
and
f^{\prime}

to the two points of
\partial\|\Delta[1]\|=\{0\}\sqcup\{1\}
.
We then have that
v_{0}
and
v_{1}
are the maps
\textup{sing}(\xi_{0})\to\textup{reg}(f_{0})

and
\textup{sing}(\xi_{1})\to\textup{reg}(f_{1})
induced by
\xi_{0}\pitchfork f_{0}
and

\xi_{1}\pitchfork f_{1}
.
We use that
\textup{reg}:\cramped{\dot{\textup{M}}}^{1}\to\Delta
is a trivial fibration and extend
f^{\prime}
to an open
1
-mesh bundle
f:{M}\to\|\Delta[k]\|
with
\textup{reg}(f)=\beta
.

We construct an extension of
\xi^{\prime}
to a closed
1
-mesh bundle
\xi:{X}\to\|\Delta[1]\|
by specifying a sequence
h_{i}:{|\Delta[1]|}\to\mathbb{R}
determining the heights of the singular strata of
\xi
for each
i\in[a_{1}]=\textup{sing}(\xi_{1})
.
Let
i\in[a_{1}]
be the index of such a singular stratum and suppose by induction that we have already determined
h_{j}
for all
0\leq j<i
.
Let
x_{0},x_{1}\in{X}^{\prime}
be the singular points of
\xi^{\prime}
over
0,1\in\|\Delta[1]\|
corresponding to the indices
\alpha(i)\in[a_{0}]
and
i\in[a_{1}]
.
By transversality of
\xi^{\prime}
and
f^{\prime}
we have that
x_{0}
and
x_{1}
must lie in regular strata of
f^{\prime}
, with indices
v_{0}(\alpha(i))
and
v_{1}(i)
.
Because
\textup{reg}(f)=\beta
and
\beta(v_{0}(\alpha(i)))=v_{1}(i)
,
there must exist a section
s:\|\Delta[1]\|\to{M}
of
f

with
s(0)=x_{0}
and
s(1)=x_{1}
, traversing only regular strata of
{M}
.
We can nudge this section on the interior of
\|\Delta[1]\|
to be higher in the framing than the singular strata we have constructed so far,
and denote the result by
h_{i}
.

The resulting closed
1
-mesh bundle
\xi
must be transverse to
f
by construction and the transverse configuration
\xi\pitchfork f

determines a solution of the lifting problem.

3.

When
k\geq 2
we are given a map
v:[k]^{\textup{op}}*[k]\to\Delta

together with a transverse configuration
\xi^{\prime}\pitchfork f^{\prime}
of
a closed
1
-mesh bundle
\xi^{\prime}:{X}^{\prime}\to\partial\|\Delta[k]\|

and an open
1
-mesh bundle
f^{\prime}:{M}^{\prime}\to\partial\|\Delta[k]\|
.
We let
\alpha:[k]^{\textup{op}}\to\Delta
and
\beta:[k]\to\Delta

denote the restrictions of
v
to the two components of the join

[k]^{\textup{op}}*[k]
.

We use that the map
\textup{reg}:\cramped{\dot{\textup{M}}}^{1}\to\Delta
is a trivial fibration and extend
f^{\prime}
to an open
1
-mesh bundle
f:{M}\to\|\Delta[k]\|
with
\textup{reg}(f)=\beta
.
Analogously, we use that by Proposition
3.2.1.13
the map
\textup{sing}:\cramped{\bar{\textup{M}}}^{1}\to\Delta^{\textup{op}}
is a trivial fibration to extend
\xi^{\prime}
to a closed
1
-mesh bundle
\xi^{\prime\prime}:{X}^{\prime\prime}\to\|\Delta[k]\|
with
\textup{sing}(\xi^{\prime\prime})=\beta
.

The
1
-mesh bundles
\xi^{\prime\prime}
and
f
are not transverse in general, but
there is an open collar neighbourhood
{U}
of the boundary
\partial\|\Delta[k]\|
so that
\xi^{\prime\prime}
and
f
are transverse over
{U}
.
Since we assumed that
k\geq 2
we have that
{U}
is connected.
Therefore the singular strata of
\xi^{\prime\prime}
over
{U}\setminus\partial\|\Delta[k]\|
must lie within the same regular stratum of
f
.
Using the trivialisation of
f
over the
k
th stratum of
\|\Delta[k]\|
we then adjust
\xi^{\prime\prime}
to an equivalent closed
1
-mesh bundle
\xi:{X}\to\|\Delta[k]\|
that agrees with
\xi^{\prime\prime}
over
{U}
and is transverse to
f
.
Then
\xi\pitchfork f
represents a solution to the lifting problem.∎

Lemma 3.6.3.4
.

There is a unique functor which fits into the diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cramped{\bar{\textup{T}}}^{1}_{*}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\operatorname{Tw}(\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{1}_{*})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{1}_{*}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cramped{\bar{\textup{M}}}^{1}_{*}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\textup{Conf}^{1}_{\textup{LR}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cramped{\dot{\textup{M}}}^{1}_{*}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cramped{\bar{\textup{T}}}^{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\operatorname{Tw}(\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{1})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{1}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cramped{\bar{\textup{M}}}^{1}}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}

(3.21)

Proof.

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{E}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{1}_{*}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[k]^{\textup{op}}*[k]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Delta}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\Phi}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces F}
{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varphi}

We then need to construct a section

1

F

The maps
\cramped{\bar{\textup{M}}}^{1}_{*}\to\cramped{\bar{\textup{T}}}^{1}_{*}

S_{0}
,

to the two components

[k]^{\textup{op}}

[k]

We therefore look for an

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[k]^{\textup{op}}\sqcup[k]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{E}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[k]^{\textup{op}}*[k]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{[k]^{\textup{op}}*[k]}}

Since the join

is already uniquely determines as a map of sets.

Suppose that
t\in[k]
and
let us denote by
\varphi_{t}

\varphi(t^{\circ})\to\varphi(t)
.
We verify by case distinction that there is a unique map

\Phi(S_{0}(t))\to\Phi(S_{1}(t))
in

over

,

.
For reference, we refer back to the Definition
3.3.2.1

.

1.

If
\Phi(S_{0}(t))=\bar{\textup{s}}_{i}[p]=\dot{\textup{r}}_{i}[p]

then the

is contained in the

and so

.

.

is contained in the

and the

over

.

-mesh bundle, the

over

must be surrounded by the

over

and

are the indices of those regular strata, we must therefore have

.

\Phi(S_{0}(t))=\bar{\textup{r}}_{i}[p]=\dot{\textup{s}}_{i}[p]

over

.

is again surrounded by the

over

of because

and

.
Then we must have
\varphi_{t}(i)=j_{0}\leq j<j_{1}=\varphi_{t}(i+1)
.

Finally the case that

and

is impossible since the transversality
condition prevents the point

to be singular in both

and

.
∎

Lemma 3.6.3.5
.

The map
\textup{Conf}^{1}_{\textup{LR}}\to\operatorname{Tw}(\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{1}_{*})
is a trivial fibration.

Proof.

Since
\operatorname{Tw}(\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{1})
is a
1
-category and
\textup{Conf}^{1}_{\textup{LR}}
is a quasicategory by Observation
3.6.2.6
,
the map must be an inner fibration already by Lemma
2.1.2.7
.
It therefore suffices to show that the map is a categorical equivalence.

To see that the map is essentially surjective,
let
\hat{\alpha}
be a map in
\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n}_{*}
which is sent to
the order-preserving map
\alpha:[n]\to[m]
by
\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{1}_{*}\to\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{1}
.
By Proposition
3.6.3.3
we can construct a transverse configuration
(\xi,f)
of
a closed
1
-mesh bundle
\xi:{X}\to\|\Delta[0]\|
and an open

1
-mesh bundle
f:{M}\to\|\Delta[0]\|
which is sent to
\alpha

by
\textup{Conf}^{1}\to\operatorname{Tw}(\Delta)
.
It remains to show that there exists a point
x\in{X}\cap{M}

such that
\textup{Conf}^{1}_{\textup{LR}}\to\operatorname{Tw}(\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{1}_{*})
sends
(\xi,f)
together with
x

to
\hat{\alpha}
.
We verify this with a case distinction.

1.

Suppose that
\hat{\alpha}:\dot{\textup{r}}_{i}[n]\to\dot{\textup{r}}_{j}[n]
.
We then have
\alpha(i)=j
and so the
i
th singular stratum of
{X}

must intersect the
j
th regular stratum of
{M}
.
Then the point
x\in{X}\cap{M}
corresponding to the
i
th singular
stratum of
{X}
is sent to
\hat{\alpha}
.

2.

Suppose that
\hat{\alpha}:\dot{\textup{s}}_{i}[n]\to\dot{\textup{r}}_{j}[n]
. Then
we have
\alpha(i)\leq j\leq\alpha(i+1)
.
This entails that the
i
th and
(i+1)
st singular strata of
{X}
must intersect
regular strata of
{M}
that are above and below, respectively, of the
j
th
regular stratum of
{M}
.
In particular the
i
th regular stratum of
{X}
intersects the
j
th regular stratum of
{M}
non-trivially, and any point in this intersection is sent to
\hat{\alpha}
.

3.

Suppose that
\hat{\alpha}:\dot{\textup{s}}_{i}[n]\to\dot{\textup{s}}_{j}[n]
.
Then
\alpha(i)\leq j<\alpha(i+1)
.
The
j
th singular stratum of
{M}
is surrounded by the
j
th and
(j+1)
st regular strata.
The
i
th singular stratum of
{X}
intersects a regular stratum of
{M}
below the
j
th regular stratum, and the
(i+1)
st singular stratum of
{X}
intersects a regular stratum that is above the
(j+1)
st regular stratum.
Therefore the
i
th regular stratum of
{X}
must cross the
j
th singular stratum of
{M}
.
This intersection point is then sent to
\hat{\alpha}
.

4.

The case
\hat{\alpha}:\dot{\textup{r}}_{i}[n]\to\dot{\textup{s}}_{j}[n]
is impossible since there are no maps from regular to singular elements in
\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{1}_{*}
.

For faithfulness it suffices to observe that an equivalence of
transverse configurations can not change which strata intersect each other
since this would require passing singular strata of the closed and open mesh across each other.
Finally fullness can again be verified via a case distinction similar to one ones above.
∎

Lemma 3.6.3.6
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a
1
-category.
Then there exists an equivalence

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\cramped{\bar{\textup{M}}}^{1}(\mathcal{C})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\textup{Conf}^{1}(\mathcal{C})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\cramped{\dot{\textup{M}}}^{1}(\mathcal{C})}}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{1}(\mathcal{C})}}

which is natural in

.

Proof.

Let us begin by constructing the analogue of the diagram (

The diagonal maps in the diagram (

Therefore, by Construction

\hat{\textup{T}}(\mathcal{C})
.
We obtain an induced map between the limits

.
Since

-category, the limits are homotopy limits and
so the induced map

We now show that there is an isomorphism of simplicial sets

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\hat{\textup{T}}(\mathcal{C})}}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cong}

We first make some auxiliary constructions derived from a

-simplex

.
There is a diagram of simplicial sets

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{E_{0}^{\textup{op}}}}

,

By the definition of

.

in which the diagonal squares are pullback squares and

The posets

agree with their earlier construction.
The twisted arrow construction
\operatorname{Tw}(-):\textup{sSet}\to\textup{sSet}
is a right

We apply

to the middle pullback square in (

) and the further

to obtain the diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\hat{E}}}

The two squares in this diagram compose to the middle square of the diagram

.

A

-simplex of

over
\tau
now is determined

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{E_{0}}}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{1}}

(3.25)

while a

-simplex of

over

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{1}}

(3.26)

The maps in (
3.25
) determine the maps in (
3.26
) by letting
L=\operatorname{Tw}(R)\circ I
.
This defines the map
\hat{\textup{T}}(\mathcal{C})\to\operatorname{Tw}(\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{1}(\mathcal{C})
.
For the other direction, we first use that
\mathcal{C}
is a
1
-category
and
F
a flat categorical fibration to reduce to the case that
k=1
.
We then construct a functor of
1
-categories
R:E\to\mathcal{C}
as follows.
On objects we let
R(e_{0})=L_{0}(e_{0})
when
e_{0}\in E_{0}\subseteq E
and

R(e_{1})=L_{1}(e_{1})
for
e_{1}\in E_{1}\subseteq E
.
To define the action of
R
on the maps of
E
,
suppose that
a,b\in E
with
a\leq b
. We then proceed by a case distinction:

1.

When
a,b\in E_{0}
we let
R(a\leq b):=L_{0}(a\leq b)
.

2.

When
a,b\in E_{1}
we let
R(a\leq b):=L_{1}(a\leq b)
.

3.

Suppose that
F(a)=i^{\circ}
and
F(b)=i
for some
i\in[1]
.
Then the interval
[a,b]
is an element of the poset
\hat{E}
and so
L
sends

[a,b]
to an object of the twisted arrow category
\operatorname{Tw}(\mathcal{C})
.
By commutativity of (
3.26
) this object of

\operatorname{Tw}(\mathcal{C})
is a map
L_{0}(a)\to L_{1}(b)
in
\mathcal{C}
. We then let

R(a\leq b):=L([a,b])
be this map.

4.

Suppose that
F(a)=0^{\circ}
and
F(b)=1
.
Since
F
is flat we can find an element
e\in E
such that
a\leq e\leq b

and
F(e)=0
. We then let

R(a\leq b):=L_{1}(e\leq b)\circ L([a,e]).

The element
e
is not unique and so we need to verify that the definition
of
R(a\leq b)
does not depend on the chosen factorisation.
Flatness of
F
not only guarantees existence of the factorisation but also
weak contractibility of the category of factorisations.
In particular any two factorisations are connected by a zigzag of maps.
Considering one step of the zigzag at a time, suppose that we have two factorisations

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{e_{0}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{a}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{b}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{e_{1}}}

where
F(e_{0})=F(e_{1})=0
.
We then have a diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{L_{1}(e_{0})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{L_{0}(a)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{L_{1}(b)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{L_{1}(e_{1})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\varphi}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{1}(e_{0}\leq b)}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L([a,e_{0}])}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L([a,e_{1}])}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces L_{1}(e_{1}\leq b)}

which is rendered commutative by
\varphi=L([a,e_{0}]\leq[a,e_{1}])=L_{1}(e_{0}\leq e_{1})
.

5.

The remaining case is
F(a)=1^{\circ}
and
F(b)=0
.
Analogously to the previous case we pick a factorisation

a\leq e\leq b
with
F(e)=0^{\circ}
and let

R(a\leq b):=L([e,b])\circ L_{0}(a\leq e).

Functoriality of
R
follows from its construction. We see that
the diagrams (
3.25
) and (
3.26
)
uniquely determine each other.
∎

Remark 3.6.3.7
.

We have shown Lemma
3.6.3.6
for the case that
\mathcal{C}

is a
1
-category to simplify the proof. We expect that it also holds
in the more general case when
\mathcal{C}
is a quasicategory, but this would
require a more sophisticated proof. Because
\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n}
is a
1
-category
for all
n\geq 0
the current form of Lemma
3.6.3.6
is
sufficient for our purpose of demonstrating an equivalence

\textup{Conf}^{n}\simeq\operatorname{Tw}(\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n})
via the packing construction below.

3.6.4
Packing for Configurations of
n
-Meshes

The goal in this section is to construct an equivalence
\textup{Conf}^{n}\simeq\operatorname{Tw}(\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n})
.
We do so inductively using the ability to label transverse configurations,
transferring one dimension at a time into the open truss by a packing
construction similar to that for closed and open meshes.

Lemma 3.6.4.1
.

Let
\mathcal{C}
be a
1
-category.
Then there exists an equivalence

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\cramped{\bar{\textup{M}}}^{n+1}(\mathcal{C}^{\textup{op}})}}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\cramped{\dot{\textup{M}}}^{n+1}(\mathcal{C})}}

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\textup{Conf}^{n}(\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{1}(\mathcal{C}))}}

\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}

which is natural in

.

Proof.

A

-simplex of

is a labelled transverse configuration
of

-mesh bundles over

. We present the closed

The labelling of the transverse configuration

Corollary 3.6.4.3

There exists an equivalence of

3.6.5
Orthogonality

We wish to extend our concept of transversality to pairs consisting of a closed
n
-mesh

{X}
and any stratification
{E}
of
\mathbb{R}^{n}
that does not need to be
an open
n
-mesh itself.
In the cases that
{E}
is meshable we would want that transversality of

{X}
and
{E}
implies transversality of
{X}
with the coarsest
refining mesh of
{E}
.
However, as illustrated below, there is no local
criterion that we can impose on the intersection of the strata in
{X}
and
{E}
which would guarantee this property.

Example 3.6.5.1
.

Consider the
3
-dimensional diagram, presented in projection as follows:

We have an essentially tame
3
-framed stratification
{E}
, drawn in black, and
a closed
3
-mesh
{X}
, drawn in red.
When we take the coarsest
refining mesh
{M}
of
{E}
,
the result is not a transverse configuration of
{X}
and
{M}
.

The issue arises from the braid in
{E}
that induces a
stratum in
{M}
intersecting
{X}
non-tranversally.
We can not place a local condition on
{E}
and
{X}

which excludes this situation since the braid is not within
any arbitrarily small neigbourhood of
{X}
.

We resolve this issue by imposing a stronger compatibility condition on the pair

({X},{E})
which is preserved by replacing
{E}
with
its coarsest refining mesh. We call this condition orthogonality and define
it inductively as follows.

Definition 3.6.5.2
.

A closed
(n+1)
-mesh
{X}
and a stratification

{E}
of
\mathbb{R}^{n+1}
are
\varepsilon
-orthogonal

for some
\varepsilon>0
when they satisfy:

1.

For each singular height
h
of
{X}
,
x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}
and

t\in{(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)}
we have

\cramped{\mathbb{s}}({{M}})(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},h)=\cramped{\mathbb{s}}({{M}})(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},h+t)

2.

For each height
h\in\mathbb{R}
the slices

{X}\cap(\mathbb{R}^{n}\times\{h\})

and

{E}\cap(\mathbb{R}^{n}\times\{h\})

are
\varepsilon
-orthogonal.

In the base case
n=0
the unique closed
0
-mesh is
\varepsilon
-orthogonal to the
unique stratification of
\mathbb{R}^{0}
for any
\varepsilon>0
.
When
{X}
and
{M}
are
\varepsilon
-orthogonal we write
{X}\perp_{\varepsilon}{M}

and call the pair
({X},{M})
an
\varepsilon
-orthogonal configuration.

Definition 3.6.5.3
.

Let
\xi:{X}\to{B}
be a closed
n
-mesh bundle and

\varphi:{E}\to{B}
an
n
-framed stratified bundle so that

\operatorname{U}({E})=\operatorname{U}({B})\times\mathbb{R}^{n}
.
We say that
\xi
and
\varphi
are
\varepsilon
-orthogonal

for some
\varepsilon>0
when for every

b\in{B}
the fibres
\xi^{-1}(b)
and
\varphi^{-1}(b)

are
\varepsilon
-orthogonal.
In this case we write
\xi\perp_{\varepsilon}\varphi
and call the pair
(\xi,\varphi)

an
\varepsilon
-orthogonal configuration.

Definition 3.6.5.4
.

Let
\xi:{X}\to{B}
be a closed
n
-mesh bundle and

\varphi:{E}\to{B}
an
n
-framed stratified bundle so that

\operatorname{U}({E})=\operatorname{U}({B})\times\mathbb{R}^{n}
.
We say
\xi
and
\varphi
are
orthogonal
when there exists a

\varepsilon>0
such that
\xi
and
\varphi
are
\varepsilon
-orthogonal.
We then write
\xi\perp\varphi
and call the pair
(\xi,\varphi)
an
orthogonal configuration.

Observation 3.6.5.5
.

Suppose that
{X}
is a closed
n
-mesh and
p:{E}\to{K}
an open meshable
n
-framed stratified bundle such that
{X}\perp p^{-1}(b)
for every
b\in{K}
.
Let
f:{M}\to{B}
be the coarsest open
n
-mesh bundle
over a PL stratified pseudomanifold which refines
p
.
Then we also have
{X}\perp f^{-1}(b)
for all
b\in{B}
,
since else we could coarsen
f
further.

Observation 3.6.5.6
.

Let
(\xi,f)
be an orthogonal configuration of a closed

n
-mesh bundle
\xi:{X}\to{B}
and an open

n
-mesh bundle
f:{M}\to{B}
. Then
(\xi,f)
is a transverse
configuration.

The orthogonal configurations of closed and open
n
-mesh bundles therefore
form a simplicial subset
\textup{Conf}^{n}_{\perp}
of the quasicategory
\textup{Conf}^{n}
.
We show that
\textup{Conf}^{n}_{\perp}
is itself a quasicategory and equivalent
to
\textup{Conf}^{n}
itself.
In particular the equivalence
\textup{Conf}^{n}\simeq\operatorname{Tw}(\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n})

restricts to an equivalence
\textup{Conf}^{n}_{\perp}\simeq\operatorname{Tw}(\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n})
.

Definition 3.6.5.7
.

We denote by
\textup{Conf}^{n}_{\perp}
the simplicial subset of
\textup{Conf}^{n}
whose

k
-simplices consist of a pair
(\xi,f)
of a closed
n
-mesh bundle

\xi:{X}\to\|\Delta[k]\|
and an open
n
-mesh bundle

f:{M}\to\|\Delta[k]\|
such that
\xi\perp f
.

Lemma 3.6.5.8
.

The projection
\textup{Conf}^{n}_{\perp}\to\cramped{\bar{\textup{M}}}^{n}
is a cocartesian
fibration. Moreover a map in
\textup{Conf}^{n}_{\perp}
is cocartesian for the
projection map
\textup{Conf}^{n}_{\perp}\to\cramped{\bar{\textup{M}}}^{n}
if and only if it
is sent to an equivalence by the other projection
\textup{Conf}^{n}_{\perp}\to\cramped{\dot{\textup{M}}}^{n}
.

Proof.

Analogous to Lemma
3.6.1.5
.
∎

Lemma 3.6.5.9
.

The inclusion map
\textup{Conf}^{n}_{\perp}\hookrightarrow\textup{Conf}^{n}

is a categorical equivalence.

Proof.

Both projection maps
\textup{Conf}^{n}_{\perp}\to\cramped{\bar{\textup{M}}}^{n}

and
\textup{Conf}^{n}\to\cramped{\bar{\textup{M}}}^{n}
are cocartesian fibrations.
It therefore suffices to show that for every closed
n
-mesh
{X}
,
the induced map on fibres

\textup{Conf}^{n}_{\perp}\times_{\cramped{\bar{\textup{M}}}^{n}}\{{X}\}\longrightarrow\textup{Conf}^{n}\times_{\cramped{\bar{\textup{M}}}^{n}}\{{X}\}

is a categorical equivalence.
This can be demonstrated by stretching out transverse configurations
within a neighbourhood of the singular strata of
{X}

so that they become orthogonal.
∎

Remark 3.6.5.10
.

We also have a projection map
\textup{Conf}^{n}_{\perp}\to\cramped{\dot{\textup{M}}}^{n}

which sends an orthogonal configuration
\xi\perp f
to the
open
n
-mesh bundle
f
. This map is not an inner fibration,
in contrast to the corresponding
projection map
\textup{Conf}^{n}\to\cramped{\dot{\textup{M}}}^{n}
.

Chapter 4
Diagrammatic Higher Categories

4.1
Diagrammatic Spaces

The
n
-fold Segal space model for
(\infty,n)
-categories uses the
n
-fold product

\Delta^{n}
of the simplex category as its category of shapes.
A diagram in an
n
-fold Segal space is glued together from little cubes
with shape
[k_{1},\ldots,k_{n}]
where
0\leq k_{i}\leq 1

that represent a morphism of dimension
k_{1}+\cdots+k_{n}
.
For instance a
2
-morphism
\alpha
in a
2
-fold Segal space
\mathcal{C}
is a point
in the space of maps
[1,1]\to\mathcal{C}
.
The source and target
1
-morphisms of
\alpha
are obtained by restricting

[1,1]\to\mathcal{C}
along the two inclusions
[1,0]\hookrightarrow[1,1]
.
The collection of shapes offered by
\Delta^{n}
is therefore quite limited,
and does not allow us to ask directly for
n
-morphisms whose source or target is a composite
or even includes an isotopy.
In this section we show how we can use open
n
-trusses to generalise the shapes
with which
(\infty,n)
-categories can be probed.

Observation 4.1.0.1
.

By Construction
3.3.2.8
we have a fully faithful functor
\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}}:\Delta^{n}\hookrightarrow\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n}

from the
n
-fold product of
\Delta
with itself.
For brevity of notation we omit the dimension
n
from the name of this functor.
We then get an adjunction of
\infty
-categories of space-valued presheaves

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\textup{P}(\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\textup{P}(\Delta^{n})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}})^{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}})_{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptscriptstyle\dashv}

given by restriction
(\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}})^{*}
and right Kan extension
(\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}})_{*}
.
Because
\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}}
is fully faithful, so is the right adjoint
(\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}})_{*}
.
The
n
-simplicial spaces therefore embed into presheaves on
\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n}
.

Example 4.1.0.2
.

Suppose that
\mathcal{C}
is a
2
-uple Segal space and that

A
is the
2
-dimensional atom which realises to the open mesh

Then a point in
(\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}})_{*}\mathcal{C}(A)
is a compatible family of cells in
\mathcal{C}
,
consisting of a map
[k_{1},k_{2}]\to\mathcal{C}
for every map
[k_{1},k_{2}]\to A
.
We illustrate this geometrically by using transverse configurations,
rendering
A
in black and the closed mesh associated to some
[k_{1},k_{2}]\in\Delta^{2}

in red.
We only list the elements which are non-degenerate.

•

Objects
[0,0]\to\mathcal{C}
for each

•

Horizontal
1
-morphisms
[1,0]\to\mathcal{C}
between the objects for each

•

Vertical
1
-morphisms
[0,1]\to\mathcal{C}
between the objects for each

•

A
2
-morphism
[1,1]\to\mathcal{C}
for

•

A witness of composition of horizontal
1
-morphisms
[2,0]\to\mathcal{C}

which composes to the chosen
1
-morphism
[1,0]\to\mathcal{C}
from above

A point in
(\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}})_{*}\mathcal{C}(A)
therefore is a
2
-morphism of
\mathcal{C}

whose domain factors as the composite of two chosen
1
-morphisms.
In this way the presheaf
(\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}})_{*}\mathcal{C}
lets us produce compatible families
of morphisms in
\mathcal{C}
according to each truss
T\in\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{2}
interpreted
as a string diagram.

Definition 4.1.0.3
.

A presheaf
\mathcal{F}\in\textup{P}(\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n})
satisfies the

Segal condition
when for every open
n
-truss
T
the atomic covering
diagram
U:\textup{Exit}(T)^{\textup{op},\triangleright}\to\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n}
is sent to a
limit diagram
U\circ\mathcal{F}
.
We denote by
\operatorname{Seg}(\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n})
the reflective subcategory of
\textup{P}(\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n})

consisting of the presheaves that satisfy the Segal condition.

The Segal condition on
\textup{P}(\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n})
restricts to the Segal condition
on
\textup{P}(\Delta^{n})
for
n
-uple Segal spaces,
wherefore the restriction functor
\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{*}
induces a functor

\operatorname{Seg}(\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n})\to\operatorname{Seg}(\Delta^{n})
.
To see that the functor
(\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}})_{*}
also preserves the Segal condition,
we make the following observation.

Definition 4.1.0.4
.

Let
E\in\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n}
be an open
n
-truss. We then write

\textup{Grid}(E):=\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n}(\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}}(-),E).

for the restricted representable functor.

Lemma 4.1.0.5
.

Let
E\in\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n}
be an open
n
-truss.
Then
\textup{Grid}(E)
is the free
n
-uple Segal space with one generator
for each atom
A\hookrightarrow E
.

Proof.

The claim is trivial for
n=0
.
When
n>0
we use the isomorphism
\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n}\cong\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{1}(\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n-1})
to write
E
as an open
1
-truss labelled in
\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n-1}

and therefore a sequence of spans

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{R_{0}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{S_{0}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{R_{1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{S_{1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{R_{2}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cdots}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{R_{k}}}

(4.1)

By induction we have that
\textup{Grid}(R_{i})
is the free
(n-1)
-uple Segal space
generated by the atoms in
R_{i}
for all
0\leq i\leq k
,
and analogously
\textup{Grid}(S_{i})
is the free
(n-1)
-uple Segal space
generated by the atoms in
S_{i}
for all
0\leq i<k
.
Via the maps of (
4.1
) we then get a graph
in the
\infty
-category of
(n-1)
-fold Segal spaces:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{G_{1}:=\coprod_{0\leq i<k}\textup{Grid}(S_{i})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\coprod_{0\leq i\leq k}\textup{Grid}(R_{i})=:G_{0}}}

Then
\textup{Grid}(E)
is the free Segal object in
\operatorname{Seg}(\Delta^{n-1})
generated
by this graph, and the generators of
\textup{Grid}(E)
are the generators of the
free
(n-1)
-fold Segal spaces of vertices
G_{0}
and edges
G_{1}
.
When
A\hookrightarrow E
is an atom with
\textup{stype}(A)_{n}=0
,
then
A\hookrightarrow E
factors through a regular slice
R_{i}\hookrightarrow E
for some

0\leq i\leq k
. Therefore, the atom induces a generator in
G_{0}
.
When
A\hookrightarrow E
is an atom with
\textup{stype}(A)_{n}=1
,
then there is some
0\leq i<k
and a diagram of open
(n-1)
-trusses

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A_{0}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A_{1}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{A_{2}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{R_{i}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{S_{i}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{R_{i+1}}}

where the vertical maps are inert and
A_{1}
is an atom.
Therefore,
A\hookrightarrow E
corresponds exactly to the atom

A_{1}\hookrightarrow S_{i}
and therefore to a generator in
G_{1}
.
∎

Corollary 4.1.0.6
.

Let
E\in\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n}
be an open
n
-truss.
When

U:\textup{Exit}(E)^{\textup{op},\triangleright}\to\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n}

is the atomic covering diagram of
E
,
the induced diagram

\textup{Grid}(U(-))

is a colimit diagram in the
\infty
-category
\operatorname{Seg}(\Delta^{n})

of
n
-uple Segal spaces.

Proof.

This follows from Lemma
4.1.0.5
since

\textup{Grid}(E)
is freely generated as an
n
-uple Segal space with one generator
for every atom of
E
.
∎

Proposition 4.1.0.8
.

The adjunction of
\infty
-categories of space-valued presheaves

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\textup{P}(\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\textup{P}(\Delta^{n})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}})^{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}})_{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptscriptstyle\dashv}

induced by the inclusion functor
\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}}:\Delta^{n}\to\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n}

restricts to an adjunction

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\operatorname{Seg}(\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\operatorname{Seg}(\Delta^{n})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptscriptstyle\dashv}

Proof.

The left adjoint
(\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}})^{*}
trivially preserves Segal objects,
so it remains to show that
(\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}})_{*}
does so as well.
Let
\mathcal{F}\in\textup{P}(\Delta^{n})
be an
n
-uple Segal space.
Then the value of the presheaf
(\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}})_{*}\mathcal{F}\in\textup{P}(\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n})

on some
E\in\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n}
is the space of maps
\textup{Grid}(E)\to\mathcal{F}

in
\textup{P}(\Delta^{n})
.
Let
U:\textup{Exit}(E)^{\triangleright}\to\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n}
be the atomic covering
diagram of
E
, then by Corollary
4.1.0.6
we have that

\textup{Grid}(U(-))
is a colimit diagram in
\operatorname{Seg}(\Delta^{n})
.
It therefore follows that

(\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}})_{*}\mathcal{F}(U(-))\simeq\textup{P}(\Delta^{n})(\textup{Grid}(U(-)),\mathcal{F})\simeq\operatorname{Seg}(\Delta^{n})(\textup{Grid}(U(-)),\mathcal{F})

is a limit diagram. Hence,
(\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}})_{*}\mathcal{F}
satisfies the Segal condition.
∎

Example 4.1.0.9
.

While the induced functor
\operatorname{Seg}(\Delta^{n})\to\operatorname{Seg}(\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n})
is fully faithful,
it is not essentially surjective.
Let us illustrate this by giving an example of a Segal object
\mathcal{F}\in\operatorname{Seg}(\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{2})
that is not in the essential image.
Suppose that
A
is the atom

Construction 4.1.0.10
.

For an atom
A\in\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n}
we write
\partial A
for the presheaf
on
\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n}
that is the colimit of the representable presheaves

\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n}(-,B)
for all embeddings
B\hookrightarrow A
except for the identity.
When
\mathcal{F}
is a presheaf on
\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n}
, we write
\mathcal{F}(\partial A)

for the space of maps of presheaves
\partial A\to\mathcal{F}
, i.e. the limit of
\mathcal{F}(B)
for all non-trivial embeddings
B\hookrightarrow A
.

We also recall the singular shape construction from §
3.5.5
which assigns
to every mesh atom
{A}
the mesh atom
\square{{A}}:=\cramped{\boxplus}_{\scriptscriptstyle\dot{\textup{M}}}^{n}(\textup{stype}({A}))
together with an active bordism
\square{{A}}\mathrel{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hfil$\mapstochar\mkern 5.0mu$\hfil\cr$\to$\cr}}}{A}
.
Via the equivalence between open meshes and open trusses, the singular shape
construction transfers to truss atoms. We note that for every truss atom
A
,
the singular shape
\square{A}
is within the image of
\cramped{\boxplus}_{\scriptscriptstyle\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n}:\Delta^{n}\hookrightarrow\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n}
.

Definition 4.1.0.11
.

A presheaf
\mathcal{F}\in\textup{P}(\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n})
is
regular

when for every atom
A\in\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n}
the induced diagram of spaces

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{F}(A)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{F}(\square{A})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{F}(\partial A)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{F}(\partial\square{A})}}

is a pullback square. The presheaf
\mathcal{F}
is an

n
-diagrammatic space
when it is regular and satisfies the Segal condition.
We denote by
\operatorname{Seg}^{\textup{r}}(\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n})
the full subcategory of

\textup{P}(\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n})
consisting of the
n
-diagrammatic spaces.

Lemma 4.1.0.12
.

Let
0\leq n\leq\infty
and
A\in\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n}
an atom. Then

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\textup{Grid}(\partial\square{A})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\textup{Grid}(\partial A)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\textup{Grid}(\square{A})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\textup{Grid}(A)}}

is a pushout square in the
\infty
-category
\operatorname{Seg}(\Delta^{n})

of
n
-uple Segal spaces.

Proof.

By Lemma
4.1.0.5

the
n
-uple Segal space
\textup{Grid}(A)
is freely generated
with one generator for each atom embedded in
A
, including the
identity embedding
\textup{id}:A\to A
.
The boundary
\textup{Grid}(\partial A)
is also freely generated
as an
n
-uple Segal space with the same generators except
A
itself.
The pushout adds the missing generator.
∎

Theorem 4.1.0.13
.

The adjunction of
\infty
-categories of space-valued presheaves

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\textup{P}(\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\textup{P}(\Delta^{n})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}})^{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces(\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}})_{*}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptscriptstyle\dashv}

induced by the inclusion functor
\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}}:\Delta^{n}\hookrightarrow\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n}

restricts to an adjoint equivalence

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\operatorname{Seg}^{\textup{r}}(\textup{T}^{n})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\operatorname{Seg}(\Delta^{n})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\scriptscriptstyle\simeq}

between the
\infty
-categories of
n
-diagrammatic spaces and
n
-uple Segal spaces.

Proof.

The restriction functor
(\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}})^{*}
preserves the Segal condition.
For the other direction, suppose that
\mathcal{F}\in\operatorname{Seg}(\Delta^{n})
is an
n
-uple
Segal space. By Proposition
4.1.0.8
we already know
that
(\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}})_{*}\mathcal{F}
also satisfies the Segal condition.
Regularity of
(\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}})_{*}\mathcal{F}
then follows from Lemma
4.1.0.12
.

Therefore, the adjunction
(\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}})^{*}\dashv(\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}})_{*}
restricts to an adjunction

\operatorname{Seg}^{\textup{r}}(\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n})\rightleftarrows\operatorname{Seg}(\Delta^{n})
;
it remains to show that this adjunction is an equivalence.
Because
\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}}
is fully faithful, the counit
(\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}})^{*}(\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}})_{*}\to\textup{id}

is a natural equivalence and therefore
(\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}})^{*}(\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}})_{*}\mathcal{F}\to\mathcal{F}

is an equivalence for each
\mathcal{F}\in\operatorname{Seg}(\Delta^{n})
.
Now let
\mathcal{G}\in\operatorname{Seg}^{\textup{r}}(\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n})
.
We show that for every open
n
-truss
E\in\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n}
the value of
the unit
\mathcal{G}(E)\to(\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}})_{*}(\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}})^{*}\mathcal{G}(E)
is an equivalence,
using induction on the structure of
E
.
The base case of
E=[0]^{n}
is clear.
If
E
is an atom, then we get an induced diagram

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{(\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}})_{*}(\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}})^{*}\mathcal{G}(E)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{(\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}})_{*}(\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}})^{*}\mathcal{G}(\square{E})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{G}(E)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{G}(\square{E})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{(\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}})_{*}\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{*}\mathcal{G}(\partial E)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{(\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}})_{*}(\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}})^{*}\mathcal{G}(\partial\square{E})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{G}(\partial E)}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\mathcal{G}(\partial\square{E})}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\simeq}

The front square is a pullback square because
\mathcal{G}
is regular by assumption,
and the back square is a pullback square because
(\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}})_{*}
sends any
presheaf on
\Delta^{n}
to a regular presheaf on
\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n}
as shown above.
The diagonal maps on the right are equivalences since
\square{E}
is within the
image of
\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}}
.
The diagonal map on the bottom right is an equivalence by induction.
Therefore, it follows that the diagonal map on the top left must be an equivalence.

When
E
is not an atom, then there is a covering diagram

U:\textup{Entr}(E)^{\triangleright}\to\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n}
which covers
E
with atoms.
By induction on the number of atoms in the open truss we have that
\mathcal{G}(U(i))\to(\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}})_{*}(\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}})^{*}\mathcal{G}(U(i))

is an equivalence for each
i\in\textup{Entr}(E)
.
We have that
\mathcal{G}
is Segal by assumption
and
(\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}})_{*}(\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}})^{*}\mathcal{G}
is Segal because both functors preserve
Segal objects, as shown above.
Therefore, it follows that
\mathcal{G}(E)\to(\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}})_{*}(\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}})^{*}\mathcal{G}(E)

must be an equivalence.
This concludes the proof that the unit
\mathcal{G}\to(\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}})_{*}(\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}})^{*}\mathcal{G}

is an equivalence.
∎

4.1.0.14
.

Suppose that
\mathcal{F}
is an
n
-diagrammatic space.
We then say that
\mathcal{F}
is globular when the
n
-uple Segal space
(\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}})^{*}\mathcal{F}

is globular, i.e. an
n
-fold Segal space.
Similarly, we say that
\mathcal{F}
is complete when the
n
-uple Segal space

(\cramped{\boxplus}_{\dot{\textup{T}}})^{*}\mathcal{F}
is complete.
Then the
\infty
-category
\textup{Cat}_{(\infty,n)}
of
(\infty,n)
-categories is the reflective
subcategory of
\operatorname{Seg}^{\textup{r}}(\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n})
consisting of the globular and complete
objects.

4.1.0.15
.

We have so far defined
n
-diagrammatic spaces as presheaves on
\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n}

satisfying the regularity and the sheaf condition.
The sequence of equivalences

\cramped{\dot{\textup{M}}}^{n}\simeq\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n}\simeq\cramped{\bar{\textup{T}}}^{n,\textup{op}}\simeq\cramped{\bar{\textup{M}}}^{n,\textup{op}}

induces a sequence of equivalences between the
\infty
-categories of presheaves

\textup{P}(\cramped{\dot{\textup{M}}}^{n})\simeq\textup{P}(\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n})\simeq\textup{P}(\cramped{\bar{\textup{T}}}^{n,\textup{op}})\simeq\textup{P}(\cramped{\bar{\textup{M}}}^{n,\textup{op}}).

We say that a presheaf in any of these
\infty
-categories is an
n
-diagrammatic
space if it becomes an
n
-diagrammatic space as a presheaf on
\cramped{\dot{\textup{T}}}^{n}

by applying the equivalences.
In particular in §
4.2
, we will construct an
n
-diagrammatic space of manifold diagrams
as a presheaf on
\cramped{\bar{\textup{M}}}^{n,\textup{op}}
, i.e. as a functor
\cramped{\bar{\textup{M}}}^{n}\to\textup{S}
.

4.2
Manifold Diagrams

Open
n
-meshes capture all the shapes that we would expect from an
n
-manifold diagram
calculus and, via diagrammatic spaces, we can probe any
(\infty,n)
-category with
open
n
-meshes. However, the space of automorphisms of any open
n
-mesh is contractible.
This conflicts with our goal of an
n
-dimensional graphical calculus in which the weak interchange
law of higher categories is captured by the space of isotopies.
Below we describe a notion of
n
-manifold diagrams that generalises string diagrams and
surface diagrams and admits enough isotopies.

In §
4.2.1
we characterise the local properties of
n
-manifold
diagrams so that their strata correspond to shapes of cells in
(\infty,n)
-categories.
In particular the strata are manifolds of varying dimension and satisfy a generalisation
of the progressivity condition of string diagrams.
In §
4.2.2
we define
n
-manifold diagrams supported on any closed
n
-mesh
{X}
. When
{X}
is a closed
n
-cube, this specialises to a globular
n
-manifold diagram. Other choices of
{X}
lead to a natural definition of a pasting diagram of
n
-manifold diagrams.
Moving beyond individual diagrams, we define isotopies of
n
-manifold diagrams
in §
4.2.3
. We show how
n
-manifold diagrams on a closed
n
-mesh

{X}
together with their isotopies define a space
\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n}({X})
.
In §
4.2.4
we see that these spaces organise into a functor

\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n}(-):\cramped{\bar{\textup{M}}}^{n}\to\textup{S}
which we show to be an
n
-diagrammatic
space in §
4.2.5
.
Finally, we explore an alternative but equivalent presentation of
n
-manifold diagrams in §
4.2.6

that will be useful when combinatorialising manifold diagrams in §
4.3
.

4.2.1
The Local Geometry of Manifold Diagrams

As the first step towards characterising
n
-manifold diagrams
we study the local conditions that such a diagram should satisfy.
To give justice to the name, every stratum of an
n
-manifold diagram should be a
k
-manifold
for some
k\in[n]
.
We will work with
n
-framed stratified spaces
{M}

that are equipped with a labelling map
\ell({M}):\textup{Exit}({M})\to[n]
.
A priori this map is arbitrary, but once we have placed the appropriate local conditions
on
{M}
the labelling map will indicate the dimension of the strata
of
{M}
.

A
k
-dimensional stratum of an
n
-manifold diagram should correspond to an

(n-k)
-dimensional cell of an
(\infty,n)
-category.
Via our discussion of
n
-diagrammatic spaces in §
4.1
we have identified
atoms as appropriate shapes for such cells.
We therefore require an
n
-manifold diagram to be covered by neighbourhoods

{U}
that each admit a refinement map
r:{A}\to{U}
from
some atom
{A}
.

String diagrams satisfy the progressivity condition which guarantees that
the edges progress upwards, in the direction from the source to the target boundary,
without turning around or having sections that are horizontal.
Equivalently, the height function is injective when restricted to any edge of
the string diagram.
An
n
-manifold diagram should satisfy a generalisation of the progressivity
condition for strata of all dimensions.
We achieve this by placing a condition on the atoms that refine the local
neighbourhoods of the diagram.
Recall from Observation
3.5.5.2
that the singular depth of an atom

{A}\in\cramped{\dot{\textup{M}}}^{n}([n])
is the largest
d\geq 0
such that
there is an atom
{B}\in\cramped{\dot{\textup{M}}}^{n-d}([n])
and an isomorphism

{A}\cong{B}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}

of labelled
n
-framed stratified spaces.

Definition 4.2.1.1
.

An atom
{A}\in\cramped{\dot{\textup{M}}}^{n}([n])
is
progressive
when
its singular depth
\textup{sdepth}({A})
agrees with its label
\ell({A})(\bot_{{A}})
and every proper subatom of
{A}
is progressive.

Definition 4.2.1.2
.

An
n
-framed basic
is an
n
-framed stratified space
{U}

with a conservative labelling
\ell({U}):\textup{Exit}({U})\to[n]

such that there exists a progressive atom
{A}\in\cramped{\dot{\textup{M}}}^{n}([n])

together with a refinement map
r:{A}\to{U}
of labelled

n
-framed stratified spaces.

.

-categories.

.

. Colouring

,

we would render the map

in a string diagram for

like this:

Example 4.2.1.5
.

The following is a framed basic that represents a
3
-dimensional cell
for a (directed) associativity law of a binary operation:

3
2
1

This definition of a framed basic implies that the strata are manifolds
whose dimension agrees with the label in
[n]
. Moreover, each stratum
is progressive in a sense that generalises the progressivity condition of
string diagrams.
Because both of these properties are local conditions, they are then
automatically satisfied by any
n
-manifold diagram that is covered with framed basics.

Observation 4.2.1.6
.

Let
{U}
be an
n
-framed basic and
i\in\cramped{\mathbb{P}}({{U}})
a stratum
labelled with
k\in[n]
.
Then the projection
\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{k}
to the last
k
dimensions
restricts to an open immersion
{U}_{i}\to\mathbb{R}^{k}
.
In particular
{U}_{i}
is a topological
k
-manifold.

Example 4.2.1.7
.

There are framed basics that do not interact well with projection.
Consider for example the following
3
-framed basic in which the

1
-strata are arranged to lie within the same
(3,1)
-plane:

3
2
1

Taking the projection to the last two coordinate directions
produces a diagram in which the orange
1
-stratum completely obscures the blue one:

In the string diagram calculus for braided monoidal categories, such arrangements
are prohibited in order to avoid confusion.
Similarly, we want to avoid framed basics like this from appearing within
manifold diagrams.

We restrict manifold diagrams to only contain framed basics whose framed stratified isomorphism type is stable under small perturbations.
This is not the case for Example
4.2.1.7
since the two overlapping
1
-strata may be slightly nudged so that they can be distinguished in the projection.

Definition 4.2.1.8
.

A
perturbation
of an
n
-framed stratified space

{M}
is an
n
-framed stratified bundle

f:{E}\to{|\Delta[1]|}
that satisfies the following conditions:

1.

{M}
is the fibre of
f
over
0\in{|\Delta[1]|}
.

2.

f
is a stratified trivial bundle after forgetting the framing.

3.

f
is an
n
-framed stratified submersion.

A compact
n
-framed stratified space
{M}
is
stable

when for every perturbation
f:{E}\to{|\Delta[1]|}
of

{M}
there exists an
\varepsilon>0
such that
f
restricts to
an
n
-framed stratified trivial bundle over the subinterval

{[0,\varepsilon)}\subset{|\Delta[1]|}
:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{{M}\times{[0,\varepsilon)}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{{E}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{{[0,\varepsilon)}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{{|\Delta[1]|}}}
{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}

An
n
-framed stratified space
{M}
is
stable
if
every compact subspace
{K}\subseteq{M}
is stable.

4.2.2
The Global Geometry of Manifold Diagrams

We have characterised the local properties that an
n
-framed stratified
space
{M}
should satisfy in order to be an
n
-manifold diagram.
We now turn to the global conditions.
An
n
-manifold diagram contains information that is not directly detected by just the stratification, but by the relative arrangement of the strata in the ambient space.
This arrangement determines which coherence structure of an
(\infty,n)
-category
\mathcal{C}

should be used when interpreting the diagram in
\mathcal{C}
.
To keep this information finite, we require an
n
-manifold diagram to be essentially tame
as a
n
-framed stratified space according to Definition
3.1.0.14
.

Remark 4.2.2.1
.

Framed basics are refined by atoms and are therefore always essentially tame.
Therefore, when an
n
-framed stratified space
{M}
is covered by framed basics,
every point in
{M}
has an open neighbourhood that is essentially tame.
However, this is not sufficient for
{M}
to be essentially tame itself.
For instance the
3
-framed stratification containing two
1
-strata
given by the subsets

\{(-1,0,t)\mid t\in\mathbb{R}\},\{(1,t\sin(t^{-1}),t)\mid t\in\mathbb{R}\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{3}

is covered by framed basics but is not essentially tame because the two
1
-strata
cross over each other an infinite number of times.
Such a diagram would be impossible to interpret in an arbitrary

(\infty,3)
-category without assuming additional structure.

String diagrams are often defined as stratifications of a closed
2
-cube
{[0,1]}^{2}
.
The surface diagrams for Gray categories of
[
BMS18
]
similarly
are defined as stratifications of the closed
3
-cube
{[0,1]}^{3}
.
A natural continuation would be to define
n
-manifold diagrams as stratifications
of the closed
n
-cube
{[0,1]}^{n}
.
That choice, however, would prevent us from defining a semi-strict composition
operation on
n
-manifold diagrams and therefore nullify one of their major
technical advantages.

Manifold diagrams are composed by juxtaposition or, in other words, by placing diagrams
next to each other along shared boundaries.
The composition of two
1
-manifold diagrams on
{[0,1]}
should be a
1
-manifold diagram on the longer interval
{[0,2]}
.
This appears insubstantial at first, since
{[0,1]}
and
{[0,2]}
are
isomorphic, but there is no way in which we can rescale the composite diagram to fit into
the unit interval

{[0,1]}
and simultaneously retain associativity of the composition.
Similarly, strict unitality of diagram composition can only be achieved when we allow diagrams that have a length of zero in the direction of composition.

We therefore do not pick any particular subspace of
\mathbb{R}^{n}
on which to define

n
-manifold diagrams but allow their underlying space to vary.
In particular, we have a concept of
n
-manifold diagrams supported on any
closed
n
-mesh
{X}
.
Notably this includes the closed subspaces

{[a_{1},b_{1}]}\times\cdots\times{[a_{n},b_{n}]}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}

for all choices of
a_{i}\leq b_{i}
, enabling semistrict composition.
Other choices of closed
n
-meshes will turn out to be meaningful as well.

For technical convenience we let an
n
-manifold diagram
{M}

that is supported on a closed
n
-mesh
{X}
overshoot the boundary
of
{X}
so that the underlying unstratified space
\operatorname{U}({M})
is an open subspace of
\mathbb{R}^{n}
that contains

\operatorname{U}({X})
.
With that convention every point of an
n
-manifold diagram can have an open
neighbourhood that is a framed basic.
We identify two
n
-manifold diagrams on
{X}
when they agree on
their intersection with
{X}
.

The globularity condition of a
2
-dimensional string diagram controls the interaction of
the diagram’s strata with the boundary. In particular, it ensures that the
vertices of the diagram must lie within the interior and the edges may only
intersect the top and bottom boundaries.
For a
3
-dimensional string diagram, the globularity condition also guarantees
that all braids must occur within the diagram’s interior.
For an
n
-manifold diagram
{M}
on a closed
n
-mesh
{X}
we ensure globularity
by requiring that
{M}
is orthogonal to
{X}
in the sense of
§
3.6.5
.

Definition 4.2.2.2
.

An
n
-manifold diagram
is an essentially tame
n
-framed stratified space

{M}
with labels in
[n]
that is covered with stable framed basics.
When
{X}
is a closed
n
-mesh, an
n
-manifold diagram on
{X}

is an
n
-manifold diagram
{M}
that is orthogonal to
{X}
.
When
{M}_{0}
,
{M}_{1}
are two
n
-manifold diagrams on
{X}

we write
{M}_{0}\sim_{X}{M}_{1}
whenever

\ell({M}_{0})(x)=\ell({M}_{1})(x)

for all
x\in\operatorname{U}({X})
.
We denote the equivalence classes for this relation by
[-]_{{X}}
.

Observation 4.2.2.3
.

For the closed
n
-mesh
\mathbb{I}^{n}
we can characterise the orthogonality
condition in a more direct way.
Suppose that
{M}
is a stratified space such that

{[-1,1]}^{n}\subseteq\operatorname{U}({M})\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}
.
Then
{M}
is orthogonal to
\mathbb{I}^{n}
exactly if there
is an
\varepsilon>0

such that for every
x\in{M}
with
\|x\|_{\infty}\in{(1-\varepsilon,1+\varepsilon)}

the stratification of
{M}
satisfies

\cramped{\mathbb{s}}({{M}})(x)=\cramped{\mathbb{s}}({{M}})(\|x\|_{\infty}^{-1}x)
.

2

\mathbb{I}^{2}

[
BDSV15

When the closed
2

{X}

2

4.2.3
Isotopies of Manifold Diagrams

The interpretation of a string diagram in a monoidal category is invariant under isotopy: however we might deform a string diagram, it represents the same morphism.
This is the content of the coherence theorems of
[
JS91
]
and is implicitly relied on wherever string diagrams are used.
Isotopy invariance becomes algebraically significant for string diagrams in
\mathbb{R}^{3}
and
\mathbb{R}^{4}
for braided and symmetric monoidal categories,
in which the braiding operation together with the coherence axioms are encoded into geometric arrangements.
In higher dimensions, the isotopies of
n
-manifold diagrams should capture all the coherence information that is part of having a weak interchange law.

Isotopies of braided and symmetric monoidal categories are more restricted than general isotopies of the diagrams interpreted as stratified spaces.
The order of edges entering a vertex matters,
but a stratified isotopy can permute these edges freely.
If this was valid in any symmetric monoidal category, every monoid would have to be automatically commutative.
For braided and symmetric monoidal categories the solution is relatively straightforward:
We require an isotopy to preserve the order of edges as seen in a projection.

Example 4.2.3.1
.

Trimble’s notes on surface diagrams
[
Tri10
]
described an example of a deformation of surface diagrams that should be excluded from the valid deformations.

Starting with two braided
1
-strata that end in a
0
-stratum,
we continuously push the height at which the braiding occurs upwards.
In the limit we reach the diagram in which the two
1
-strata are not braided
any longer.
The notes do not mention how to avoid this situation in general, but do hint at a solution involving coincidences where two strata agree in some coordinates.

Manifold diagrams can have strata of any dimension and arrangements that are more complicated than just their order.
Requiring isotopies of manifold diagrams to preserve the framing would prevent this problem but would also be too strict, as it would prohibit even braids.
Instead, we demand that an isotopy preserves the framing locally by being
a framed stratified submersion.

Definition 4.2.3.2
.

An
n
-manifold diagram bundle
is an essentially tame
n
-framed stratified submersion

p:{E}\to B
with labels in
[n]
where
B
is an unstratified space and every fibre of
p
is an
n
-manifold diagram.
An
isotopy of
n
-manifold diagrams
is an
n
-manifold diagram bundle
over the interval
{|\Delta[1]|}
.

By combining the requirements that each fibre must be an
n
-manifold diagram
and that the bundle is a framed stratified submersion, we have the following
more direct characterisation of
n
-manifold diagram bundles after unpacking the definitions.

Observation 4.2.3.3
.

Suppose that
p:{E}\to B
is an essentially tame
n
-framed stratified bundle
with labels in
[n]

such that
B
is an unstratified space.
Then
p
is an
n
-manifold diagram bundle if and only if for every point

x\in{E}
there exists a framed basic
{U}
, an open
neighbourhood
V\subseteq B
of
f(x)
and an open embedding of
labelled
n
-framed stratified spaces

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{{U}\times{V}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{{E}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{V}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{B}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces I}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces p}

such that
I(\bot_{{U}},f(x))=x
.

Definition 4.2.3.4
.

Let
{X}
be a closed
n
-mesh.
An
n
-manifold diagram bundle on
{X}
is an
n
-manifold
diagram bundle
p:{E}\to B
that is fibrewise orthogonal to
{X}
.
When
p_{0}:{E}_{0}\to B
and
p_{1}:{E}_{1}\to B
are two

n
-manifold diagram bundles on
{X}
we write
p_{0}\sim_{X}p_{1}
whenever

\ell({E}_{0})(x,b)=\ell({E}_{1})(x,b)

for all
x\in\operatorname{U}({X})
and
b\in B
.
We write
[-]_{{X}}
for the equivalence classes.

Definition 4.2.3.5
.

Let
{X}
be a closed
n
-mesh.
The
space of
n
-manifold diagrams on
{X}

is the simplicial set
\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n}({X})
whose
k
-simplices
consist of an equivalence class
[p]_{{X}}
of an
n
-manifold
diagram bundle
p:{E}\to{|\Delta[k]|}
on
{X}
.

Lemma 4.2.3.6
.

Let
{X}
be a closed
n
-mesh.
Then
\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n}({X})
is a Kan complex.

Proof.

Suppose we have a lifting problem

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Lambda^{i}[k]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Delta[k]}}

By unpacking the definitions and picking a representative,
we have an
\varepsilon>0
and an
n
-manifold diagram
bundle
f_{0}:{E}_{0}\to{|\Lambda^{i}[k]|}
that is fibrewise
\varepsilon
-orthogonal to

{X}
and defined on

\operatorname{U}({E}_{0})=\{(e,b)\mid\exists x\in{X}.\ \|e-x\|_{\infty}<\varepsilon\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}\times{|\Lambda^{i}[k]|}.

We then pick any piecewise linear retraction
R:{|\Delta[k]|}\to{|\Lambda^{i}[k]|}

and let
f_{1}:{E}_{1}\to{|\Delta[k]|}
be the pullback of
f_{0}
along

R
.
Then
f_{1}
represents a solution to the lifting problem.
∎

Example 4.2.3.7
.

Paths in the space
\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{2}(\mathbb{I}^{2})
are isotopies of string diagrams:

For any
m\geq 0
the space
\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{2}(\mathbb{I}^{2})
contains as
a connected component the unordered configuration space of
m
points in the plane.

Definition 4.2.3.8
.

Let
{X}
be a closed
n
-mesh and
\varepsilon>0
.
We let
\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n,\varepsilon}({X})
be the simplicial set
whose
k
-simplices consist of an
n
-manifold diagram bundle

p:{E}\to{|\Delta[k]|}

that is fibrewise
\varepsilon
-orthogonal to
{X}
and defined on the open subset

\operatorname{U}({E})=\{(e,b)\mid\exists x\in{X}.\ \|e-x\|_{\infty}<\varepsilon\}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}\times{|\Delta[k]|}.

Whenever
\varepsilon_{0}>\varepsilon_{1}>0
we have an induced monomorphism of simplicial sets

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n,\varepsilon_{0}}({X})}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n,\varepsilon_{1}}({X}).}

Observation 4.2.3.9
.

For every closed
n
-mesh
{X}
the simplicial set

\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n}({X})

is the filtered colimit of

\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n,\varepsilon}({X})

for all
\varepsilon>0
.
In particular for every
\varepsilon>0
there is a map

\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n,\varepsilon}({X})\to\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n}({X})

which sends an
n
-manifold diagram bundle
p
to its equivalence class

[p]_{{X}}
.
Moreover, for any sufficiently small
\varepsilon>0
the map

\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n,\varepsilon}({X})\to\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n}({X})

is the inclusion of a deformation retract.

4.2.4
Functoriality in the Closed Mesh

For any equivalence of closed
n
-meshes
{X}\simeq{Y}

we obtain an equivalence between the spaces of
n
-manifold diagrams

\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n}({X})\simeq\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n}({Y})
.
More generally, the assignment of
\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n}({X})
to any closed
n
-mesh
{X}

extends to a functor
\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n}(-):\cramped{\bar{\textup{M}}}^{n}\to\textup{S}
.
We construct this functor as a left fibration of simplicial sets.

Definition 4.2.4.1
.

Suppose that
\xi:{X}\to{B}
is a closed
n
-mesh bundle.
Let
p_{0}:{E}_{0}\to\operatorname{U}({B})
and

p_{1}:{E}_{1}\to\operatorname{U}({B})
are
n
-manifold diagram bundles
that are orthogonal to
\xi
.
We write
p_{0}\sim_{\xi}p_{1}
whenever

\ell({E}_{0})(x,b)=\ell({E}_{1})(x,b)

for all
(x,b)\in\operatorname{U}({X})
.
We denote the equivalence classes by
[-]_{\xi}
.

Definition 4.2.4.2
.

We let
\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n}
denote the simplicial set whose
k
-simplices consist of
a pair
(\xi,[p]_{\xi})
where

\xi:{X}\to\|\Delta[k]\|
is a closed
n
-mesh bundle and

p:{E}\to{|\Delta[k]|}
an
n
-manifold diagram bundle orthogonal to
\xi
.
There is a canonical projection map
\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n}\to\cramped{\bar{\textup{M}}}^{n}
which sends
the pair
(\xi,[p]_{\xi})
to the closed
n
-mesh bundle
\xi
.

Proposition 4.2.4.3
.

The projection map
\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n}\to\cramped{\bar{\textup{M}}}^{n}
is a left fibration.

Proof.

Suppose we have a lifting problem

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Lambda^{i}[k]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Delta[k]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\cramped{\bar{\textup{M}}}^{n}}}

for some
0\leq i<k
.
After unpacking the definitions,
we have an
n
-manifold diagram bundle
f^{\prime}:{M}^{\prime}\to{|\Lambda^{i}[k]|}

and a closed
n
-mesh bundle
\xi:{X}\to\|\Delta[k]\|
such that

f^{\prime}
is orthogonal to the restriction of
\xi
over
\|\Lambda^{i}[k]\|
.
We pick a retraction
R:{|\Delta[k]|}\to{|\Lambda^{i}[k]|}
of the inclusion

{|\Lambda^{i}[k]|}\hookrightarrow{|\Delta[k]|}
and let
f^{\prime\prime}
be the pullback
of
f^{\prime}
along
R
:

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{{M}^{\prime\prime}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{{M}^{\prime}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{{|\Delta[k]|}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{{|\Lambda^{i}[k]|}}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{\prime\prime}}
{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces f^{\prime}}

The
n
-manifold diagram bundle
f^{\prime\prime}
will in general not be orthogonal to
\xi
.
However, there exists an open neighbourhood
{U}
of
\|\Lambda^{i}[k]\|

in
\|\Delta[k]\|
such that
f^{\prime\prime}
and
\xi
are orthogonal over
{U}
.
We can then use the trivialisation of
\xi
over the
k
th stratum of

\|\Delta[k]\|
to modify
f^{\prime\prime}
into an
n
-manifold diagram bundle

f:{M}\to{|\Delta[k]|}
such that
f\perp\xi
.
Then
(\xi,[f]_{\xi})
is a solution to the lifting problem.
∎

Observation 4.2.4.4
.

As a left fibration, the map

\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n}\to\cramped{\bar{\textup{M}}}^{n}

induces a functor

\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n}(-):\cramped{\bar{\textup{M}}}^{n}\to\textup{S}

and therefore a space
\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n}({X})
for any closed
n
-mesh
{X}
.
The space
\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n}({X})
can be computed explicitly as a Kan complex by taking the
pullback of simplicial sets

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n}({X})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Delta[0]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\cramped{\bar{\textup{M}}}^{n}}}
{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\lrcorner}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{X}}

We therefore see that the space
\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n}({X})
is modelled by the Kan
complex of
n
-manifold diagrams supported on
{X}
which we defined earlier in
Definition
4.2.3.5
.

.

The image of
e
is the lower left corner in
{Y}
.
The functor
\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{2}({Y})\to\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{2}({X})
,
induced by the inert map
{Y}\mathrel{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hfil$\mapstochar\mkern 5.0mu$\hfil\cr$\to$\cr}}}{X}
associated to
e
,
restricts a string diagram on
{Y}
to its subdiagram on
{X}
.

4.2.5
The Diagrammatic Space of Manifold Diagrams

So far we have constructed a functor
\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n}(-):\cramped{\bar{\textup{M}}}^{n}\to\textup{S}

which sends a closed
n
-mesh
{X}
to the space
\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n}({X})
of
n
-manifold diagrams on
{X}
.
Via functoriality in
{X}
we have seen how to restrict and compose manifold diagrams.
In this section we prove the following result.

Theorem 4.2.5.1
.

The functor
\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n}(-):\cramped{\bar{\textup{M}}}^{n}\to\textup{S}
is an
n
-diagrammatic space.

Proof.

The functor satisfies the Segal condition by
Lemma
4.2.5.9

and the regularity condition by Lemma
4.2.5.10
,
which we state and prove below.
∎

Corollary 4.2.5.2
.

The functor
\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n}(-)
restricts to an
n
-uple Segal space

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Delta^{n,\textup{op}}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\cramped{\bar{\textup{M}}}^{n}}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\textup{S}.}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cramped{\boxplus}_{\scriptscriptstyle\bar{\textup{M}}}^{n}}
\scriptstyle{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n}(-)}

The Segal condition of an
n
-diagrammatic space requires us to demonstrate that for any closed
n
-mesh
{X}
, the space

\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n}({X})
of
n
-manifold diagrams on
{X}
is the homotopy limit of the spaces of
n
-manifold
diagrams on every cell of
{X}
individually.
This guarantees that by gluing together manifold diagrams along common boundaries,
we have a composition operation that interacts well with isotopies of diagrams.
For any
n
-cell
{X}
we write
\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n}(\partial{X})
for
the limit of the simplicial sets
\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n}({C})
for each cell

{C}\hookrightarrow{X}
, except for
{X}

itself.
To help with calculating the homotopy limit as an ordinary limit of simplicial sets, we show then show that the restriction to the boundary

\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n}({X})\to\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n}(\partial{X})

is a Kan fibration.
We gradually build up to this result, starting with the
n
-cube
{X}=\mathbb{I}^{n}
for which we can
write down the stratifications of lifts directly.
The regularity condition for
\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n}(-)
follows from intermediate results.

Lemma 4.2.5.3
.

The map
\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n}(\mathbb{I}^{n})\to\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n}(\partial\mathbb{I}^{n})
is a Kan fibration.

Proof.

Suppose that we have a lifting problem

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Lambda^{i}[k]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n}(\mathbb{I}^{n})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Delta[k]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n}(\partial\mathbb{I}^{n})}}

Unpacking the given data and picking representatives,
we have an
\varepsilon>0
and an
n
-manifold diagram bundle

f_{0}:{E}_{0}\to{|\Delta[k]|}
that is fibrewise orthogonal to

\mathbb{I}^{n}
and defined on

\displaystyle\operatorname{U}({E}_{0})=

\displaystyle\ \{(e,b)\mid 1-\varepsilon<\|e\|_{\infty}<1+\varepsilon\}

\displaystyle\cup

\displaystyle\ \{(e,b)\mid\|e\|_{\infty}<1+\varepsilon\land b\in{|\Lambda^{i}[k]|}\}.

We define
\tau:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to{[0,1]}
be the piecewise linear function:

\displaystyle\tau(e)

\displaystyle:=0

(when
\|e\|_{\infty}<1-2\varepsilon
)

\displaystyle\tau(e)

\displaystyle:=\tfrac{1}{\varepsilon}(\|e\|_{\infty}-(1-2\varepsilon))

(when
1-2\varepsilon\leq\|e\|_{\infty}\leq 1-\varepsilon
)

\displaystyle\tau(e)

\displaystyle:=1

(when
1-\varepsilon<\|e\|_{\infty}
)

Let
R:{|\Delta[k]|}\to{|\Lambda^{i}[k]|}
be a piecewise linear retraction of the inclusion
{|\Lambda^{i}[k]|}\hookrightarrow{|\Delta[k]|}
.
We then define a retraction

P:{[-1-\varepsilon,1+\varepsilon]}^{n}\times{|\Delta[k]|}\to\operatorname{U}({E}_{0})

as follows:

P(e,b):=(e,\tau(e)b+(1-\tau(e))R(b))

We let
{E}_{1}
be the stratification of
{[-1-\varepsilon,1+\varepsilon]}^{n}\times{|\Delta[k]|}

defined by
\cramped{\mathbb{s}}({{E}_{1}})=\cramped{\mathbb{s}}({{E}_{0}})\circ P

and let
f_{1}:{E}_{1}\to{|\Delta[k]|}
be the projection.
Then
f_{1}
is an
n
-manifold diagram bundle which extends
f_{0}
and
is orthogonal to
\mathbb{I}^{n}
.
Therefore, the equivalence class
[f_{1}]_{\mathbb{I}^{n}}
is a solution to the lifting problem.
∎

Lemma 4.2.5.4
.

Let
s_{1},\ldots,s_{n}\in[1]
and let

{X}:=\{(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})\mid\forall 1\leq i\leq n.\ s_{i}=0\Rightarrow x_{i}=0\}\subseteq\mathbb{I}^{n}

be the
n
-framed stratified subspace.
Then
\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n}({X})\to\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n}(\partial{X})

is a Kan fibration.

Proof.

Suppose that we have a lifting problem

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Lambda^{i}[k]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n}({X})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Delta[k]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n}(\partial{X})}}

Unpacking the definitions, we have some
0<\varepsilon<1
and an
n
-manifold diagram bundle

f_{0}:{E}_{0}\to{|\Delta[k]|}
that is
\varepsilon
-orthogonal to
{X}
and defined on the subspace

\displaystyle\operatorname{U}({E}_{0})=

\displaystyle\ \{(e_{1},\ldots,e_{n},b)\mid\forall 1\leq i\leq n.\ s_{i}-\varepsilon<|e_{i}|<s_{i}+\varepsilon\}

\displaystyle\cup

\displaystyle\ \{(e_{1},\ldots,e_{n},b)\mid\forall 1\leq i\leq n.\ |e_{i}|<s_{i}+\varepsilon\land b\in{|\Lambda^{i}[k]|}\}.

We let
{D}_{0}
be a stratification with underlying space

\displaystyle\operatorname{U}({D}_{0})=

\displaystyle\ \{(e,b)\mid 1-\varepsilon<\|e\|_{\infty}<1+\varepsilon\}

\displaystyle\cup

\displaystyle\ \{(e,b)\mid\|e\|_{\infty}<1+\varepsilon\land b\in{|\Lambda^{i}[k]|}\}.

The stratifying map of
{D}_{0}
is derived from
{E}_{0}
by stretching

{E}_{0}
into the coordinate directions where
s_{i}=0
so that the result
is defined around the
n
-cube:

\cramped{\mathbb{s}}({{D}_{0}})(e_{1},\ldots,e_{n},b)=\cramped{\mathbb{s}}({{E}_{0}})(s_{1}e_{1},\ldots,s_{n}e_{n},b).

Then the projection
g_{0}:{D}_{0}\to{|\Delta[k]|}
is an

n
-manifold diagram bundle
and fibrewise orthogonal to
\mathbb{I}^{n}
.
It classifies a lifting problem

{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Lambda^{i}[k]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n}(\mathbb{I}^{n})}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\Delta[k]}}
{\lx@inpgf@ignorespaces{\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n}(\partial\mathbb{I}^{n})}}

which has a solution by Lemma
4.2.5.3
.
Such a solution is given by an
n
-manifold diagram bundle

g_{1}:{D}_{1}\to{|\Delta[k]|}
that is orthogonal to
\mathbb{I}^{n}

and extends
g_{0}
.

We then let
{E}_{1}
be the extension of
{E}_{0}
so that

\operatorname{U}({E}_{1})=\{(e_{1},\ldots,e_{n},b)\mid\forall 1\leq i\leq n.\ |e_{i}|<s_{i}+\varepsilon\}

and the stratification is defined by

\cramped{\mathbb{s}}({{E}_{1}})(e_{1},\ldots,e_{n},b)=\cramped{\mathbb{s}}({{D}_{1}})(s_{1}e_{1}+(1-s_{1}),\ldots,s_{n}e_{n}+(1-s_{n}),b).

The term
1-s_{i}
in each coordinate ensures that when
s_{i}=0
,
we sample the stratification of
{D}_{1}
along the boundary where
it is required to be orthogonal to
\mathbb{I}^{n}
.
The projection
f_{1}:{E}_{1}\to{|\Delta[k]|}
then is an

n
-manifold diagram bundle
that is orthogonal to
{X}
and extends
f_{0}
.
Therefore,
[f_{1}]_{{X}}
is a solution to the lifting problem.
∎

Lemma 4.2.5.5
.

Let
{X}
be an
n
-cell. Then
\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n}(\square{{X}})\to\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n}(\partial\square{{X}})
is a Kan fibration.

Proof.

This follows directly from Lemma
4.2.5.4
since
\square{{X}}
is of the required shape.
∎

We wish to use the result of Lemma
4.2.5.5
to imply that also

\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n}({X})\to\cramped{\mathbb{D}}^{n}(\partial{X})
is a Kan fibration.
For that we recall the bordism of closed
n
-meshes
{X}\mathrel{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hfil$\mapstochar\mkern 5.0mu$\hfil\cr$\to$\cr}}}\square{{X}}

from Construction
3.5.5.7
. For any
t\in\|\Delta[1]\|
we denote by
\square_{t}{{X}}

the fibre of the active bordism
{X}\mathrel{\vtop{\halign{#\cr\hfil$\mapstochar\mkern 5.0mu$\hfil\cr$\to$\cr}}}\square{{X}}
over
t
.
